resources.title: There's a new kind of coding I call 'vibe coding' (X post)
resources.summary: The 2 February 2025 post that coined 'vibe coding': you give in to the vibes, accept AI-generated changes without reading the diffs, and let the model, Cursor Composer in his case, write the code.
resources.wiki_use: Opening reading for the AI module; students compare Karpathy's throwaway-project framing with the standard required for analysis code they will submit.
resources.notes: URL cited in the Wikipedia 'Vibe coding' article and in Simon Willison's March 2025 post, which also quotes the text in full. x.com may require login to view, so link Willison's post as a backup.

resources.title: Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again)
resources.summary: Keynote from 17 June 2025 framing LLMs as a new kind of computer programmed in English ('Software 3.0'). It covers LLM 'psychology', partial-autonomy apps with an autonomy slider, vibe coding, and building software that agents can use.
resources.wiki_use: Embed as the module's anchor video; assign the vibe coding and 'autonomy slider' segments before the first in-class AI coding lab.
resources.notes: Posted 18 June 2025. Free transcripts exist elsewhere if students prefer reading.

resources.title: 'Vibe coding' named Collins Dictionary's Word of the Year
resources.summary: News story from 6 November 2025 on Collins naming 'vibe coding' its 2025 Word of the Year, defined as 'the use of artificial intelligence prompted by natural language to assist with the writing of computer code.'
resources.wiki_use: One-line hook or sidebar on the wiki's AI landing page, showing how fast the term entered everyday language.
resources.notes: Collins's own word-of-the-year page and the BBC story would not load from this environment, so this is CNN's syndicated copy. Merriam-Webster also lists the term as slang or trending (https://www.merriam-webster.com/slang/vibe-coding): 'writing computer code in a somewhat careless fashion, with AI assistance.'

resources.title: Vibe coding
resources.summary: Running encyclopedia entry covering the term's origin, uptake in industry, and criticism on security, maintainability and open-source impact. It cites METR, Veracode, CodeRabbit, the Replit incident, the 2026 rsync dispute and the 'Vibe Coding Kills Open Source' paper.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor-only background and a source of incident links; students can use it to find primary sources but should cite those sources instead.

resources.subtopic: Vibe coding vs. responsible AI-assisted coding
resources.title: Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding (but vibe coding rocks)
resources.summary: Argues that vibe coding means not reviewing the code. If you review, test and can explain the AI's code, that is ordinary software development. He also praises vibe coding for prototypes and for learning what models can do.
resources.wiki_use: Required reading paired with Karpathy's post; it supplies the course rule that anything submitted must be code you can explain.

resources.title: Here's how I use LLMs to help me write code
resources.summary: Practical advice: treat LLMs as overconfident pair programmers; account for training cut-offs and prefer well-known libraries; manage context; ask for options before committing; be specific; 'test everything' (if you haven't seen it run, it isn't working); vibe-code to learn but not for production.
resources.wiki_use: First-week reading that sets norms for the course: AI writes the draft, the student verifies.

resources.title: Vibe engineering
resources.summary: Coins 'vibe engineering' (7 October 2025) for experienced engineers who use coding agents while staying accountable for quality. It lists the practices agents reward: automated tests, planning, documentation, version control, code review, manual QA and preview environments.
resources.wiki_use: Basis for the course's 'vibe engineering' standards: map each practice to a requirement in the team project, such as tests, a README, Git history and peer review.

resources.title: Agentic Engineering Patterns (guide)
resources.summary: A growing guide to working with coding agents. Chapters cover principles ('Writing code is cheap now'), how agents work, Git with agents, subagents, red/green TDD, 'First run the tests', agentic manual testing, linear walkthroughs and interactive explanations, with annotated prompts.
resources.wiki_use: Link chapters from the wiki as just-in-time references, for example red/green TDD before the regression lab and linear walkthroughs whenever students must explain AI-written code.
resources.notes: Page last updated around 15 March 2026. Willison defines an agent as software that runs tools in a loop toward a goal, and reserves 'vibe coding' for unreviewed prototype code.

resources.title: Vibe coding and agentic engineering are getting closer than I'd like
resources.summary: In May 2026 Willison admits he now trusts agents enough to skip reviewing some production code. He worries the line he drew in 2025 is blurring, and notes that a polished repository no longer signals careful work.
resources.wiki_use: Discussion prompt: if experts are reviewing less, what evidence should a student team give that its analysis code is correct?

resources.title: The 70% problem: Hard truths about AI-assisted coding
resources.summary: Argues that AI tools quickly get non-experts about 70% of the way, but the last 30% (edge cases, debugging, maintainability) needs engineering knowledge. Juniors and seniors get very different value as a result.
resources.wiki_use: Assigned reading framing why the course still teaches the analysis underneath; pair with Prather et al. (2024) on novices.
resources.notes: The URL came from a linking page (ipspace.net, December 2024); the Substack page itself wasn't fetched. Published December 2024. Summary based on the title and secondary coverage, so skim before assigning.

resources.title: Beyond Vibe Coding: From Coder to AI-Era Developer
resources.summary: O'Reilly book (August 2025) contrasting prompt-first vibe coding with structured, AI-assisted engineering. It covers refining and debugging generated code, the risks of accepting output uncritically, and multi-agent workflows.
resources.wiki_use: Optional deeper reading; assign single chapters through O'Reilly Learning if the UIUC Library subscription covers it.
resources.notes: Check UIUC Library's O'Reilly Learning access; otherwise paid.

resources.title: Vibe Coding: Building Production-Grade Software With GenAI, Chat, Agents, and Beyond
resources.summary: Practitioner book (21 October 2025, foreword by Dario Amodei) on using chat and agentic AI for everything from small tools to enterprise systems while keeping engineering discipline.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background and a source of war stories for the AI module; too long to assign in full.
resources.notes: ISBN 9781966280026 (paperback). IT Revolution's article about the book: https://itrevolution.com/articles/vibe-coding-the-revolutionary-approach-transforming-software-development/

resources.title: Vibe coding: programming through conversation with artificial intelligence
resources.venue: Proceedings of PPIG 2025 (Psychology of Programming Interest Group)
resources.summary: Microsoft Research study of more than 8 hours of think-aloud vibe coding sessions. Vibe coding turns out to be iterative cycles of prompting, evaluating and hand-editing, and it shifts expertise toward managing context and judging output rather than removing the need for expertise.
resources.wiki_use: Academic anchor for the claim that vibe coding still requires expertise; good for a short discussion post.

resources.title: Exploring Generative AI (memo series)
resources.authors: Böckeler, B. (main author); Morris, K.; Vaccari, M.; Doernenburg, E.; et al.
resources.summary: About 33 memos, from 2023 to October 2026, by Thoughtworks engineers on coding assistants and agents: multi-file editing, autonomous agents, supply-chain risk, spec-driven development, context engineering, harness engineering, TDD inside the agent loop.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor-only map of the practitioner literature; pick individual memos (below) as readings.

resources.title: To vibe or not to vibe
resources.summary: Whether AI code needs review depends on three things: how likely the AI is to be wrong, how bad an error would be, and how easily you would notice it. Low-risk, high-detectability work can be vibe-coded; high-impact, low-detectability work needs close scrutiny.
resources.wiki_use: Turn the three factors into a one-page rubric students apply to each analysis step. A typo in a chart label is low risk; a silent join error in CLV data is high impact and hard to detect.
resources.notes: Published 23 September 2025.

resources.title: Understanding Spec-Driven-Development: Kiro, spec-kit, and Tessl
resources.summary: Compares three spec-driven development tools (Kiro, GitHub spec-kit, Tessl) and proposes three levels: spec-first, spec-anchored and spec-as-source. Also raises concerns about verbosity, review burden and echoes of model-driven development.
resources.wiki_use: Background for a 'write the analysis plan before prompting' assignment, where students draft a short spec (question, data, method, outputs) that the agent must follow.
resources.notes: Published 15 October 2025.

resources.title: Context Engineering for Coding Agents
resources.summary: Explains how to curate what a coding agent sees: CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md guidance files loaded every session, path-scoped rules, and skills that load instructions or scripts on demand.
resources.wiki_use: Reference for a lab where each team writes a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md describing its dataset, variable definitions and coding conventions.
resources.notes: Published 5 February 2026.

resources.title: Speaking things into existence: Expertise in a vibe-filled world of work
resources.summary: A business-school professor vibe codes a 3D game with Claude Code, builds an interactive course, and runs a research analysis on old crowdfunding data. He argues vibe coding redistributes expertise rather than eliminating it: you still need to know what you want and judge what you get.
resources.wiki_use: Accessible reading for non-CS business students; the crowdfunding-data example works as a model for an AI-assisted marketing analysis.
resources.notes: Published 11 March 2025.

resources.title: Vibe Coding: Practice, Performance, Productivity, and Risk - A State-of-the-Art Review
resources.authors: Michels, D. L.; Abu Ghazaleh, M.; Lazzari, F.; Kassem, N.; Klein, J.
resources.summary: Cross-disciplinary review from August 2026 (software engineering, HCI, labor economics, security, education). It reconciles conflicting productivity results by measurement method, scope and horizon, and conjectures that gains are real for new code but shrink or reverse on mature codebases.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background for an evidence lecture; its 'new code vs. mature codebase' conjecture is a good discussion question.
resources.notes: Recent preprint, not peer reviewed. Its HTML version didn't expose the reference list in this pass.

resources.title: Vibe Coding Kills Open Source
resources.authors: Koren, M.; Békés, G.; Hinz, J.; Lohmann, A.
resources.summary: Economic model with entry and quality choice. Vibe coding makes reusing open-source code cheaper but cuts the user engagement that pays maintainers, so wider adoption can mean fewer and lower-quality open-source projects and lower welfare despite higher productivity.
resources.wiki_use: Case for the 'Current Topics' module on platform and ecosystem externalities of AI tools; Békés also co-wrote a widely used data analysis textbook.
resources.notes: Submitted 21 January 2026.

resources.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
resources.authors: Peng, S.; Kalliamvakou, E.; Cihon, P.; Demirer, M.
resources.summary: Controlled experiment in which developers with GitHub Copilot finished an HTTP server in JavaScript 55.8% faster than the control group.
resources.wiki_use: Classic early RCT; use in M6 as a worked example of a two-arm experiment and of what a narrow, well-specified task can and cannot tell us.

resources.title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
resources.authors: Cui, Z. K.; Demirer, M.; Jaffe, S.; Musolff, L.; Peng, S.; Salz, T.
resources.summary: Three randomized field experiments (Microsoft, Accenture, an anonymous Fortune 100 firm; 4,867 developers) find a 26.08% (SE 10.3%) increase in completed tasks with an AI coding assistant (GitHub Copilot).
resources.wiki_use: Academic anchor in Management Science for M6 (field experiments, staggered rollout, pooling estimates) and the AI module's evidence page.
resources.notes: The INFORMS page didn't show volume or issue, so check the final citation. SSRN version: https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=4945566. The paper also reports heterogeneity by developer experience; check the abstract before quoting.

resources.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
resources.authors: Becker, J.; Rush, N.; Barnes, E.; Rein, D. (METR)
resources.summary: RCT with 16 experienced open-source developers on 246 real issues in their own large repositories. Allowing AI made tasks take 19% longer, yet developers expected a 24% speedup and afterwards believed AI had sped them up by 20%.
resources.wiki_use: Centerpiece case on perception vs. measurement; students contrast it with Cui et al. and discuss task, population and tool differences.
resources.notes: METR now flags these results as out of date; always pair with the February 2026 update.

resources.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
resources.authors: Becker, J.; Rush, N.; Cunningham, T.; Rein, D.; Mahamud, K. (METR)
resources.summary: Late-2025 follow-up (57 developers, 800+ tasks). Point estimates now show speedups (-18% time for returning developers, -4% for new ones), but METR calls them weak evidence. Developers increasingly refused to work without AI, causing selection, and METR is redesigning the study.
resources.wiki_use: Excellent M6 teaching case on selection, attrition and non-compliance when the treatment becomes indispensable; pair with the 2025 study.
resources.notes: Published 24 February 2026. METR calls the central estimate 'a bad proxy for the real productivity impact'.

resources.title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
resources.authors: Kwa, T.; West, B.; Becker, J.; et al. (METR)
resources.summary: Introduces the '50% time horizon', the length of tasks (in human-expert time) that agents complete with 50% reliability, and finds it doubled roughly every 7 months over six years.
resources.wiki_use: M3 tie-in: students fit the log-linear trend themselves; also frames why the tools change mid-semester.
resources.notes: METR says the static March 2025 figures are dated. Current methodology (Time Horizon 1.1, January 2026) is at https://metr.org/time-horizons/

resources.title: How much does AI impact development speed? An enterprise-based randomized controlled trial
resources.authors: Paradis, E.; Grey, K.; Madison, Q.; Nam, D.; Macvean, A.; Meimand, V.; Zhang, N.; Ferrari-Church, B.; Chandra, S.
resources.summary: RCT with 96 Google engineers on an enterprise-grade task: AI features cut time on task by about 21%, with a wide confidence interval, and gains were larger for developers who spend more hours a day coding.
resources.wiki_use: Third data point beside Peng and METR for an in-class 'meta-analysis by hand' exercise.

resources.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
resources.authors: Dell'Acqua, F.; McFowland III, E.; Mollick, E. R.; Lifshitz-Assaf, H.; Kellogg, K.; Rajendran, S.; Krayer, L.; Candelon, F.; Lakhani, K. R.
resources.summary: Preregistered experiment with BCG consultants: GPT-4 improved speed and quality on tasks inside the AI 'frontier' but reduced correctness on a task just outside it. Introduces 'centaur' and 'cyborg' work styles.
resources.wiki_use: Core business-school reading on why AI help is uneven; students map which Marketing Analytics tasks sit inside or outside the frontier.
resources.notes: The SSRN page wouldn't load directly; URL and PDF come from search results. Author list as given in Shen & Tamkin (2026). A later journal version couldn't be confirmed.

resources.title: Generative AI at Work
resources.authors: Brynjolfsson, E.; Li, D.; Raymond, L.
resources.summary: Staggered rollout of an AI assistant to 5,172 customer-support agents raised issues resolved per hour by about 15% on average. The largest gains went to less experienced and lower-skilled workers; top workers gained little.
resources.wiki_use: Economics anchor for the heterogeneity theme (who gains from AI); useful in M6 as a staggered-adoption design.
resources.notes: Customer support, not coding. Published in QJE 2025 (article qjae044, as cited in Shen & Tamkin 2026); the QJE landing page wasn't checked here.

resources.title: Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI
resources.authors: Daniotti, S.; Wachs, J.; Feng, X.; Neffke, F.
resources.summary: Trains a classifier to detect AI-written Python functions in 30M+ GitHub commits from about 170,000 developers. About 29% of US Python functions are AI-written; AI raises quarterly output by about 3.6%, and gains go mostly to experienced programmers.
resources.wiki_use: M7 tie-in (a classifier used as a measurement tool) and evidence that AI may widen skill gaps.

resources.title: 2025 DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development report
resources.summary: Annual DORA survey reframed around AI. It argues that AI amplifies an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses, and introduces a seven-practice DORA AI Capabilities Model.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background; the 'AI as amplifier' framing works as a slide for business students thinking about adoption.
resources.notes: Download gated by a contact form. Headline adoption figures weren't visible on the landing page.

resources.title: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025: AI
resources.summary: Survey of 49,000+ developers: 84% use or plan to use AI tools, but 46% distrust their accuracy. 66% cite 'almost right' solutions as their top frustration, and about 77% say vibe coding isn't part of their professional work.
resources.wiki_use: Data for a quick M2 visualization exercise (trust vs. use) and a reality check on how professionals use AI.
resources.notes: Released 29 July 2025. Press release: https://stackoverflow.co/company/press/archive/stack-overflow-2025-developer-survey/. The raw data download page may also serve as a class dataset (not checked).

resources.title: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2026: AI
resources.summary: Sixteenth survey (30,903 responses, 169 countries). Coding assistants and agents are now the top AI use case (66%); Claude Code (66%) and GitHub Copilot (59%) lead among coding agents; 48% trust AI only when they can easily check the answer.
resources.wiki_use: Pair with the 2025 survey to show year-over-year change; the 'trust when verifiable' finding motivates the course's verification habits.
resources.notes: No release date on the page. Figures are as summarized from the page in October 2026, so recheck before citing, especially the trust comparisons with 2025.

resources.title: Anthropic Economic Index: AI's impact on software development
resources.summary: Analysis of coding conversations from April 2025: about 79% of Claude Code conversations were automation (AI does the task) vs. 49% on Claude.ai. Web languages dominate; Python was 14% and SQL 6%; startups were early Claude Code adopters.
resources.wiki_use: Shows how privacy-preserving text classification of conversations (M5 methods) produces economic evidence.
resources.notes: Published 28 April 2025. One-week sample covering Free and Pro only; the startup vs. enterprise shares are inconsistent within the post.

resources.title: Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise
resources.authors: Hitzig, Z.; Massenkoff, M.; Lyubich, E.; Zhang, S.; Heller, R.; McCrory, P. (Anthropic)
resources.summary: About 400,000 Claude Code sessions (October 2025 to April 2026): users make about 70% of planning decisions but only about 20% of execution decisions. Domain experts succeed more often, non-software occupations succeed at nearly the same rates as engineers, and data analysis is a growing share of use.
resources.wiki_use: Key evidence for business students that domain expertise, not syntax, drives success with agents; a good opener for the course's 'you decide what, the agent decides how' framing.
resources.notes: Published 16 June 2026. The companion Economic Index report 'Cadences' (26 June 2026) is at https://www.anthropic.com/research/economic-index-june-2026-report

resources.title: Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
resources.authors: Pearce, H.; Ahmad, B.; Tan, B.; Dolan-Gavitt, B.; Karri, R.
resources.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2022
resources.summary: Generated 1,689 programs with Copilot across 89 security-relevant scenarios and found about 40% vulnerable.
resources.wiki_use: Classic citation for 'AI code can look right and be unsafe'; a short discussion item in the AI module.

resources.title: GenAI Code Security Report (October 2025 update)
resources.summary: Industry test of code from 100+ LLMs in Java, JavaScript, Python and C#: AI-generated code introduced risky security flaws in 45% of tests.
resources.wiki_use: Headline statistic for a slide on why students must not paste credentials or trust generated data-access code.
resources.notes: Vendor report; methodology detail is behind the download. Registration not confirmed on the page.

resources.title: We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs
resources.authors: Spracklen, J.; Wijewickrama, R.; Sakib, A. H. M. N.; Maiti, A.; Viswanath, B.; Jadliwala, M.
resources.summary: 576,000 code samples from 16 LLMs: commercial models hallucinate nonexistent packages at least 5.2% of the time and open-source models 21.7%, producing 205,474 unique fake package names that attackers can register ('slopsquatting').
resources.wiki_use: Concrete rule for M1 setup labs: verify every pip install suggested by AI against PyPI before running it.
resources.notes: No standalone 'slopsquatting' source was verified in this pass; the Thoughtworks memo 'Coding Assistants Threaten the Software Supply Chain' (https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/software-supply-chain-attack-surface.html, May 2025) covers the same risk for practitioners.

resources.title: Vibe coding service Replit deleted user's production database, faked data, told fibs galore
resources.summary: July 2025 incident in which Replit's agent deleted SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin's production database despite instructions not to touch it, generated fake data to hide bugs, and wrongly claimed the data couldn't be restored.
resources.wiki_use: Short case for a 'guardrails' discussion: separate dev and prod data, use version control, never give an agent write access to the only copy of your data.
resources.notes: Business Insider coverage of the Replit CEO's apology: https://www.businessinsider.com/replit-ceo-apologizes-ai-coding-tool-delete-company-database-2025-7

resources.title: Our new report: AI code creates 1.7x more problems (State of AI vs Human Code Generation)
resources.summary: Analysis of 470 open-source pull requests: AI-co-authored PRs averaged 10.83 issues vs. 6.45 for human-only PRs, with logic errors 75% more common and readability problems more than 3x.
resources.wiki_use: Motivates readability and logic-review items on the course's code-review rubric.
resources.notes: Published 17 December 2025. Vendor study; AI authorship was inferred from co-author tags, so some 'human' PRs may involve AI.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.subtopic: AI for economic and empirical research
resources.title: Generative AI for Economic Research: Use Cases and Implications for Economists
resources.summary: Catalog of LLM use cases for researchers (ideation, writing, background research, coding, data analysis, math), with example prompts, a rating of each use case, and a replication package.
resources.wiki_use: Anchor reading for using LLMs in analysis work; students try two coding or data use cases on course data and compare with Korinek's ratings.
resources.notes: Replication package: https://doi.org/10.3886/E194623V1. Updates: June 2024 (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles/materials/21298) and December 2024 'LLMs Learn to Collaborate and Reason' (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles/materials/22146). Access to the JEL article may depend on AEA or library access, but the updates are open.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: AI Agents for Economic Research: August 2025 Update
resources.venue: Journal of Economic Literature (online update to Korinek 2023)
resources.summary: Update to the JEL article on agentic AI for research: what agents are, how economists can use them (deep research, coding agents) and worked examples.
resources.wiki_use: Bridge reading from chat-based help to agentic workflows (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI) for empirical analysis.
resources.notes: Direct file link: https://www.aeaweb.org/content/file?id=23290. Contents summarized from the title and landing page, so skim before assigning.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: How Do Analysts Understand and Verify AI-Assisted Data Analyses?
resources.authors: Gu, K.; Shang, R.; Althoff, T.; Wang, C.; Drucker, S. M.
resources.summary: Qualitative study of 22 analysts using a design probe that shows AI explanations, code, plots and interactive tables. It documents how analysts verify AI analyses that can look right but reach wrong conclusions, and how their backgrounds shape their checks.
resources.wiki_use: Basis for a 'verify the AI's analysis' lab: give students an AI-produced regression or segmentation with a planted error and have them apply the paper's verification behaviors.
resources.notes: Published at CHI 2024; the link is the arXiv version (v2, March 2024).

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: BLADE: Benchmarking Language Model Agents for Data-Driven Science
resources.authors: Gu, K.; Shang, R.; Jiang, R.; Kuang, K.; et al.; Heer, J.; Althoff, T.
resources.summary: Benchmark of 12 datasets and research questions with expert-coded ground truth on analytic choices. LLM agents tend to stick to basic analyses and explore fewer defensible alternatives than experts.
resources.wiki_use: Connects to many-analyst and garden-of-forking-paths themes: ask an agent and a teammate to analyze the same question and compare the choices they make.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: DSBench: How Far Are Data Science Agents from Becoming Data Science Experts?
resources.authors: Jing, L.; Huang, Z.; Wang, X.; Yao, W.; Yu, W.; Ma, K.; Zhang, H.; Du, X.; Yu, D.
resources.summary: Benchmark of realistic data analysis and modeling tasks; at publication the best agent solved only 34.12% of data analysis tasks.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background; one or two DSBench-style tasks could be adapted as in-class challenges.
resources.notes: Scores are from 2024 to 2025 models and are now outdated.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: DA-Code: Agent Data Science Code Generation Benchmark for Large Language Models
resources.authors: Huang, Y.; Luo, J.; Yu, Y.; Zhang, Y.; Lei, F.; Wei, Y.; He, S.; Huang, L.; Liu, X.; Zhao, J.; Liu, K.
resources.summary: Agent-based data science benchmark (wrangling, EDA, ML); the best LLMs reached 30.5% accuracy at release.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background on which data-science steps agents fail most.
resources.notes: Project site: https://da-code-bench.github.io. Repository license not checked.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: Benchmarking Data Science Agents (DSEval)
resources.authors: Zhang, Y.; Jiang, Q.; Han, X.; Chen, N.; Yang, Y.; Ren, K.
resources.summary: Introduces DSEval, an evaluation paradigm and benchmarks covering the full data science lifecycle, with a summary of common agent failure modes.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background; its failure taxonomy can seed a 'common AI mistakes in pandas' checklist.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: DS-1000: A Natural and Reliable Benchmark for Data Science Code Generation
resources.authors: Lai, Y.; Li, C.; Wang, Y.; Zhang, T.; Zhong, R.; Zettlemoyer, L.; Yih, S. W.; Fried, D.; Wang, S.; Yu, T.
resources.summary: 1,000 StackOverflow-derived data science problems across seven Python libraries (NumPy, pandas, etc.), graded by execution; Codex-002 scored 43.3% at release.
resources.wiki_use: Sample problems make good warm-up exercises: students solve one with and without AI and check against the tests.
resources.notes: Project site: https://ds1000-code-gen.github.io. Published at ICML 2023 per common citation, which wasn't confirmed on the arXiv page.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: CORE-Bench: Fostering the Credibility of Published Research Through a Computational Reproducibility Agent Benchmark
resources.authors: Siegel, Z. S.; Kapoor, S.; Nadgir, N.; Stroebl, B.; Narayanan, A.
resources.summary: 270 tasks from 90 papers in CS, social science and medicine test whether agents can reproduce published results from code and data. The best agent reached 21% on the hardest tasks.
resources.wiki_use: Frames the team project's GitHub deliverable: can an agent, or a classmate, reproduce your blog post's results from your repo?
resources.notes: v2 dated 22 June 2026.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: Is GPT-4 a Good Data Analyst?
resources.authors: Cheng, L.; Li, X.; Bing, L.
resources.summary: Early test of GPT-4 as an end-to-end data analyst against professional human analysts; it was comparable on the paper's metrics, though the authors stop short of saying it can replace analysts.
resources.wiki_use: Historical marker for how quickly 'AI analyst' claims evolved; pair with Gu et al. on verification.

resources.section: AI for data analysis and empirical research
resources.title: Automated Social Science: Language Models as Scientist and Subjects
resources.authors: Manning, B. S.; Zhu, K.; Horton, J. J.
resources.summary: An LLM system generates hypotheses, builds structural causal models, runs simulated experiments with LLM agents (negotiation, bail, interviews, auctions) and estimates effects. The LLM gets effect directions right but not magnitudes until it is given the fitted model.
resources.wiki_use: M6/M8 discussion of AI-run experiments and synthetic subjects; links to marketing debates on synthetic respondents.

resources.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
resources.authors: Bastani, H.; Bastani, O.; Sungu, A.; et al.
resources.summary: Field experiment with about 1,000 Turkish high school math students: unrestricted GPT-4 ('GPT Base') raised practice scores 48% but lowered later unassisted exam scores 17%. A tutor version with teacher-designed hints ('GPT Tutor') raised practice 127% with no exam penalty.
resources.wiki_use: Required reading for the course's AI policy: explains why labs use hint-first tutors and unassisted checkpoints. Also a clean M6 example of a three-arm field experiment.
resources.notes: The PNAS pages wouldn't load from this environment, so the URL is the SSRN working paper 'Generative AI Can Harm Learning', linked from Wharton Knowledge (https://knowledge.wharton.upenn.edu/article/without-guardrails-generative-ai-can-harm-education/) and from Mollick's 'Post-apocalyptic education'. PNAS title and venue as given in the brief; DOI and full author list not verified here.

resources.title: How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills (paper: How AI Impacts Skill Formation)
resources.summary: RCT with 52 mostly junior Python engineers learning the Trio library. Those with an AI assistant scored about 17 points lower on a follow-up quiz (about 50% vs. 67%), with the biggest gap on debugging, and weren't significantly faster. People who asked conceptual questions kept their learning; those who fully delegated did not.
resources.wiki_use: Central evidence for the course's 'ask for explanations, not just code' norm; show the six interaction patterns and have students self-classify their own AI logs.
resources.notes: Anthropic blog post 29 January 2026; arXiv v1 28 January 2026, v2 1 February 2026.

resources.title: Studying the Effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners in Introductory Programming
resources.authors: Kazemitabaar, M.; Chow, J.; Ma, C. K. T.; Ericson, B. J.; Weintrop, D.; Grossman, T.
resources.summary: Controlled study of 69 learners aged 10 to 17 on 45 Python tasks: Codex access raised completion (about 1.15x) and scores (about 1.8x) without hurting manual code-modification skills. Retention a week later was slightly, not significantly, higher.
resources.wiki_use: A counterweight to the harm studies; discuss what differs (scaffolded tasks, novices, manual-modification checks).

resources.title: The Widening Gap: The Benefits and Harms of Generative AI for Novice Programmers
resources.authors: Prather, J.; Reeves, B.; Leinonen, J.; MacNeil, S.; Randrianasolo, A. S.; Becker, B.; Kimmel, B.; Wright, J.; Briggs, B.
resources.summary: Eye-tracking and interview study of 21 novices: students who already had a plan used GenAI to speed up, while struggling students were further derailed, often ending with an 'illusion of competence'.
resources.wiki_use: Motivates mandatory 'plan first, then prompt' steps and short self-explanation checks in labs; shows students the gap they may fall into.
resources.notes: Published at ICER 2024; the link is the arXiv preprint.

resources.title: Computing Education in the Era of Generative AI
resources.authors: Denny, P.; Prather, J.; Becker, B. A.; Finnie-Ansley, J.; Hellas, A.; Leinonen, J.; Luxton-Reilly, A.; Reeves, B. N.; Santos, E. A.; Sarsa, S.
resources.summary: Accessible overview of what code-generating models mean for programming instructors, summarizing studies of model performance on intro problems and of AI-generated learning resources.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor-only background for course design decisions.
resources.notes: Published in Communications of the ACM (2024). The link is the arXiv preprint (June 2023) because the ACM Digital Library blocked automated access.

resources.title: From 'Ban It Till We Understand It' to 'Resistance is Futile': How University Programming Instructors Plan to Adapt as More Students Use AI Code Generation and Explanation Tools such as ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot
resources.summary: Interviews with university programming instructors on short- and long-term plans for AI coding tools, from banning them to fully embracing them.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor-only map of policy options; useful when writing the syllabus AI section.
resources.notes: Related: Lau & Guo, 'The Design Space of LLM-Based AI Coding Assistants: An Analysis of 90 Systems' (VL/HCC 2025), https://pg.ucsd.edu/publications/ai-coding-assistants-design-space_VLHCC-2025.pdf

resources.title: Six Opportunities for Scientists and Engineers to Learn Programming Using AI Tools such as ChatGPT
resources.summary: Short essay on how people who program as a means to an end (scientists, engineers, and by extension analysts) can use AI tools to learn programming.
resources.wiki_use: Good fit for the course's non-CS audience; assign in Week 1 alongside Willison.

resources.title: Teaching CS50 with AI: Leveraging Generative Artificial Intelligence in Computer Science Education
resources.authors: Liu, R.; et al. (Harvard CS50; Malan, D. J.)
resources.summary: How Harvard's CS50 deployed AI tools, including the CS50 Duck rubber-duck debugger, built to guide students toward solutions rather than hand them answers, and how students responded.
resources.wiki_use: Model for a course-specific hint-first AI tutor (for example a Claude Project or custom GPT with a 'don't give full solutions' system prompt) for Marketing Analytics labs.
resources.notes: Full author list not captured, so check the PDF. Follow-up: 'Improving AI in CS50: Leveraging Human Feedback for Better Learning' (SIGCSE 2025), https://cs.harvard.edu/malan/publications/fp0627-liu.pdf

resources.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
resources.authors: Kosmyna, N.; Hauptmann, E.; Yuan, Y. T.; Situ, J.; Liao, X.-H.; Beresnitzky, A. V.; Braunstein, I.; Maes, P.
resources.summary: EEG study of 54 participants writing essays with an LLM, a search engine, or no tools. LLM users showed the weakest brain connectivity, the lowest sense of ownership and trouble quoting their own essays; the authors call this 'cognitive debt'.
resources.wiki_use: Use as a critical-reading exercise: students evaluate the design (small sample, 18 in the crossover session, essay task, preprint) before accepting the headlines.
resources.notes: Not peer reviewed as of v2 (31 December 2025). MIT Media Lab project page: https://www.media.mit.edu/projects/your-brain-on-chatgpt/overview/. Published critiques couldn't be verified in this pass because the search budget ran out; the course should add one before assigning.

resources.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers
resources.authors: Lee, H.-P.; Sarkar, A.; Tankelevitch, L.; Drosos, I.; Rintel, S.; Banks, R.; Wilson, N.
resources.summary: Survey of 319 knowledge workers (936 examples): more confidence in GenAI predicts less critical thinking, more self-confidence predicts more. GenAI shifts effort toward verifying, integrating and 'stewarding' output.
resources.wiki_use: Short reading for business students on how over-trust erodes review; supports building verification into every assignment.

resources.title: Anthropic Education Report: How University Students Use Claude
resources.summary: Privacy-preserving analysis of student conversations: CS students are heavily overrepresented, about 47% of conversations are 'direct' (answer-seeking), and Claude mostly performs higher-order Bloom's tasks (creating, analyzing), raising concerns about offloading.
resources.wiki_use: Discussion opener on how students actually use AI, and an M5 example of classifying text at scale.
resources.notes: Published 8 April 2025. The CS share appears as both 36.8% and 38.6% within the report.

resources.title: Anthropic Education Report: How educators use Claude
resources.summary: About 74,000 higher-education conversations plus Northeastern faculty interviews: curriculum development dominates, educators build interactive artifacts (simulations, quizzes, dashboards), and grading is the use faculty trust least.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background and validation for building the course itself as interactive HTML artifacts.
resources.notes: Published 27 August 2025.

resources.title: CS146S: The Modern Software Developer
resources.summary: Stanford course, first offered Fall 2025 and again in Fall 2026, on building software with LLM coding agents: MCP, agent skills, spec-driven development, loop engineering and the 'software factory', with hands-on assignments, industry guest talks and a final project.
resources.wiki_use: Benchmark for topic coverage and sequencing; borrow the spec-driven and context-engineering units at a business-analytics level.
resources.notes: Fall 2025 archive: https://themodernsoftware.dev/fall2025. No AI policy, weekly syllabus or GitHub repo visible from the fetched pages.

resources.title: Claude Code: A Highly Agentic Coding Assistant (DeepLearning.AI)
resources.summary: A 2-hour course (10 video lessons) built with Anthropic: exploring, testing, refactoring and debugging codebases; MCP servers (Playwright, Figma); CLAUDE.md, context management, planning, subagents, worktrees, GitHub integration and hooks. Projects include refactoring a Jupyter notebook into a dashboard.
resources.wiki_use: Core assigned course. The notebook-to-dashboard project maps directly onto the M2 visualization module.
resources.notes: Fetched via https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/claude-code-a-highly-agentic-coding-assistant/, which declares this canonical URL. Prerequisites: Python and Git. Free 'for a limited time during the platform beta'; graded work needs Pro. Year approximate (2025).

resources.title: Vibe Coding 101 with Replit (DeepLearning.AI)
resources.summary: A 1h34m beginner course: principles of agentic coding (one task at a time, fresh sessions per feature), PRDs and wireframes as prompts, building and deploying two apps, debugging, persistent storage, and reviewing what the agent built.
resources.wiki_use: Good first exposure for non-CS students. Its 'review what the agent built' habit sets up the verification lessons.
resources.notes: Year approximate (2025). Free 'for a limited time during the platform beta'. Certificate needs Pro.

resources.title: Solve It With Code (Solveit)
resources.authors: Howard, J.; Whitaker, J.; Ries, E. (Answer.AI)
resources.summary: Five-week course and platform built around the 'Solveit method': use AI to become a better problem solver rather than outsource thinking. Write one or two lines at a time, check results right away, then package working steps into functions. Draws on Pólya's How to Solve It.
resources.wiki_use: Pedagogical model for small-step, check-as-you-go AI coding in Colab labs.
resources.notes: Signups were closed when checked; the page gives conflicting price information ($500 course vs. $10/month platform).

resources.title: Assigning AI: Seven Approaches for Students, with Prompts
resources.summary: Seven roles for AI in courses (tutor, coach, mentor, teammate, tool, simulator, student), each with sample prompts, benefits and risks, plus risk-management advice that keeps students 'in the loop'.
resources.wiki_use: Framework for labeling each wiki activity by the AI role it uses; the AI-student role (students teach or correct the AI) suits code review.

resources.title: Claude Code and What Comes Next
resources.summary: Mollick watches Claude Code (Opus 4.5) build and deploy a working sales website from one request. He explains context compaction, Skills and subagents, and argues that agentic coding tools preview changes to all knowledge work.
resources.wiki_use: Accessible intro to agents for business students before the first Claude Code lab.
resources.notes: Published 7 January 2026. Related: 'A Guide to Which AI to Use in the Agentic Era' (https://www.oneusefulthing.org/p/a-guide-to-which-ai-to-use-in-the), updated periodically.

resources.title: Post-apocalyptic education
resources.summary: Argues that the 'homework apocalypse' has arrived and describes two illusions: that teachers can detect AI work, and that students learn from AI answers. Suggests tutor-style prompts and in-class verification instead.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background for the assessment plan. A reader comment by Tyler Ransom describes AI-permitted coding assignments followed by one-on-one oral exams, a model worth copying.
resources.notes: Published 30 August 2024. Links to research on AI detection and to the Bastani SSRN paper.

resources.title: AI Pedagogy Project
resources.summary: Curated, open-access library of about 40 classroom assignments that use AI critically, plus an AI Guide (AI Starter, LLM comparison, resources).
resources.wiki_use: Source of adaptable activities, for example 'Questioning the Bot' (https://aipedagogy.org/assignment/questioning-the-bot-socratic-chats-with-ai-2/) recast as interrogating an AI's regression interpretation.
resources.notes: Few coding- or data-specific assignments on the first page of the listing. Reuse terms are on https://aipedagogy.org/using-our-content/

resources.title: The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS)
resources.authors: Perkins, M.; Furze, L.; Roe, J.; MacVaugh, J.
resources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (diagrams and resource assets only)
resources.summary: Widely adopted five-level scale for how much AI an assessment allows: No AI, AI Planning, AI Collaboration, Full AI, AI Exploration. Now at version 2.1.
resources.wiki_use: Tag every Marketing Analytics assignment with an AIAS level on the wiki (for example, concept checks at Level 1, labs at Level 3 or 4, the team project at Level 5).
resources.notes: Updated paper 'Reimagining the AIAS' (JUTLP 2025): https://doi.org/10.53761/rrm4y757. Resources: https://aiassessmentscale.com/resources/

resources.title: 4 Steps to Design an AI-Resilient Learning Experience (with Data Analytics toolkit example)
resources.summary: Backward-design guide: learners, outcomes (Bloom's higher levels), assessments (AI required, allowed or banned for each), activities. Comes with a Word toolkit and a worked Data Analytics course example.
resources.wiki_use: Use the Data Analytics toolkit example (https://mitsloanedtech.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/AIHub_ToolkitExampleDataAnalytics.pdf) as a template when redesigning each Marketing Analytics module.
resources.notes: Toolkit files dated March 2024; page modified September 2026. Toolkit (docx): https://mitsloanedtech.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/AIHub_AI-ResilientLXDesignToolkit.docx

resources.title: AI Detectors Don't Work. Here's What to Do Instead.
resources.summary: Business-school guidance explaining why AI detectors are unreliable and offering strategies for academic honesty in their place.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor reference that backs the decision not to use detectors, consistent with Illinois guidance.
resources.notes: Original publication year not shown (page modified 14 September 2026).

resources.title: claude-code-transcripts: tools for publishing transcripts of Claude Code sessions
resources.summary: Command-line tool (uvx claude-code-transcripts) that turns local Claude Code session files into paginated HTML transcripts, with a timeline of prompts and commits.
resources.wiki_use: Make it the standard way students attach AI-use logs to team-project repos, so graders can see the prompts behind each commit.
resources.notes: Launched around 25 December 2025. The 'web' commands were broken at the time of checking (unofficial API changes); the 'local' command is what students would use.

resources.title: Linear walkthroughs (Agentic Engineering Patterns)
resources.summary: A pattern for having an agent produce a structured, step-by-step walkthrough of a codebase so a human can actually understand code they didn't write. The companion chapter 'Interactive explanations' covers the same goal interactively.
resources.wiki_use: Required step before submission: students generate a walkthrough of their own analysis notebook, then annotate where they agree or disagree, which serves as a comprehension check.
resources.notes: Posted 25 February 2026. Summary based on the chapter title and guide context; the chapter text itself wasn't fetched. Companion: https://simonwillison.net/guides/agentic-engineering-patterns/interactive-explanations/

resources.title: Introducing Claude for Education (learning mode)
resources.summary: April 2025 announcement of Claude for Education and its 'learning mode', which guides students' reasoning with Socratic questions instead of giving answers.
resources.wiki_use: Option for a hint-first course tutor, but note that UIUC does not list Claude among licensed tools, so students would need personal accounts.

resources.title: Enterprise GenAI: AI Apps (University of Illinois)
resources.authors: University of Illinois, Office of the CIO
resources.summary: Official list of approved AI tools and data classifications. For students: Microsoft Copilot Chat, Illinois Chat, Google Gemini, Google NotebookLM and Zoom AI Companion, plus Illinois Computes for grad students. Faculty and staff only: Illinois ChatGPT ($11/month), Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on, and GitHub Copilot (security review advised).
resources.wiki_use: Link from the wiki's 'Tools and accounts' page; Gemini (Internal and Public data) is the licensed path for Colab-adjacent work, and Claude and ChatGPT Edu are not on the student list.
resources.notes: Checked 2026-10-23: Claude isn't listed; ChatGPT is faculty and staff only. Gemini page (https://genai.illinois.edu/ai-apps-google-gemini/) says Public and Internal data only, Illinois-managed account required, and doesn't mention Gemini in Colab or Gemini CLI. Illinois Chat: https://chat.illinois.edu/. Students can get GitHub Copilot separately through GitHub Education (not verified here).

resources.title: Best Practices in Teaching and Learning (Enterprise GenAI, Illinois)
resources.authors: University of Illinois, Office of the CIO
resources.summary: Campus framework of principles (GenAI literacy, academic integrity, keeping humans active, inclusion, data privacy) with practice pages: notify learners of expectations, acknowledge AI use, foster critical evaluation, use AI for assessment and feedback.
resources.wiki_use: Cite in the syllabus AI policy so it lines up with campus expectations.
resources.notes: No date on the page. Expectations page: https://genai.illinois.edu/best-practice-notify-learners-of-expectations-for-using-generative-ai-to-support-learning/

resources.title: Best Practice: Acknowledge AI Use and Cite AI-Generated Content (Illinois)
resources.authors: University of Illinois, Office of the CIO
resources.summary: Campus guidance on disclosure: name the tool, how it was used and how much it shaped the result, optionally with prompts. Links an AI-use worksheet (draft and Google Forms versions) and discourages AI detectors and AI-plagiarism accusations.
resources.wiki_use: Base the course's AI-use statement template (blog-post footer plus README section) on this page and its worksheet.
resources.notes: No date on the page; the linked citation-style guidance was current as of March 2024.

resources.title: Integrate AI into your Teaching (CITL, Illinois)
resources.authors: Center for Innovation in Teaching & Learning, University of Illinois
resources.summary: CITL guidance (updated 17 August 2026): avoid blanket bans, specify when and how AI may be used, and redesign assignments toward presentations, applied group work and visible learning. Links syllabus resources, including Gies syllabus guidance and College of Law sample statements.
resources.wiki_use: Primary campus reference for the syllabus and assessment design; CITL also offers consultations and departmental workshops.
resources.notes: The older CITL ChatGPT page linked from genai.illinois.edu now redirects to the CITL home page. Related: AI Curriculum and Training (https://citl.illinois.edu/ai-curriculum-and-training), Generative AI Fluency Modules (https://citl.illinois.edu/generative-ai-fluency-modules), College of Law sample syllabus statements (https://publish.illinois.edu/ai-law-teaching/syllabus-statements/).

resources.title: Gies Generative AI Guiding Principles
resources.authors: Gies College of Business, University of Illinois
resources.summary: College-level infographic and links for instructors, including Gies syllabus guidance on setting permitted AI uses, having students document and cite AI use, and checking AI output for accuracy.
resources.wiki_use: Make sure the Marketing Analytics AI policy is consistent with college principles; link from the syllabus.
resources.notes: Created 19 May 2023; last updated 6 November 2025. Some linked tool names (for example Google Bard) are dated.

resources.title: Claude Code documentation: overview and quickstart
resources.summary: The official Claude Code docs. The quickstart covers the native installer (macOS, Linux, WSL, Windows), login, a first session, Git use, and essential commands. Claude Code also runs on the web, in a desktop app, in VS Code and JetBrains, in Slack, and in GitHub Actions.
resources.wiki_use: Link it from the M1 setup page. Students install Claude Code and complete the quickstart's 'explore a repo, make a change, commit' loop on the course starter repo.
resources.notes: Quickstart fetched at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/quickstart.md; the overview link appears in it. Requires a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise), a Console (API) account, or a cloud provider. The Free claude.ai plan does not include Claude Code (see claude-pricing-plans). The quickstart links free 'Claude Code 101' and other courses on Claude Academy. The full page index is at https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt.

resources.title: Best practices for Claude Code
resources.summary: Anthropic's guide to agentic coding. Topics: give Claude a check it can run (tests, scripts, screenshots); explore, then plan, then code (plan mode); write a short CLAUDE.md; manage context aggressively (/clear, /compact, subagents); use checkpoints and rewind; run a writer/reviewer pattern; avoid common failures such as the 'trust-then-verify gap'.
resources.wiki_use: Assigned reading before the first vibe-coding lab. Turn its 'Avoid common failure patterns' list into a classroom checklist for AI-generated analysis code.
resources.notes: The old Anthropic Engineering post at https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-best-practices now returns HTTP 302 to this docs page, so cite this URL. I did not re-verify the original post's publication date or byline.

resources.title: Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs)
resources.summary: A skill is a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter and markdown instructions, kept in ~/.claude/skills/, .claude/skills/, a plugin, or synced from claude.ai. Claude loads skills automatically when relevant, or you call one with /skill-name. Claude Code skills follow the open Agent Skills standard and add extensions.
resources.wiki_use: Demo: the instructor ships a course skill (for example 'marketing-analysis-checks', which runs assertions and reproduces headline numbers) in the starter repo so every student's agent follows the same verification routine.
resources.notes: Anthropic Academy also runs a free 'Introduction to agent skills' course at https://anthropic.skilljar.com/introduction-to-agent-skills (seen on the Skilljar catalog; I did not open the course page itself).

resources.title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills
resources.authors: Zhang, B.; Lazuka, K.; Murag, M. (Anthropic)
resources.summary: Introduces Agent Skills: folders of instructions, scripts and resources that agents load through progressive disclosure. The agent sees only the metadata at startup, reads the full SKILL.md when a skill is relevant, and opens other files only as needed. The post advises auditing skills from less-trusted sources.
resources.wiki_use: Background reading for the wiki page on 'how agents get context', paired with the context-engineering post.
resources.notes: Published October 16, 2025. An update note on the page says Agent Skills was published as an open standard (agentskills.io).

resources.title: Agent Skills: open format specification
resources.summary: The canonical site for the open Agent Skills format: a skill is a folder with a SKILL.md (name and description at minimum) plus optional scripts/, references/ and assets/. It explains progressive disclosure (discovery, activation, execution) and links the specification, a quickstart and a list of client tools that support skills.
resources.wiki_use: Cite it as the vendor-neutral definition of a skill. The same skill folder works across Claude Code, Antigravity, VS Code and other compatible agents.
resources.notes: Spec and discussion repo: https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills (link seen on the page; I did not check its license). Agent Skills is now listed as a project of the Agentic AI Foundation (https://aaif.io), which also hosts MCP and AGENTS.md.

resources.title: anthropics/skills: public repository of Agent Skills
resources.license: Apache-2.0 for many skills; the docx/pdf/pptx/xlsx document skills are source-available, not open source
resources.summary: Anthropic's example skills (about 183k stars). They cover creative, technical, enterprise and document work (docx, pdf, pptx, xlsx), and each is a folder with a SKILL.md.
resources.wiki_use: Use it as a template gallery when students write their own analysis skill, for example for a team project's data-cleaning conventions.
resources.notes: Check each skill folder's license before you redistribute it on the wiki.

download.license: Apache-2.0 (per skill; exclude the source-available document skills)

resources.subtopic: Claude Code on the web and desktop
resources.title: Use Claude Code in the cloud (Claude Code on the web) and the Claude Code desktop app
resources.summary: Cloud sessions run Claude Code on Anthropic-managed VMs. You start them from claude.ai/code in a browser, from the mobile app, from the desktop app's Code tab, or with `claude --cloud`. They clone a GitHub repository and can open pull requests. The desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux beta) gives a graphical interface for parallel sessions, diff review and pull-request management.
resources.wiki_use: A no-terminal on-ramp: students who struggle with local installs can run their project repo in a cloud session from a browser or the desktop app.
resources.notes: Cloud sessions are available on Pro, Max and Team plans, and for Enterprise users with premium seats or Chat + Claude Code seats. They share rate limits with other Claude usage, with no separate compute charge. Repo cloning and PRs require GitHub. Desktop docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop (fetched). Before sharing a session publicly from a Pro or Max account, check it for credentials.

resources.title: How Claude remembers your project (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, auto memory)
resources.summary: Explains CLAUDE.md files at project, user and organization scope, .claude/rules/ for rules scoped to file types, and auto memory, which holds notes Claude writes itself. It states that Claude Code can read a repository's AGENTS.md in place of CLAUDE.md.
resources.wiki_use: Give every team a starter CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md for the semester project (data paths, 'never print raw customer rows', test command), and use this page to explain how it works.
resources.notes: These instructions are advisory context, not enforced configuration. For hard rules the docs point to hooks (for example a PreToolUse hook).

resources.title: Claude Code security (permission modes, prompt-injection safeguards, MCP and cloud security)
resources.summary: Covers Claude Code's permission architecture (read-only by default in Manual mode; auto mode uses a classifier model to review actions), sandboxed bash, the working-directory boundary, prompt-injection protections, MCP server trust, isolation of cloud sessions, and best practices for untrusted content.
resources.wiki_use: Required reading for the 'running agents safely' wiki page. Students configure /permissions and /sandbox before the first assignment that touches course data.
resources.notes: Related pages: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes and https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing. As of v2.1.283, auto mode is the default starting permission mode for interactive terminal sessions, so instructors may want to recommend Manual mode or plan mode at first.

resources.title: Beyond permission prompts: making Claude Code more secure and autonomous
resources.summary: Explains Claude Code's sandbox, which combines filesystem isolation with network isolation through a domain-allowlisting proxy, enforced with OS tools (bubblewrap on Linux, seatbelt on macOS). It argues that both are needed to stop a compromised agent from exfiltrating data.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background for teaching why sandboxing matters and how it reduces 'approval fatigue'.
resources.notes: Published October 20, 2025. Open-source runtime: https://github.com/anthropic-experimental/sandbox-runtime (link from the post; I did not check its license).

resources.title: Claude Code data usage (training, retention, telemetry)
resources.summary: Free, Pro and Max (consumer) accounts choose whether their data trains future models. With the setting on, retention is 5 years; with it off, 30 days. Team, Enterprise and API (commercial) data is not used for training by default, and standard retention is 30 days. Local transcripts are stored in plaintext under ~/.claude/projects/ for 30 days.
resources.wiki_use: Use it on the data-privacy wiki page to show why personal accounts differ from institutional ones, and have students check their claude.ai privacy setting before using course or client data.
resources.notes: Transcripts sent with /feedback are retained for 5 years. Telemetry can be disabled with environment variables. Point out to students that local plaintext transcripts can contain any data the agent has read.

resources.section: AI inside notebooks and data apps
resources.title: Create and edit files with Claude (code execution and file creation)
resources.summary: Claude can run code in a sandbox to analyze uploaded CSV/TSV files (up to 30 MB) and create Excel, PowerPoint, Word, PDF, Python and PNG chart outputs. The feature is available on Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise, across web, desktop and mobile.
resources.wiki_use: The zero-install option for M1/M2 labs: students upload a sample customer CSV, ask for an RFM table and chart, then download and inspect the Python that produced it.
resources.notes: On by default on Free, Pro and Max, with network egress on. The article warns about prompt injection through hidden instructions in files or websites, and notes that file creation uses more of the plan's usage. The older URL support.anthropic.com/en/articles/12111783-create-and-edit-files-with-claude appeared in search results. Hands-on review: Simon Willison, 'My review of Claude's new Code Interpreter, released under a very confusing name' (September 9, 2025; https://simonwillison.net/2025/Sep/9/claude-code-interpreter, fetched). He found a Python/Node sandbox with about 9 GB RAM and PyPI installs, needed several rounds of prompting for a usable chart, and planned to avoid using it with data he would not want leaked. A good short M2 reading.

resources.title: Claude plans and pricing
resources.summary: As of 2026-10-23: Free $0 (no Claude Code); Pro $20/month monthly or $17/month billed annually, with Claude Code included in all paid plans; Max from $100/month (5x or 20x Pro usage); Team standard seats $20 (annual) or $25 (monthly), premium seats $100 or $125; Enterprise $20/seat/month plus usage at API rates.
resources.wiki_use: Use it for the 'which tool should I pay for?' table on the M1 setup page.
resources.notes: The page mentions an Education plan for whole universities with 'discounted rates', but gives no price and no individual student discount.

resources.title: Claude for Education (Claude for higher education)
resources.summary: Anthropic's higher-education offering is a university-wide plan bought by institutions. Students cannot sign up individually. It includes learning mode, which tutors Socratically, and points students to a free 'AI Fluency for students' course.
resources.wiki_use: State plainly on the wiki that UIUC does not list Claude among its approved AI apps, so students would use personal Free or Pro accounts. Pair this with the privacy guidance.
resources.notes: anthropic.com/education 302-redirects here. Original announcement: https://www.anthropic.com/news/introducing-claude-for-education (April 2, 2025), which describes learning mode, campus-wide agreements (Northeastern, LSE, Champlain), Campus Ambassadors and API credits for student builders. The current page does not mention API credits or a student discount. See uiuc-genai-approved-apps. Free student course: 'AI Fluency for students' on Anthropic Academy (https://anthropic.skilljar.com/ai-fluency-for-students; from the catalog listing, not opened), suitable as pre-course homework for non-CS students.

resources.title: Claude Code in Action (Anthropic Academy)
resources.summary: A free self-paced course on running longer, less-supervised Claude Code sessions. Lessons: steering long sessions, a CLAUDE.md the agent actually follows, verification skills, permission modes, hooks, routines and headless runs, GitHub Actions code review, verifying unsupervised runs, and plugins. Ends with a quiz.
resources.wiki_use: Optional certificate-style module after students finish the basics; its 'verifying unsupervised runs' lesson fits the course's emphasis on checking AI-generated analysis.
resources.notes: Marked 'Register | FREE'. The page gives no duration and does not confirm a certificate. The beginner course 'Claude Code 101' is at https://anthropic.skilljar.com/claude-code-101 (catalog listing; also linked from the Claude Code quickstart as academy.claude.com/courses/claude-code-101).

resources.title: Prompt engineering overview and Prompting best practices (Claude Platform docs)
resources.summary: Anthropic's entry point to prompting. Before tuning a prompt, define success criteria and a way to test against them. Techniques (clarity, examples, XML structure, roles, thinking, chaining) are collected in the 'Prompting best practices' reference.
resources.wiki_use: Link it from the prompting page, and use its 'define success criteria first' framing to teach students to specify expected numbers or tests before asking for analysis code.
resources.notes: docs.claude.com/... 302-redirects here. Best-practices page: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices. An interactive tutorial is at https://github.com/anthropics/prompt-eng-interactive-tutorial, written for Claude 3, so some advice is dated, and I did not check its license. A metaprompt notebook can be opened in Colab from the claude-cookbooks repo.

resources.title: Claude Cookbooks (anthropics/claude-cookbooks)
resources.summary: Jupyter notebooks and recipes for the Claude API: tool use, SQL queries, JSON or structured extraction, PDF summarization, reading charts, classification, RAG, skills and the Agent SDK.
resources.wiki_use: Embed selected notebooks in the wiki. misc/how_to_make_sql_queries.ipynb and the JSON-mode or structured-extraction recipes suit M5 text analysis; multimodal/reading_charts_graphs_powerpoints.ipynb suits M2.
resources.notes: Running these notebooks needs an Anthropic API key, which costs money. The README links still point to the old anthropics/anthropic-cookbook name, so the repo appears to have been renamed.

resources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
resources.authors: Rajasekaran, P.; Dixon, E.; Ryan, C.; Hadfield, J. (Anthropic Applied AI)
resources.summary: Argues that for multi-turn agents the job shifts from wording prompts to curating 'the smallest useful set of tokens' in a limited context window. Covers system prompts, tools, examples, retrieval at run time, compaction, structured note-taking and sub-agents.
resources.wiki_use: Canonical source for the wiki's 'context engineering' concept page. It explains why students should give the agent a data dictionary rather than paste in a 100k-row CSV.
resources.notes: Published September 29, 2025.

resources.title: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? (official docs)
resources.summary: MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external data, tools and workflows, described as 'a USB-C port for AI applications'. Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor and others support it. The docs cover building servers and clients and MCP Apps. The current docs version is dated 2026-07-28.
resources.wiki_use: Concept page: show how an agent could query a course SQL database or Google Drive through MCP instead of students pasting data into chat.
resources.notes: Anthropic's launch post (November 25, 2024): https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol. MCP is now listed as a project of the Agentic AI Foundation, under the Linux Foundation (https://aaif.io). Free courses: DeepLearning.AI 'MCP: Build Rich-Context AI Apps with Anthropic' (https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/mcp-build-rich-context-ai-apps-with-anthropic) and Anthropic Academy 'Introduction to Model Context Protocol' (https://anthropic.skilljar.com/introduction-to-model-context-protocol); both URLs came from catalog listings. Claude Code MCP setup: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp. Security: the MCP Security Best Practices page (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tutorials/security/security_best_practices.md, fetched) covers confused deputy, token passthrough, SSRF and local-server compromise; its local-server section is a good warning against installing random MCP servers. Governance: the Agentic AI Foundation (https://aaif.io, fetched) hosts MCP, AGENTS.md, Agent Skills, A2A, goose and others.

resources.title: AGENTS.md: a simple, open format for guiding coding agents
resources.authors: Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation); originally OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google Jules, Cursor, Factory
resources.summary: AGENTS.md is a plain-Markdown 'README for agents' with no required fields. Codex, Jules, Gemini CLI, Cursor, VS Code, GitHub Copilot coding agent, Windsurf, Zed, Aider and others read it. The Agentic AI Foundation now stewards it.
resources.wiki_use: Have each team commit an AGENTS.md (with a CLAUDE.md that points to it) so the project works the same whether a teammate uses Claude Code, Codex, Copilot or Cursor.
resources.notes: Repo: https://github.com/agentsmd/agents.md (link from the site). Codex docs on how AGENTS.md files are discovered and merged: https://learn.chatgpt.com/codex/agent-configuration/agents-md. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md (see claude-code-memory-claude-md).

resources.title: GitHub Spec Kit: toolkit for spec-driven development
resources.summary: An open-source toolkit that runs inside an agent's chat as /speckit-* skills: constitution (project principles), specify, plan, tasks, implement and converge, plus optional bug-fix and idea-assessment extensions. It turns 'vibe coding' into a spec, then plan, then tasks, then implement workflow.
resources.wiki_use: Use it for the team project kickoff: students write a constitution and spec for their analytics blog post before any code is generated.
resources.notes: Docs: https://github.github.io/spec-kit/. The README examples use Copilot, and other agents plug in through an integration key. I could not verify a GitHub blog post on spec-driven development because the search budget ran out.

resources.title: Spec-Driven Development with Coding Agents (DeepLearning.AI short course)
resources.summary: A 1h16m beginner course: compares vibe coding with spec-driven development, then covers writing project constitutions and feature specs, a plan-implement-verify loop, replanning, building an MVP, applying the method to legacy code, and packaging the workflow as an agent skill.
resources.wiki_use: Assign it before the project proposal milestone.
resources.notes: Last updated April 18, 2026. The page does not say whether viewing is free; quizzes, graded work and certificates need DeepLearning.AI Pro.

resources.title: Cursor plans and pricing (restructured October 2026)
resources.summary: An AI-first code editor (a VS Code fork) with agent, chat, tab completion, MCP and rules. As of 2026-10-23 the plans are Free (limited agent and chat requests), Plus $8/month (Grok models only), Premium $30 (4x Plus, cloud agents, third-party models billed at API list price), Super $100, Ultra $200, Teams $30+/user and Enterprise.
resources.wiki_use: List it as an alternative IDE. Warn students that the cheap tier now uses only xAI Grok models and that Claude or GPT models cost extra.
resources.notes: SHAKY, FAST-MOVING. SpaceX/xAI agreed to buy Anysphere for $60B (Techzine, June 16, 2026: https://www.techzine.eu/news/devops/142197/spacex-acquires-cursor-for-60-billion/, expected to close Q3 2026). PricingSaaS reports the rebuilt lineup around Oct 13-19, 2026 (https://pricingsaas.com/news/article/cursor-rebuilds-its-pricing-around-grok-and-x-with-plans-from-8-to-200); the old lineup was Individual $20 with Pro/Pro+/Ultra options and Teams $40. Cursor MCP docs: https://cursor.com/docs/context/mcp (link from the MCP docs; not opened).

resources.title: Cursor for Students
resources.summary: Cursor's student page currently says anyone can start free, with upgrades offered through promotions at campus and online events 'this fall' and a campus newsletter. It does not describe a standing free-Pro-for-students offer, a duration, eligibility or verification.
resources.wiki_use: Tell students not to count on free Cursor Pro. The Free plan or other tools are the safe default.
resources.notes: In 2025 Cursor offered one year of free Pro to verified university students (Cursor forum threads such as https://forum.cursor.com/t/major-bug-verified-students-get-one-year-of-free-cursor-pro/88376 appeared in search results). The current page no longer describes that offer, so treat it as ended or changed.

resources.title: GitHub Copilot plans (Free, Pro, Pro+, Max; usage-based AI credits)
resources.summary: As of 2026-10-23: Free $0 (2,000 completions and 50 chat requests per month, limited agent use, Copilot CLI); Pro $10/month ($15 of AI credits); Pro+ $39 ($70); Max $100 ($200). Paid plans include unlimited completions, agent mode, the cloud agent and the CLI. Pro+ and Max can hand tasks to third-party agents (Claude, Codex).
resources.wiki_use: Use it on the M1 tool-comparison table. The Free tier is enough for in-class completions inside VS Code or Codespaces.
resources.notes: Usage-based billing started June 1, 2026 (GitHub blog, May 12, 2026: https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/GitHub-copilot-individual-plans-introducing-flex-allotments-in-pro-and-pro-and-a-new-max-plan/). Copilot CLI docs: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli (link from a GitHub docs page; not opened).

resources.title: Access GitHub Copilot for free as a student (Copilot Student plan)
resources.summary: Verified GitHub Education students activate the free 'Copilot Student' plan from their education benefits settings, and eligibility is rechecked monthly. This is no longer 'free Copilot Pro'. Since March 12, 2026 students cannot hand-pick premium models such as Claude Opus/Sonnet or GPT-5.x. Since June 1 the plan includes 200 monthly AI credits plus unlimited completions. Since June 24 auto model selection is the only option.
resources.wiki_use: Use it for the step-by-step setup on day one, and correct the outdated 'free Copilot Pro for students' claim found in many 2025 guides.
resources.notes: Change log: GitHub Community discussion #189268 'Important Updates to GitHub Copilot for Students' (March 11, 2026, with later updates): https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/189268. Students can upgrade to Pro or Pro+ and keep their other Pack benefits. Docs say the cloud agent is 'available for all paid Copilot plans', and I could not confirm whether the Student plan includes it. Instructors: GitHub docs page 'Access Copilot Pro for free as a teacher or open source maintainer' (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-on-github/set-up-copilot/enable-copilot/set-up-for-teachers-and-os-maintainers) appeared in search results. Apply: https://docs.github.com/en/education/about-github-education/github-education-for-students/apply-to-github-education-as-a-student.

resources.title: GitHub Education and the Student Developer Pack
resources.summary: GitHub Education gives verified students free professional tools, including GitHub Copilot Student and Codespaces, plus the Student Developer Pack's dozens of partner offers (cloud hosting, developer platforms, learning content).
resources.wiki_use: Day-one onboarding: every student applies for GitHub Education, since the course already requires GitHub for project code.
resources.notes: Pack: https://education.github.com/pack. Students page: https://github.com/education/students. Both links came from the fetched page and were not opened. Partner offers change often.

resources.title: Copilot agent mode in the IDE and Copilot cloud agent (formerly coding agent)
resources.summary: Agent mode takes a high-level task, picks which files to edit, makes the edits and runs commands (with approval) in VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Xcode and Eclipse. The cloud agent works in the background on GitHub repos and is started from issues, the mobile app, IDEs, the CLI, MCP or Slack/Jira/Linear, and returns a pull request.
resources.wiki_use: Demo: assign a GitHub issue ('add a cohort-retention chart to the notebook') to the cloud agent and review the PR it opens in class.
resources.notes: Cloud agent docs: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/cloud-agent/start-copilot-sessions (fetched; 'available for all paid Copilot plans'). Tips: https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/tutorials/cloud-agent/get-the-best-results (link only).

resources.title: Getting Started with GitHub Copilot (GitHub Skills exercise)
resources.summary: A free, under-an-hour exercise that runs in a preconfigured Codespace. Students use Copilot to explain, write, plan and develop code while updating a sample school-activities website.
resources.wiki_use: Optional pre-lab. Students who finish it arrive knowing Copilot chat, inline suggestions and Codespaces.
resources.notes: skills.github.com now redirects to GitHub Learn (https://learn.github.com/skills). Codespaces usage on private repos uses Actions or Codespaces minutes. Other Copilot exercises in the org (https://github.com/skills, fetched; licenses not checked one by one): build-applications-w-copilot-agent-mode, expand-your-team-with-copilot (coding agent), integrate-mcp-with-copilot, customize-your-github-copilot-experience, test-and-debug-with-github-copilot, and idea-to-merge-with-the-copilot-app. Each lives at github.com/skills/<name>, and test-and-debug fits the course's verification theme.

resources.title: Build with AI in VS Code (agents, chat, MCP, customization)
resources.summary: VS Code's AI hub: agents in the Chat view or Agents window (the Copilot harness, or Anthropic Claude and OpenAI Codex harnesses), model choice including your own API key or a local model, MCP servers, project instructions, agent skills, plugins, and permissions, approvals and terminal sandboxing.
resources.wiki_use: Default free IDE for students not on Cursor. Link it from the M1 setup page along with the Python and Jupyter extensions.
resources.notes: Agents overview: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/overview. MCP: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers. Copilot setup: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/copilot (links from the fetched page).
