resources.notes: Default branch is 'oct_2024'. The repository is the style guide's website source (about 157 MB, mostly images), so it is linked rather than downloaded. Jon Schwabish (PolicyViz) discusses style guides at https://policyviz.com/2016/11/30/style-guides.

resources.section: Data visualization: practitioners, guides and code
resources.title: VisEval: benchmark for LLM-generated visualizations (code)
resources.summary: Code and data for evaluating whether charts generated by language models are valid, legal for the data and readable, the benchmark behind the VisEval paper already in this folder.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background for the 'audit the AI's chart' activity; its checklist of failure types adapts well to a student rubric.

resources.section: Data visualization: practitioners, guides and code
resources.title: storytelling-with-data: Python/Matplotlib recreations of Knaflic's figures
resources.summary: Notebooks that rebuild figures from 'Storytelling with Data' in Matplotlib, showing the before-and-after decluttering steps in code.
resources.wiki_use: Strong model for a 'declutter this chart with AI, then explain each change' exercise. Link only.
resources.notes: The repository has no LICENSE file (all rights reserved by default), so it was not downloaded.

resources.section: Data visualization: practitioners, guides and code
resources.title: From Data to Viz: a decision tree for choosing charts
resources.summary: Decision tree that leads from the type of data you have to suitable chart types, with a page per chart on caveats and common mistakes. Its sister site is the Python Graph Gallery.
resources.wiki_use: Pair with the FT Visual Vocabulary: one organizes charts by message, the other by data type.
resources.notes: The repository is the website's source (mostly HTML and images), so it was catalogued rather than downloaded.

resources.section: Data visualization: practitioners, guides and code
resources.title: Datawrapper blog: guides to color in data visualization
resources.summary: Practical, well-illustrated posts on using fewer colors, building palettes, color keys and style-guide colors.
resources.wiki_use: Short readings for the design part of M2. Related posts: https://www.datawrapper.de/blog/create-good-color-palettes and https://www.datawrapper.de/blog/colors-for-data-vis-style-guides.

resources.section: Data visualization: practitioners, guides and code
resources.title: Visualization Analysis and Design: course page and lecture slides (CPSC 547)
resources.summary: Tamara Munzner's UBC graduate course built on her textbook 'Visualization Analysis and Design', with free slides on the what-why-how framework, marks and channels, and evaluation.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background for the conceptual framing of M2 (marks and channels, effectiveness rankings).

resources.section: Data visualization: practitioners, guides and code
resources.title: PyNarrative: A Python Library for Data Storytelling
resources.summary: Describes a Python library built on Altair for adding narrative structure (titles, annotations, story steps) to charts.
resources.wiki_use: Optional tool for students who want annotated, story-style charts in their final blog.
resources.notes: The paper's author list was not confirmed in search results; check it before citing.

resources.title: Marketing Analytics for Data-Rich Environments
resources.summary: Widely cited JM review of how marketing analytics evolved and how data-rich environments change models for CRM, the marketing mix, personalization and privacy, ending with a research agenda.
resources.wiki_use: Assigned framing reading for week 1; its sections map onto the course modules and give students a vocabulary for the whole semester.
resources.notes: Citation confirmed on an AMA summary page. Won the 2017 Sheth/JM award per a UMD news page seen in search. No verified open-access copy.

resources.title: Editorial: Marketing Science and Big Data
resources.authors: Chintagunta, P.; Hanssens, D.M.; Hauser, J.R.
resources.summary: Two-page editorial arguing that big data does not replace marketing science; theory, causal identification and managerial relevance still matter.
resources.wiki_use: Short opening reading next to Wedel and Kannan; a good prompt for a discussion on 'data vs. models'.

resources.title: MSI Research Priorities (booklet)
resources.summary: MSI's current priority list from member firms. 'Marketing Analytics: AI, models, measurement, and communication' is the first of four themes, and it includes integrating AI into analytics and combining disparate data sources.
resources.wiki_use: Show on the course home page as evidence of what practitioners say they need: AI, measurement, and communicating results.
resources.notes: The PDF does not state a year range; the upload folder dates it to October 2025. The earlier 2024 announcement (same four themes) is at https://www.msi.org/article/msi-announces-2024-research-priorities/

resources.title: A Strategic Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Marketing
resources.venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 49, 30-50
resources.summary: Open-access framework that sorts AI into mechanical, thinking and feeling types and maps each onto research, STP strategy and the 4Ps.
resources.wiki_use: Gives students an open-access framework for placing each later module (and each AI tool) in the marketing process.
resources.notes: Published online March 2020; issue year 2021.

resources.title: Cutting-Edge Marketing Analytics: Real World Cases and Data Sets for Hands On Learning
resources.authors: Venkatesan, R.; Farris, P.; Wilcox, R.T.
resources.summary: Darden case-based text with technical notes and real datasets on resource allocation, marketing mix, pricing, customer and digital analytics, and dashboards.
resources.wiki_use: Source of case narratives that students can redo in Python; suggested textbook on the old syllabus.
resources.notes: No Python companion found. The O'Reilly page does not say which software the data exercises assume. Free Pearson sample pages appeared in search: https://ptgmedia.pearsoncmg.com/images/9780133552522/samplepages/9780133552522.pdf . O'Reilly Learning is often available through university libraries; check UIUC access.

resources.title: Principles of Marketing Engineering and Analytics (3rd ed.)
resources.authors: Lilien, G.L.; Rangaswamy, A.; De Bruyn, A.
resources.summary: Model-based marketing decision-making text (segmentation, positioning, conjoint, forecasting, CLV, resource allocation) built around the browser-based Enginius software.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background, and a source of model templates that students can rebuild in Python with AI help.
resources.notes: No Python companion found. Its companion software is Enginius (https://www.enginius.biz/), a web platform with segmentation, conjoint, positioning, Bass, CLV, text and network tools; pricing is quote-based and Python is not mentioned.

resources.title: Applying Data Analytics in Marketing
resources.summary: Gies MOOC taught by Unnati Narang, about 16-20 hours with Python demos. Four modules: course intro and causal analysis (experiments, matching, IV, DiD); AI, prediction and ML including LLM applications; user, firm and AI-generated content analysis; and segmentation, conjoint, CLV and churn.
resources.wiki_use: Link as optional video backup for students who want lectures; its module order closely tracks Marketing Analytics.
resources.notes: Year is approximate: the page shows no launch date, but its LLM content suggests a 2024-2025 revision. Rated 4.5/5 (206 reviews) when fetched. Can count toward UIUC degree programs.

resources.title: 10 minutes to pandas (official quick start)
resources.summary: Official quick tour of Series and DataFrame: selection with loc and iloc, missing data, groupby, merge, pivot_table, time series, categoricals, plotting and I/O.
resources.wiki_use: Reference card for the first coding lab; students can ask an AI assistant to explain each code block.
resources.notes: The docs are now pandas 3.x, which changed copy-on-write and default string dtype behavior. Code that LLMs write from older training data may use deprecated 1.x and 2.x idioms, so students should be told to check warnings. (The license is the well-known pandas BSD-3 and was not rechecked on this page.)

resources.title: Plotting and Programming in Python (Software Carpentry)
resources.summary: Twenty-episode workshop lesson for novices using JupyterLab: variables, lists, loops and functions, reading tabular data into DataFrames, and plotting.
resources.wiki_use: Ready-made, openly licensed lesson that can be adapted into the wiki's Python bootcamp pages.
resources.notes: The year reflects the continuously updated lesson, not a fixed edition.

resources.title: Project Jupyter (JupyterLab and Jupyter Notebook)
resources.summary: Home of the notebook format, with JupyterLab, the classic Notebook, JupyterHub, Voila and Jupyter Book; includes a try-in-browser option and install docs.
resources.wiki_use: Background page explaining what a notebook is, since Colab, VS Code and Cursor all run the same .ipynb format.
resources.notes: Try online: https://jupyter.org/try ; install: https://jupyter.org/install . AI option for local JupyterLab users: the Jupyter AI extension (BSD-3-Clause), https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyter-ai , which connects agents such as Claude, Codex, Copilot and Gemini through the Agent Client Protocol.

resources.title: Anaconda Distribution
resources.summary: Bundled Python data-science distribution with conda, Jupyter Notebook and JupyterLab.
resources.wiki_use: Mention as the traditional install path, with the licensing caveat; steer students to Colab or uv first.
resources.notes: Licensing caveat: per its terms, organizations with more than 200 employees or contractors need a paid license unless eligible for free use. Check UIUC's status before recommending. Free alternative: Miniforge (conda-forge only, BSD-3-Clause) at https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge

resources.title: Version Control with Git (Software Carpentry)
resources.summary: Novice lesson on setting up Git, tracking changes, history, .gitignore, GitHub remotes, collaborating, resolving conflicts, licensing, citation and hosting.
resources.wiki_use: Adapt into the wiki's 'Git for your team project' page; the collaboration and conflict episodes fit team blog-plus-code projects.

resources.title: Introduction to GitHub (GitHub Skills exercise)
resources.summary: Self-guided, under-one-hour exercise in the browser: create a branch, commit a file, open and merge a pull request; it ends with a profile README.
resources.wiki_use: First-week graded check-in: each student completes it and submits the resulting repo link.
resources.notes: skills.github.com now redirects to GitHub Learn (https://learn.github.com/skills), which lists further exercises (GitHub Pages, Markdown, Copilot); that catalog did not render on fetch.

resources.title: Quickstart for GitHub Pages
resources.summary: Shortest path to a live site: create a username.github.io repo and publish from a branch. The default pipeline assumes Jekyll and a _config.yml.
resources.wiki_use: Baseline for the plain HTML + JS option: commit hand-written pages or single-file interactive HTML artifacts, and add an empty .nojekyll file to skip Jekyll processing.
resources.notes: The quickstart itself does not mention .nojekyll; that tip comes from Quarto's GitHub Pages guide. Plain HTML gives full control and needs no build step, but you get no built-in navigation, search, cross-references or notebook rendering. Pair it with Pagefind for search.

resources.title: RFM and CLV: Using Iso-Value Curves for Customer Base Analysis
resources.authors: Fader, P.S.; Hardie, B.G.S.; Lee, K.L.
resources.summary: Links RFM summaries to a probability model (Pareto/NBD plus gamma-gamma) so that recency, frequency and monetary value map into CLV through 'iso-value' curves.
resources.wiki_use: Academic anchor that turns M2's descriptive RFM into M4's CLV; instructor background plus a figure to show in class.
resources.notes: The fetched PDF is the authors' February 2005 working-paper version and does not name the journal. Publication in JMR 42(4), 2005, is from instructor knowledge and was not verified here; no DOI seen.

resources.title: Google Analytics demo account
resources.summary: Free, viewer-level access to live GA4 properties (Google Merchandise Store web data and the Flood-It! app) so students can explore standard reports and explorations.
resources.wiki_use: In-class walkthrough of acquisition, engagement and monetization reports before moving to raw data in Python.
resources.notes: Limits: obfuscated data, no export, no Data API access.

resources.title: [GA4] Cohort exploration
resources.summary: Defines cohort settings in GA4: inclusion criteria, return criteria, granularity, and standard, rolling or cumulative calculation.
resources.wiki_use: Concept page for cohort retention; students then build the same table from Online Retail II in pandas.
resources.notes: No verified Python cohort-analysis tutorial was found before the search budget ran out (gap).

resources.title: PyMC-Marketing CLV Quickstart (BG/NBD + Gamma-Gamma) and CLV model notebooks
resources.summary: Uses CDNOW to build an RFM summary with clv.utils.rfm_summary and a train/test split, fits BG/NBD by MAP and MCMC, and computes P(alive) and expected purchases. It then checks the Gamma-Gamma independence assumption, fits Gamma-Gamma and computes discounted CLV with uncertainty intervals.
resources.wiki_use: Main CLV lab notebook. Sibling notebooks cover Pareto/NBD, MBG/NBD, standalone Gamma-Gamma and sBG with cohorts and covariates for subscription settings.
resources.notes: BG/NBD: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/clv/bg_nbd.html. Pareto/NBD: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/clv/pareto_nbd.html. Gamma-Gamma: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/clv/gamma_gamma.html. sBG: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/clv/sbg.html. The quickstart doesn't mention migrating from lifetimes. The rfm_summary definitions of frequency and recency differ from standard RFM scoring, which is worth flagging to students.

resources.title: What is a CDP? (CDP Institute definition)
resources.summary: Industry definition of a CDP as 'software that creates and maintains a persistent, unified customer record that is accessible to other systems', with own-store, warehouse-native (composable) and hybrid deployments.
resources.wiki_use: Short reading for the 'where first-party data lives' lecture; connects identity resolution to the student datasets.
resources.notes: Vendor-neutral industry body, but not academic. Definition labeled as the 2026 version.

resources.title: The Economics of Privacy
resources.authors: Acquisti, A.; Taylor, C.; Wagman, L.
resources.summary: Survey of theory and evidence on the value of protecting versus disclosing personal data. It concludes there is no unified theory, that privacy protection can raise or lower welfare, and that consumers often cannot see how their data is used.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background and an optional reading that frames privacy as a trade-off rather than a compliance checklist.

resources.title: Protecting Personal Information: A Guide for Business
resources.summary: Five plain-language principles for handling customer data: take stock, scale down, lock it, pitch it, plan ahead.
resources.wiki_use: Data-handling rules for the team project (minimize, de-identify, never commit raw PII to GitHub or paste it into chatbots).

resources.title: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)
resources.authors: State of California Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General
resources.summary: Official summary of CCPA/CPRA consumer rights (know, delete, opt out including Global Privacy Control, correct, limit sensitive data) and business obligations.
resources.wiki_use: Reference box on the privacy page; ties opt-out signals to why first-party datasets have gaps.
resources.notes: Last updated Aug 28, 2026 at time of fetch.

resources.title: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), structured text
resources.summary: Searchable article-by-article GDPR text with linked recitals, covering lawful basis (Art. 6), consent (Art. 7), and data-subject rights including erasure, portability and profiling (Arts. 15-22).
resources.wiki_use: Quick lookup when discussing international students' home-market rules and consent-based data collection.
resources.notes: Unofficial; the site links to the authoritative EUR-Lex PDF.

resources.title: Update on Plans for Privacy Sandbox Technologies
resources.summary: Google says Chrome will keep its current approach of user choice on third-party cookies (no deprecation). It is retiring most Privacy Sandbox APIs (Topics, Protected Audience, Attribution Reporting, IP Protection and others) after low adoption, and keeping CHIPS, FedCM and Private State Tokens.
resources.wiki_use: The definitive answer to 'are cookies dead?' as of late 2026. Use it to open the measurement week and explain why first-party data, clean rooms and MMM matter anyway.
resources.notes: privacysandbox.com/news/... now redirects to privacysandbox.google.com. Check the status page (privacysandbox.google.com/overview/status) before class for any later change.

resources.title: Matplotlib Quick start guide (and official cheatsheets)
resources.summary: Official intro to Figure, Axes and Artists, and to the explicit (object-oriented) versus implicit (pyplot) interfaces, plus styling, labels, scales, dates and colormaps.
resources.wiki_use: Teach the fig, ax = plt.subplots() pattern so students can read and fix AI-generated plotting code, which often mixes the two interfaces.
resources.notes: Cheatsheet PDFs: https://matplotlib.org/cheatsheets/cheatsheets.pdf and https://matplotlib.org/cheatsheets/handout-beginner.pdf

resources.title: seaborn user guide and tutorial
resources.summary: Tutorial on statistical graphics: relational, distribution and categorical plots, error bars, regression fits, multi-plot grids, palettes, and the seaborn.objects interface.
resources.wiki_use: Default library for M2 exploratory charts of customer segments; the error-bar chapter supports M3.

resources.title: Plotly Express in Python
resources.summary: High-level px API that builds interactive figures in one call; the figures export to HTML and can be embedded in web pages and Dash apps.
resources.wiki_use: Use for interactive charts in student blog posts and in the GitHub Pages wiki.
resources.notes: The page also promotes Plotly Studio (AI app builder), a commercial product.

resources.title: Vega-Altair: Declarative Visualization in Python
resources.summary: Grammar-of-graphics library built on Vega-Lite; charts are specified as data, encodings and marks and render as interactive web graphics.
resources.wiki_use: Alternative for interactive, web-native charts on the wiki; its declarative specs are easy for LLMs to generate and for students to read.
resources.notes: Gallery: https://altair-viz.github.io/gallery/index.html

resources.title: Visualization Curriculum (interactive Altair notebooks)
resources.authors: UW Interactive Data Lab (Heer, J. et al.)
resources.summary: Seven Colab-ready notebooks teaching visualization principles through Altair: marks and encodings, transforms, scales and legends, multi-view composition, interaction, maps, plus a debugging guide.
resources.wiki_use: Embed one notebook (marks and encoding) as an in-class activity on encoding choices.
resources.notes: Year approximate; not confirmed on the page.

resources.title: The Python Graph Gallery
resources.summary: Hundreds of reproducible matplotlib, seaborn, plotly and plotnine examples grouped by chart purpose (distribution, correlation, ranking, flow), following the Data-to-Viz classification.
resources.wiki_use: Go-to reference: students find a chart type here, then ask an AI assistant to adapt the code to their own data.
resources.notes: Site source at https://github.com/holtzy/The-Python-Graph-Gallery (0BSD). Repo size not checked, so no download entry.

resources.title: From Data to Viz
resources.summary: Decision tree for choosing a chart from the data type, with 'common mistakes' notes per chart and a caveats gallery (pie charts, cut y-axes, overplotting, rainbow palettes), linked to Python code.
resources.wiki_use: In-class exercise: given a marketing question and dataset, pick the chart with the tree and defend the choice.

resources.title: Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction
resources.summary: Practical introduction to the why and how of good graphics, from perception and honesty to workflow, with a full draft readable online.
resources.wiki_use: Assign Chapter 1 ('Look at data') for perception and honesty principles; skip the R code.
resources.notes: Code is R/ggplot2, not Python. The online text is a 2018-04-25 draft. The full subtitle and the free-access status are from instructor knowledge; the page shows purchase links but no license.

resources.section: Communicating results: Pyramid Principle, SCQA, storytelling
resources.title: storytelling with data: a data visualization guide for business professionals
resources.summary: Business-oriented guide to context, choosing visuals, removing clutter, focusing attention and telling a story. The companion site adds free makeovers, a chart guide, a podcast and sample chapters.
resources.wiki_use: Core M2 reading for the blog-post deliverable; use SWD 'makeovers' as before-and-after critique exercises.
resources.notes: Year and publisher (2015, Wiley) are from instructor knowledge; the books page links to Wiley but shows no dates. Free chart guide: https://www.storytellingwithdata.com/chart-guide . Workbook 'let's practice!' has exercise solutions on the site.

resources.title: SWD + AI: data storytelling with AI
resources.authors: storytelling with data (Knaflic, C.N. et al.)
resources.summary: Free guide, videos and blog series on using AI as a 'thought partner' for data storytelling. It compares five AI tools on one dataset and shows that prompting with SWD principles improves AI-made graphs.
resources.wiki_use: Lab: students get a default chart from Gemini or ChatGPT, then re-prompt it with SWD principles and compare.
resources.notes: Year approximate; one part of the blog series was marked 'coming soon' when fetched.

resources.title: The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (2nd ed.)
resources.summary: Classic on graphical integrity, data-ink, chartjunk and small multiples (1st ed. 1983, 2nd ed. 2001).
resources.wiki_use: Short excerpts on the lie factor and data-ink ratio; students critique an AI-generated chart against Tufte's rules.

resources.section: Communicating results: Pyramid Principle, SCQA, storytelling
resources.title: The Minto Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing, Thinking and Problem Solving
resources.summary: The source text on top-down, answer-first business writing: a governing thought supported by MECE groups of ideas, opened with the Situation-Complication-Question framework.
resources.wiki_use: Core reading for M2's communication unit and the template for every project blog post and in-class readout.
resources.notes: The 1996 revised edition is the authoritative one (originally 1987; the Pearson reissue is not the revised text, per Minto). Her site calls the intro the 'SCQ Framework'; SCQA adds the Answer. The official online course costs $1,200. No free official summary.

resources.section: Communicating results: Pyramid Principle, SCQA, storytelling
resources.title: Barbara Minto: 'MECE: I invented it, so I get to say how to pronounce it'
resources.summary: Free interview in which Minto explains the pyramid (summary point over logically grouped ideas), the origin of MECE, and why thinking comes before slides.
resources.wiki_use: Free, authoritative 10-minute primer to assign in place of the book.
resources.notes: Publication date not shown on the page; the year field is the fetch year, not the publication year.

resources.section: Communicating results: Pyramid Principle, SCQA, storytelling
resources.title: Minto Pyramid (Untools)
resources.summary: One-page summary with an example: start with the conclusion (BLUF), give key supporting points, then supporting data.
resources.wiki_use: Embed as the quick-reference card; students run their draft blog post through its three steps.
resources.notes: Does not cover SCQA. All rights reserved, so link rather than copy.

resources.section: Communicating results: Pyramid Principle, SCQA, storytelling
resources.title: Minto Pyramid & SCQA (ModelThinkers)
resources.summary: Summary of SCQA (situation, complication, question, answer) as the pyramid's introduction, with action-statement recommendations and MECE support; notes the limits of answer-first framing.
resources.wiki_use: Short SCQA explainer; the free preview covers the key structure.
resources.notes: Partly paywalled (members-only sections, US$5/month). No fully open SCQA summary was verified (gap).

resources.section: Communicating results: Pyramid Principle, SCQA, storytelling
resources.title: The Cognitive Style of PowerPoint: Pitching Out Corrupts Within
resources.summary: Essay ($5 PDF) arguing that bullet-outline slideware weakens reasoning and distorts statistical analysis.
resources.wiki_use: Counterpoint reading in the communication unit, and a reason the course uses a blog post instead of a deck.
resources.notes: Year from memory (2nd ed. 2006); the page does not show it. For examples of consulting-style action titles, Analyst Academy keeps a free list of 600+ public consulting decks: https://www.theanalystacademy.com/consulting-presentations/ (verified; the site promotes paid courses).

resources.section: Communicating results: Pyramid Principle, SCQA, storytelling
resources.title: Advice to aspiring data scientists: start a blog
resources.summary: Widely shared essay on why public analysis blog posts build skills, a portfolio and feedback, and why not to wait for an audience.
resources.wiki_use: Motivation reading when introducing the blog-post-plus-GitHub project format.
resources.notes: The fetch confirmed the author and content; the title and 2017 date are from memory, not shown in the fetched text.

resources.section: Communicating results: Pyramid Principle, SCQA, storytelling
resources.title: Creating a Blog (Quarto) and Publishing to GitHub Pages
resources.summary: How to create a Quarto blog (quarto create project blog) whose posts can be Jupyter notebooks or .qmd files with frozen outputs, and how to publish it to GitHub Pages.
resources.wiki_use: Recommended toolchain for team blog posts, and a candidate engine for the course wiki itself.
resources.notes: GitHub Pages guide (verified): https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html . Three options: render to docs/, 'quarto publish gh-pages', or a GitHub Action; use freeze: auto to avoid re-running notebooks in CI.

resources.title: Communicating with Interactive Articles
resources.authors: Hohman, F.; Conlen, M.; Heer, J.; Chau, D.H.
resources.summary: Review of research on interactive articles (details-on-demand, prediction prompts, simulations, personalization) and the evidence on when interactivity helps or costs too much.
resources.wiki_use: Design reference for the interactive HTML wiki, and inspiration for ambitious team blog posts.

resources.title: LIDA: A Tool for Automatic Generation of Grammar-Agnostic Visualizations and Infographics using Large Language Models
resources.summary: Microsoft Research system that treats visualization as code generation in four stages: a Summarizer that describes the data, a Goal Explorer that proposes questions, a VisGenerator that writes, repairs and filters matplotlib, seaborn or Altair code, and an Infographer.
resources.wiki_use: Explains what Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude do under the hood when they 'make a chart'; run the tutorial notebook in Colab as a demo.
resources.notes: The README warns that LIDA executes generated code, so run it in a sandbox. Maintenance activity unclear. Supports OpenAI, Azure, PaLM, Cohere, Hugging Face and local models via llmx. No error-rate figures were confirmed on the fetched abstract pages.

resources.title: Data Formulator: AI-powered data exploration with visualizations
resources.summary: Open-source app that mixes drag-and-drop encoding with natural-language prompts, so AI agents transform data and build charts while users branch into alternative analyses. Works with OpenAI, Azure, Anthropic or Ollama models.
resources.wiki_use: Hands-on lab: students explore a customer dataset in Data Formulator, then rebuild the best chart in their own notebook code.
resources.notes: Install with 'uvx data_formulator' or pip; runs locally at localhost:5567. Latest stable 0.7 (May 2026), 0.8 beta (Aug 2026). Needs an LLM API key.

resources.title: VisEval: A Benchmark for Data Visualization in the Era of Large Language Models
resources.authors: Chen, N.; Zhang, Y.; Xu, J.; Ren, K.; Yang, Y.
resources.summary: Natural-language-to-visualization benchmark (2,524 queries over 146 databases) with automated checks of validity, legality and readability; it documents recurring LLM chart-generation failures.
resources.wiki_use: Evidence for the course rule that AI-made charts must be checked; turn its three criteria into a rubric for student chart audits.
resources.notes: The arXiv page lists no peer-reviewed venue; publication in IEEE TVCG (VIS 2024) is believed but was not verified.

resources.title: How Good (Or Bad) Are LLMs at Detecting Misleading Visualizations?
resources.summary: Tests four multimodal LLMs with nine prompting strategies on misleading real-world charts (up to 21 issue types). Detection is promising but depends heavily on the prompt.
resources.wiki_use: Exercise: students ask an AI to critique a deliberately misleading chart (truncated axis, dual axis) and compare its answer with their own.

resources.title: DABStep: Data Agent Benchmark for Multi-step Reasoning
resources.summary: Benchmark of over 450 real-world data-analysis tasks that combine tables with documentation. At launch (Feb 2025) the best agent scored only 16% on hard tasks (o3-mini; Claude Sonnet 12%).
resources.wiki_use: A sobering number for students: AI agents handle easy descriptive analysis but often fail multi-step business questions, so verify.
resources.notes: Leaderboard: https://huggingface.co/spaces/adyen/DABstep (scores have since risen; check the current state before citing). Google's Colab agent claimed 4th place in March 2025. Earlier, more optimistic baseline: Cheng, Li and Bing (2023), 'Is GPT-4 a Good Data Analyst?', https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15038 (verified).

resources.title: The Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and Causality, Chapter 13: Regression
resources.venue: Chapman & Hall/CRC (free web edition at theeffectbook.net)
resources.summary: Non-technical regression chapter: error terms and exogeneity, how to read a regression table, binary and categorical predictors, polynomials and log transforms, interactions, and a section titled 'Your Standard Errors Are Probably Wrong'. It has code in R, Stata and Python (statsmodels formula API plus stargazer).
resources.wiki_use: Core reading for the M3 review. The Python snippets can seed a first Colab warm-up that students then extend with an AI assistant.
resources.notes: The site says the web version 'will continue to be free'. No license is stated for the text. Print edition is from CRC Press (2021).

resources.title: Causal Inference: The Mixtape, Chapter 2: Probability and Regression Review
resources.summary: Review of probability, expectation and variance, the population regression model, OLS estimation and goodness of fit, the law of iterated expectations, CEF properties and the regression anatomy theorem. It includes Python code blocks (numpy, pandas, statsmodels, plotnine) alongside R and Stata.
resources.wiki_use: Optional deeper reading for students who want the 'why' behind OLS. The regression-anatomy Python example works as an in-class demo.
resources.notes: The online site is labeled the in-progress second edition and does not state access terms, but it is openly readable. The publisher (Yale University Press, 2021) is from recollection, not shown on the page.

resources.title: Regression and Other Stories
resources.authors: Gelman, A.; Hill, J.; Vehtari, A.
resources.license: PDF free to view and download for personal use only (no redistribution or derivatives). The code repo states no license.
resources.summary: Applied regression textbook with a free official PDF and R code and data for every example. It covers linear regression, transformations, interactions, logistic regression and causal inference.
resources.wiki_use: Link specific chapters (log transforms, interactions, and the predictive checks used as diagnostics) as optional reading. A good exercise is to have an AI assistant port an R example to Python and then check the port against the book's output.
resources.notes: Use the official site, which carries the latest corrections. Don't mirror the PDF or the code, because the license allows personal use only and the code has no license.

resources.title: Linear Regression in Python (QuantEcon lecture)
resources.authors: QuantEcon (Sargent, T. J.; Stachurski, J., series editors)
resources.venue: QuantEcon: Intermediate Quantitative Economics with Python
resources.summary: Worked lecture on the Acemoglu-Johnson-Robinson data: simple and multivariate OLS with statsmodels, omitted variable bias, side-by-side tables with summary_col, and 2SLS with linearmodels IV2SLS. It also explains why manual two-stage regression gives wrong standard errors.
resources.wiki_use: Short model notebook for regression syntax and tables. The default 'nonrobust' standard errors make it a good prompt for the robust-SE discussion.
resources.notes: Robust standard errors are not covered, and the output shows 'nonrobust' covariance. A copy also appears at https://stats.quantecon.org/ols.html (seen in search). The year comes from a 2017 QuantEcon announcement; the lecture is updated continuously.

resources.title: Coding for Economists: Regression
resources.summary: Practical Python regression chapter built mainly on pyfixest. It covers HC robust and one- and two-way clustered SEs, categorical and high-dimensional fixed effects, interactions and polynomials, log and asinh transforms, and IV, with statsmodels shown for comparison.
resources.wiki_use: Best single 'how do I do X in Python' reference for M3. Assign it as the syntax companion to The Effect.
resources.notes: The page states the book is under an MIT license. The GitHub source repo was not checked.

resources.title: statsmodels OLSResults.get_robustcov_results: HC0-HC3, cluster, HAC and panel covariance options
resources.summary: Reference for every cov_type in statsmodels: HC0-HC3, cluster (CRV1, with integer 'groups'), cluster-crv3, cluster-jk, HAC (maxlags), hac-groupsum (Driscoll-Kraay) and hac-panel.
resources.wiki_use: Cheat sheet for an exercise. Students take AI-generated statsmodels code, which usually keeps the default nonrobust SEs, and re-estimate with HC3 and clustered SEs to see how the inference changes.
resources.notes: In practice the same options are usually passed via fit(cov_type=..., cov_kwargs=...).

resources.title: PyFixest: fast high-dimensional fixed-effects regression in Python (quickstart, tutorials, llms.txt and agent skill file)
resources.summary: Python port of R's fixest. It offers feols, fepois, feglm and quantreg with multi-way fixed effects; iid, HC1-HC3, CRV1/CRV3, Newey-West and Driscoll-Kraay vcov; wild cluster bootstrap; DiD and event-study estimators; and etable regression tables. The docs site publishes llms.txt and a ready-made skill file meant to be saved as SKILL.md or Agent.md so LLM coding tools write correct PyFixest code.
resources.wiki_use: Recommended regression package for the course. Have teams add the provided skill file (https://pyfixest.org/skills.llms.md) to their project repo before using Claude Code or Cursor, then require them to state and justify their vcov choice.
resources.notes: Repo: https://github.com/py-econometrics/pyfixest (MIT). The skill page lists vcov options but does not say what the defaults are. Check the API docs before telling students the defaults; fixest-style packages often cluster by the first fixed effect when FEs are present. HC2 and HC3 are not supported with FEs or IV.

resources.title: linearmodels: panel data, instrumental variables and system regression for Python
resources.summary: Adds estimators missing from statsmodels: PanelOLS (one- and two-way FE), RandomEffects, FirstDifferenceOLS, BetweenOLS, Fama-MacBeth, AbsorbingLS, IV2SLS/LIML/GMM, SUR and 3SLS, plus Hausman, Kleibergen-Paap and Pesaran CD diagnostics.
resources.wiki_use: Alternative to pyfixest for panel examples. It is also what QuantEcon uses for IV.
resources.notes: License (NCSA) taken from the GitHub repo page https://github.com/bashtage/linearmodels. The maintainer name is from recollection.

resources.title: When Should You Adjust Standard Errors for Clustering?
resources.authors: Abadie, A.; Athey, S.; Imbens, G. W.; Wooldridge, J. M.
resources.venue: Quarterly Journal of Economics (NBER Working Paper 24003, 2017)
resources.summary: Argues that clustering is a design question. Clustered SEs are needed when sampling is two-stage or when treatment assignment is correlated within clusters, and the paper proposes less conservative estimators for intermediate cases.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background for the 'at what level should I cluster?' slide. Also gives students a rule to apply when an AI tool clusters 'by everything'.
resources.notes: QJE publication is suggested by search results; the volume, pages and DOI were not verified. The arXiv page was fetched.

resources.title: A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference
resources.authors: Cameron, A. C.; Miller, D. L.
resources.summary: Standard practitioner reference on cluster-robust SEs. It covers why default SEs overstate precision, FE with clustering, choosing the cluster level, two-way clustering, few-cluster corrections and the wild cluster bootstrap.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor-only reference. Sections on few clusters and choosing clusters can back short wiki call-outs.
resources.notes: The journal and year come from the PDF filename (JHR 2015). Volume and pages were not checked.

resources.title: The garden of forking paths: Why multiple comparisons can be a problem, even when there is no 'fishing expedition' or 'p-hacking' and the research hypothesis was posited ahead of time
resources.summary: Shows that data-dependent analysis choices (exclusions, codings, subgroups, interactions) invalidate p-values even without deliberate fishing. Remedies include preregistration, replication and multilevel modeling.
resources.wiki_use: Framing reading for 'vibe coding' risks. AI agents make it nearly free to try dozens of specifications, so students should log every specification an AI tool ran and report all of them.
resources.notes: The link redirects from stat.columbia.edu to sites.stat.columbia.edu; the final URL is used here.

resources.section: Marketing applications: elasticities and response models
resources.title: Regression example: log transformation and additional predictors (beer sales, own- and cross-price elasticities)
resources.authors: Nau, R. (Duke Fuqua School of Business)
resources.summary: Business-school worked example. A log-log regression of 18-pack beer sales on price gives an own-price elasticity of about -6.7, and adding other carton sizes' prices yields cross-price elasticities. It also explains reading log-unit errors as percentages.
resources.wiki_use: Interpretation reference for the log-log and elasticity lesson. Students reproduce the example in statsmodels or pyfixest with AI help and check that they get the same coefficients.
resources.notes: The original uses Excel/RegressIt, not Python. The transformation details are on the linked 'part 3' page.

resources.section: Marketing applications: elasticities and response models
resources.title: New Empirical Generalizations on the Determinants of Price Elasticity
resources.authors: Bijmolt, T. H. A.; van Heerde, H. J.; Pieters, R.
resources.summary: Meta-analysis of published price elasticities and of what drives their size (category, data type, model specification, estimation method).
resources.wiki_use: Benchmark for sanity-checking student estimates. If a regression returns a price elasticity of +0.3 or -15, that is a red flag.
resources.notes: The landing page has metadata only, with no abstract or DOI. The often-quoted mean elasticity of about -2.6 is from recollection; check it in the paper before quoting.

resources.section: Marketing applications: elasticities and response models
resources.title: Meta-Analysis of Advertising Effectiveness: New Insights from Improved Bias Corrections
resources.authors: Korkames, J.; Stanley, T. D.; Stremersch, S.
resources.venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing 43(1), 131-151
resources.summary: Meta-analysis of 538 B2C own-brand advertising elasticities. Modern publication-bias corrections cut the mean effect more than fivefold (short-term about 0.0008, long-term about 0.03), in line with RCT evidence, and internet advertising shows the highest elasticity.
resources.wiki_use: Use it with a log-log sales response regression to discuss why observational ad elasticities run high (endogeneity and publication bias).
resources.notes: The Erasmus repository offers the final PDF under the Dutch 'Article 25fa' (Taverne) provision. The classic benchmark is Sethuraman, Tellis & Briesch (2011): 872 estimates with a mean short-term elasticity of 0.12 (https://scholar.smu.edu/business_marketing_research/12; SSRN doi 10.2139/ssrn.1866002). Its repository title differs from the published JMR title 'How Well Does Advertising Work?'.

resources.section: Marketing applications: elasticities and response models
resources.title: TV Advertising Effectiveness and Profitability: Generalizable Results from 288 Brands
resources.authors: Shapiro, B. T.; Hitsch, G. J.; Tuchman, A. E.
resources.summary: Regression-based estimates of TV ad elasticities for 288 CPG brands. Elasticities are much smaller than prior literature, many are insignificant, and marginal ROI is negative for over 80% of brands.
resources.wiki_use: Flagship case for 'advertising response as regression'. Students can read the Kellogg Insight summary (https://insight.kellogg.northwestern.edu/article/tv-advertising-is-usually-not-worth-it).
resources.notes: Published in Econometrica (2021); the SSRN page does not name the journal. The study covers 288 brands. A related NBER paper, 'Generalizable and Robust TV Advertising Effects' (w27684), also exists.

resources.section: Marketing applications: elasticities and response models
resources.title: Market Response Models: Econometric and Time Series Analysis
resources.authors: Hanssens, D. M.; Parsons, L. J.; Schultz, R. L.
resources.summary: Classic monograph on sales response functions: functional forms (linear, multiplicative/log-log, saturation), carryover, and econometric and time-series estimation of marketing-mix effects.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background for the 'sales response models' framing. Assign individual chapters through the UIUC library if needed.
resources.notes: Edition and year (2nd ed., 2001) are from recollection; the Springer page was not fetched.

resources.section: Marketing applications: elasticities and response models
resources.title: Bayesian Methods for Media Mix Modeling with Carryover and Shape Effects
resources.authors: Jin, Y.; Wang, Y.; Sun, Y.; Chan, D.; Koehler, J.
resources.summary: Foundational paper on modern MMM. A regression of sales on adstocked (carryover) and saturated (shape) media spend, estimated with Bayesian methods, showing that priors dominate in small samples and the optimal mix is highly uncertain.
resources.wiki_use: Bridge from 'MMM is just a regression with transformed regressors' to modern Bayesian MMM tools.
resources.notes: Google's open-source follow-up is Meridian (https://github.com/google/meridian, Apache-2.0), with a getting-started Colab at https://developers.google.com/meridian/notebook/meridian-getting-started.

resources.section: Marketing applications: elasticities and response models
resources.title: PyMC-Marketing: Additive vs Log vs Log-Log MMMs (and the end-to-end MMM example)
resources.summary: Compares additive, log-link and log-log MMM specifications with adstock and saturation on synthetic weekly data. It explains when log-log channel coefficients can be read as elasticities and when they are semi-elasticities, then compares ROAS and budget plans against the known truth.
resources.wiki_use: Connects M3's log-log interpretation to MMM. The repo also ships AI-agent folders (.claude, .cursor, skills/mmm-modeling) and links to MMM-GPT, so it can serve as a guided vibe-coding exercise.
resources.notes: End-to-end example: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/mmm/mmm_example.html. The contents of the skills folder could not be inspected because GitHub blocked the fetch. The notebook path inside docs/source is presumed, so confirm it before mirroring.

resources.title: Are Large Language Models Good Statisticians?
resources.authors: Zhu, Y.; Du, S.; Li, B.; Luo, Y.; Tang, N.
resources.summary: StatQA benchmark (11,623 examples) on choosing and applying hypothesis tests. GPT-4o reached only about 65%. LLMs mostly make applicability errors (using a method whose assumptions fail), whereas humans mostly confuse task types.
resources.wiki_use: Supports a rule for the wiki: make the AI state each method's assumptions and check them on the data before trusting its test or regression.
resources.notes: Venue confirmed on the NeurIPS 2024 virtual site (poster, Datasets and Benchmarks Track).

resources.title: Are LLMs Capable of Data-based Statistical and Causal Reasoning? Benchmarking Advanced Quantitative Reasoning with Data
resources.authors: Liu, X.; Wu, Z.; Wu, X.; Lu, P.; Chang, K.-W.; Feng, Y.
resources.summary: QRData has 411 questions on real data sheets from textbooks, courses and papers. The best model (GPT-4) got 58%, and models were weakest on data analysis and on combining causal knowledge with the data.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background, and a source of realistic 'check the AI' questions for in-class activities.

resources.subtopic: AI pitfalls: evaluated LLM statistical code
resources.title: StatLLM: A Dataset for Evaluating the Performance of Large Language Models in Statistical Analysis
resources.authors: Song, X.; Lee, L.; Xie, K.; Liu, X.; Deng, X.; Hong, Y.
resources.summary: Open dataset of statistical-analysis tasks with verified reference SAS code, LLM-generated code (ChatGPT 3.5 and 4.0, Llama 3.1), and expert ratings of correctness, effectiveness, readability, executability and output accuracy.
resources.wiki_use: Template for a course rubric to grade AI-written regression code on whether it runs, gives the right numbers and is read correctly.
resources.notes: The code evaluated is SAS, not Python. The value for the course is the evaluation design rather than the code.

resources.title: xlogit: GPU-accelerated multinomial and mixed logit estimation in Python
resources.summary: Estimates MNL, conditional logit and mixed logit (normal, lognormal, triangular, uniform and truncated-normal mixing), handles panel and unbalanced data with Halton draws, fits WTP-space models, and runs on GPU via CuPy when available.
resources.wiki_use: Estimation engine for the CBC exercise. The WTP-space notebook (yogurt data ported from R logitr) shows WTP estimated directly, and a Colab-ready mixed logit notebook is provided.
resources.notes: WTP-space notebook: https://xlogit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/wtp_space.html. Colab: https://colab.research.google.com/github/arteagac/xlogit/blob/master/examples/mixed_logit_model.ipynb. An older alternative is pylogit (BSD-3, https://github.com/timothyb0912/pylogit), which covers MNL, nested and normal-mixing mixed logit and has notebooks in examples/; its maintenance status is unclear.

resources.title: Biogeme: maximum likelihood (and Bayesian) estimation of discrete choice models
resources.license: Distributed free of charge (no license named on the site)
resources.summary: Mature discrete choice estimation package built on pandas. Version 3.3.5 adds JAX-based evaluation, Bayesian estimation and richer diagnostics, alongside an examples gallery, a primer and YouTube tutorials.
resources.wiki_use: Pointer for students who want nested or cross-nested logit or latent-class choice models beyond xlogit.
resources.notes: Requires Python 3.12 or later (pip install biogeme). The site asks users to cite the Biogeme primer.

resources.title: Choice-Learn: discrete choice modeling with large datasets
resources.summary: Python library with conditional logit, nested logit and neural random-utility models (RUMnet, TasteNet), plus assortment and pricing optimization on top of fitted choice models (needs Gurobi or OR-Tools).
resources.wiki_use: Extension for teams linking conjoint or choice estimates to assortment and price optimization. The intro notebooks make a clean clogit tutorial.
resources.notes: Notebooks of interest: notebooks/introduction/3_model_clogit.ipynb and notebooks/auxiliary_tools/assortment_example.ipynb.

resources.title: PyMC-Marketing customer choice notebooks: Multinomial Logit and the IIA property (plus mixed logit, nested logit, MaxDiff)
resources.summary: Bayesian MNL on heating-system choice data, with counterfactual market-share simulations: raising one product's price and removing a product. It shows IIA's proportional substitution and motivates nested logit. Sibling notebooks cover mixed logit, nested logit, consideration sets, MaxDiff and Bayesian BLP.
resources.wiki_use: Market-simulator demo: change a price and watch shares move. It also gives a concrete, visible case of IIA's proportional-substitution problem.
resources.notes: The MNL notebook does not compute WTP; add -beta_attribute/beta_price yourself. Mixed logit: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/customer_choice/mixed_logit.html. MaxDiff: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/customer_choice/maxdiff.html. A simpler PyMC gallery version on the same heating data: https://www.pymc.io/projects/examples/en/latest/generalized_linear_models/GLM-discrete-choice_models.html.

resources.title: cbcTools and logitr: R packages for designing choice-based conjoint surveys and estimating preference- and WTP-space logit models
resources.venue: CRAN; logitr described in Journal of Statistical Software 105(10)
resources.summary: cbcTools covers profile generation, priors, random and D-optimal design (labeled, no-choice and dominance-removed), checks for balance, overlap and D-error, simulated choices, and power analysis. logitr fits MNL and mixed logit in preference or WTP space and predicts shares.
resources.wiki_use: The cleanest end-to-end CBC design workflow. Use it with R, or have students ask an AI assistant to reproduce a cbcTools design in Python and compare D-errors.
resources.notes: logitr docs: https://jhelvy.github.io/logitr/. The DOI is for the logitr JSS article.

resources.title: PyDOE: Design of Experiments for Python (successor to pyDOE3)
resources.summary: Python DOE toolkit covering full and fractional factorial, response-surface, space-filling (Latin hypercube, Sobol), optimal, Taguchi and sequential designs.
resources.wiki_use: Generate full or fractional factorial profile sets for a toy conjoint. For real CBC choice-set designs, prefer cbcTools or a survey platform.
resources.notes: pyDOE3 (https://github.com/relf/pyDOE3) is archived and its README tells users to migrate to pydoe/pydoe. pyDOE3 documented optimal designs (Fedorov, DETMAX; D, A and I criteria); confirm the same functions exist in PyDOE.

resources.title: Sawtooth Software Lighthouse Studio (CBC, ACBC, MaxDiff, HB estimation, market simulator)
resources.summary: Industry-standard conjoint and MaxDiff platform with CBC, Adaptive CBC, HB estimation and a market simulator for product, price and competitor scenarios. A free starter account is available.
resources.wiki_use: Industry reference point and demo. Its technical-papers library (CBC, HB, market simulators, design) is excellent free instructor background.
resources.notes: Academic access: the site lists 'Student Grants' (studentgrants@sawtooth.com) but has no public page for it, so email them about course licenses. Technical papers: https://sawtoothsoftware.com/resources/technical-papers. The home page mentions an 'AI follow-up' survey element; no synthetic-respondent feature was seen. Checked 2026-10-23: Lighthouse Studio is a quote-priced annual license with a free trial and academic discounts. The free tier (up to 50 respondents) is Sawtooth Discover, a different product.

resources.title: Conjointly: conjoint analysis for students and academics (fee waiver)
resources.summary: Online survey and conjoint platform. Its free Basic tier allows Generic Conjoint up to 20 responses. An academic fee waiver for students and teachers with an academic email gives a one-year licence with unlimited respondents, excluding panel sampling and paid services.
resources.wiki_use: Easiest way for project teams to field a real CBC. Have students apply for waivers early, since processing can take up to 4 weeks.
resources.notes: Free academic users generally get no support. The site lists an 'API and MCP' resource (https://conjointly.com/api/) that was not inspected. Pricing page: https://conjointly.com/pricing/.

resources.title: Qualtrics Conjoint projects: getting started with choice-based conjoint
resources.summary: Guide to building choice-based conjoint projects in Qualtrics. Conjoint is a separately purchased add-on that needs Choice Based Conjoint and JavaScript permissions, and analysis is capped below 10,000 responses.
resources.wiki_use: Only useful if UIUC's campus Qualtrics license includes the Conjoint add-on. Check with campus IT before recommending it.
resources.notes: Whether UIUC has the add-on was not verified. The page does not describe a simulator.

resources.title: Conjoint Analysis in Consumer Research: Issues and Outlook
resources.summary: Foundational review that brought conjoint analysis into consumer research. It covers preference models, data collection, stimulus construction, estimation and reliability.
resources.wiki_use: Classic citation for the history of conjoint. Instructor background.
resources.notes: The 1990 Journal of Marketing follow-up by the same authors was not verified here.

resources.title: Applied Conjoint Analysis
resources.summary: Comprehensive text in ten chapters: ratings-based and choice-based designs, part-worth estimation, many-attribute methods, and applications to product design, positioning, segmentation, pricing and other marketing-mix decisions.
resources.wiki_use: Main textbook reference for the conjoint unit. Assign chapters through the UIUC library's Springer access.

resources.title: Conjoint Analysis, Related Modeling, and Applications
resources.authors: Hauser, J. R.; Rao, V. R.
resources.venue: Advances in Market Research and Modeling: Progress and Prospects (Kluwer), pp. 141-168
resources.summary: Free review of the field's history, design choices, estimation methods (including HB and adaptive approaches) and applications.
resources.wiki_use: Free assigned reading that complements Rao (2014).
resources.notes: Download link taken from John Hauser's MIT 'Papers & Books' page.

resources.title: Polyhedral Methods for Adaptive Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis
resources.authors: Toubia, O.; Hauser, J. R.; Simester, D. I.
resources.summary: Adaptive question design for CBC that picks each next choice set to shrink the feasible region of part-worths as fast as possible. A key step from classic to optimization- and ML-based conjoint.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background on adaptive design. It also motivates the idea that question design and estimation interact.
resources.notes: Companion review: Toubia, Evgeniou & Hauser (2007), 'Optimization-Based and Machine-Learning Methods for Conjoint Analysis' (https://mitsloan.mit.edu/shared/ods/documents/?PublicationDocumentID=5582). See also Hauser, Eggers & Selove (2019, Marketing Science), 'The Strategic Implications of Scale in Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis' (https://mitsloan.mit.edu/shared/ods/documents/?PublicationDocumentID=5576). Toubia's recent conjoint-adjacent work on LLM digital twins appears below.

resources.title: Economic Valuation of Product Features
resources.authors: Allenby, G. M.; Brazell, J. D.; Howell, J. R.; Rossi, P. E.
resources.summary: Values a product feature as the change in equilibrium profits, using a conjoint-estimated demand system plus competitor and cost data. With digital camera data, this gives very different answers from naive WTP or welfare measures.
resources.wiki_use: Key reading for why the 'WTP = -beta/beta_price' shortcut can mislead. It motivates building market simulators with competitors.

resources.section: LLMs as survey and conjoint respondents
resources.title: Using LLMs for Market Research
resources.authors: Brand, J.; Israeli, A.; Ngwe, D.
resources.venue: Harvard Business School Working Paper 23-062 (SSRN, revised Apr 2026)
resources.summary: Draws many GPT responses per survey question to estimate WTP for product features. Estimates are sometimes close to human studies but often inaccurate and occasionally wrong-signed. Fine-tuning on past surveys helps for new features in the same category but not for new categories or segment differences.
resources.wiki_use: Anchor reading for an exercise in which teams run a synthetic-respondent conjoint with an LLM, compare it with their human CBC, and report where it diverges.
resources.notes: The abstract became more cautious over revisions: the HBS page (https://www.hbs.edu/faculty/Pages/item.aspx?num=63859, July 2024) calls the WTP estimates 'plausible', while the April 2026 SSRN revision says they are often inaccurate. Assign the latest version.

resources.section: LLMs as survey and conjoint respondents
resources.title: Frontiers: Can Large Language Models Capture Human Preferences?
resources.venue: Marketing Science (arXiv preprint 'Can LLMs Capture Human Preferences?')
resources.summary: Asks GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 intertemporal-choice conjoint-style questions across languages. Both models are far less patient than humans, and 'chain-of-thought conjoint' narrows but doesn't close the gap. The authors recommend LLMs for generating hypotheses, not as stand-ins for respondents.
resources.wiki_use: Paired reading with Brand et al. Good for a discussion of when synthetic respondents mislead.
resources.notes: Published in Marketing Science (2024). The DOI could not be confirmed because INFORMS blocked automated access.

resources.section: LLMs as survey and conjoint respondents
resources.title: AI-Human Hybrids for Marketing Research: Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) as Collaborators
resources.authors: Arora, N.; Chakraborty, I.; Nishimura, Y.
resources.summary: Frames LLMs as collaborators in qualitative research (synthetic respondents, interviews, theme coding) and quantitative research (synthetic survey data). Few-shot prompting and RAG improve quality, and a study replication was run with a Fortune 500 food company.
resources.wiki_use: Practitioner-facing JM framework for how to use LLMs in market research, rather than whether to. It fits the M4 synthetic-respondent activity.

resources.section: LLMs as survey and conjoint respondents
resources.title: The Challenge of Using LLMs to Simulate Human Behavior: A Causal Inference Perspective
resources.summary: Shows that LLM-simulated price and attribute experiments are confounded: changing the treatment in a prompt shifts unstated factors, which produces implausible demand curves in a 40-product study. Proposes 'unblinding' (revealing the design) and fine-tuning as fixes.
resources.wiki_use: Required reading before any synthetic conjoint or pricing exercise. It explains why naive prompts give wrong elasticities.

resources.section: LLMs as survey and conjoint respondents
resources.title: Twin-2K-500: A dataset for building digital twins of over 2,000 people based on their answers to over 500 questions
resources.authors: Toubia, O.; Gui, G. Z.; Peng, T.; Merlau, D. J.; Li, A.; Chen, H.
resources.summary: Four-wave survey of 2,058 US participants (demographics, psychological scales, economic preferences, behavioral-economics experiments, and a pricing survey per the paper) with a test-retest wave, released for building and testing LLM persona simulations.
resources.wiki_use: Optional project dataset for teams testing whether LLM 'twins' reproduce individual consumer answers.
resources.notes: 733 MB of Parquet on Hugging Face, so link to it rather than mirroring. The HF card does not mention the pricing survey; the arXiv abstract does.

resources.section: LLMs as survey and conjoint respondents
resources.title: Digital Twins as Funhouse Mirrors: Five Key Distortions
resources.authors: Peng, T.; Gui, G.; Brucks, M.; Merlau, D. J.; Fan, G. J.; Ben Sliman, M.; Johnson, E. J.; et al.; Toubia, O.
resources.summary: Mega-study of 19 preregistered studies and 164 outcomes. Digital twins built from 500+ answers per person beat a generic LLM only slightly and correlate weakly with real answers (mean r = 0.20). Five distortions are documented: insufficient individuation, stereotyping, representation bias, ideological bias and hyper-rationality.
resources.wiki_use: The most current large-scale validation (2025-26) of synthetic respondents. Use it as the critical counterweight in the synthetic-conjoint activity.
resources.notes: A more optimistic 2025 counterpoint is Maier et al., 'LLMs Reproduce Human Purchase Intent via Semantic Similarity Elicitation of Likert Ratings' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338). Its free-text-plus-embedding method reached about 90% of human test-retest reliability on 57 personal-care surveys. Some of its authors work in industry (Wiecki is, from recollection, at PyMC Labs).

resources.section: LLMs as survey and conjoint respondents
resources.title: Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey Data? The Perils of Large Language Models
resources.authors: Bisbee, J.; Clinton, J. D.; Dorff, C.; Kenkel, B.; Larson, J. M.
resources.summary: ChatGPT personas match ANES group averages but show too little variance, yield regression coefficients that differ significantly from the survey's, shift with small prompt changes, and drift over three months.
resources.wiki_use: Open-access critique showing that synthetic samples can get the means right but the regressions wrong, which ties M3 back to M4.
resources.notes: Optimistic counterpart: Argyle et al. (2023), 'Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples', Political Analysis 31(3), 337-351, doi 10.1017/pan.2023.2 (paywalled). Also Horton, Filippas & Manning, 'Homo Silicus', NBER w31122 (https://www.nber.org/papers/w31122).

resources.title: scikit-learn User Guide: Clustering, and Gaussian Mixture Models
resources.summary: Reference for KMeans and MiniBatchKMeans, agglomerative clustering (Ward, complete, average, single), spectral clustering, DBSCAN and HDBSCAN, OPTICS and BIRCH, with a comparison table and evaluation metrics. The mixture chapter covers GaussianMixture, BIC-based selection of k and BayesianGaussianMixture.
resources.wiki_use: Primary API reference for the segmentation lab. The BIC model-selection example answers the 'how many segments?' question.
resources.notes: GMM page: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html. The KMeans section links a silhouette-analysis example for choosing k.

resources.title: Python Data Science Handbook: In Depth: k-Means Clustering (and the following section on Gaussian Mixture Models)
resources.summary: Clear, visual explanation of k-means as EM, its caveats (local optima, choosing k, linear boundaries) and worked examples. The next section extends this to GMMs.
resources.wiki_use: Gentle pre-reading before the segmentation lab. The notebooks can be embedded directly.
resources.notes: The GMM page URL was not fetched separately. Because of the ND clause, mirror the code but link to the prose rather than adapting it.

resources.title: StepMix: latent class and latent profile analysis in Python with a scikit-learn API
resources.summary: Generalized mixture models: latent class analysis for categorical survey items, latent profile (Gaussian) for continuous data, and mixed data with FIML for missing values. It supports 1-, 2- and 3-step estimation with covariates and distal outcomes, plus BIC, AIC, BLRT and cross-validation, and has Colab tutorials.
resources.wiki_use: Latent-class segmentation of survey or attitudinal data as a model-based alternative to k-means. The Colab tutorials can be embedded.
resources.notes: Individual JSS author names were not captured. Cite it from the README's JSS reference.

resources.title: Market Segmentation Analysis: Understanding It, Doing It, and Making It Useful
resources.authors: Dolnicar, S.; Grün, B.; Leisch, F.
resources.summary: Open-access, practitioner-oriented guide to the whole segmentation process: deciding to segment, data, extracting segments (k-means, hierarchical, mixtures), profiling, describing, selecting target segments and customizing the marketing mix, with R examples.
resources.wiki_use: Main segmentation-and-targeting reading. Because the CC BY license allows it, figures and checklists can be adapted into wiki pages with attribution.
resources.notes: The companion R package (MSA on CRAN) was not verified because CRAN blocked the fetch.

resources.title: Bruce Hardie's technical notes on BG/NBD, Pareto/NBD, sBG and Gamma-Gamma models (with Excel implementations)
resources.authors: Fader, P. S.; Hardie, B. G. S.
resources.summary: Free notes and spreadsheets, including 004 (BG/NBD in Excel), 021 (P(alive)), 039 (step-by-step BG/NBD derivation), 025 (Gamma-Gamma model of monetary value, PDF and calibration xlsx), 008/009 (Pareto/NBD) and 017 (sBG with multiple cohorts).
resources.wiki_use: Use the Excel implementations to show the likelihood before switching to Python. The Gamma-Gamma note (https://www.brucehardie.com/notes/025/) is the spend-model reading.
resources.notes: Tutorial handout 'Probability Models for Customer-Base Analysis' (2016): https://www.brucehardie.com/talks/cba_tut_art_16_HO.pdf (all versions at https://www.brucehardie.com/talks.html). CDNOW data: https://www.brucehardie.com/notes/026/ covers 23,570 customers from the Q1 1997 cohort, with the full zip at https://www.brucehardie.com/datasets/CDNOW_master.zip (424 KB) and a one-tenth sample. No license is stated, so link rather than mirror.

resources.title: 'Counting Your Customers' the Easy Way: An Alternative to the Pareto/NBD Model
resources.authors: Fader, P. S.; Hardie, B. G. S.; Lee, K. L.
resources.summary: Introduces the BG/NBD buy-till-you-die model, a far easier-to-estimate alternative to the Pareto/NBD for non-contractual repeat purchasing, illustrated on CDNOW.
resources.wiki_use: Primary academic anchor for the BG/NBD model used in the PyMC-Marketing lab.
resources.notes: The original Pareto/NBD paper (Schmittlein, Morrison & Colombo, 1987, Management Science) was not verified here.

resources.title: lifetimes (archived June 2024): the original Python BTYD package, superseded by PyMC-Marketing
resources.summary: The once-standard Python BG/NBD, Pareto/NBD and Gamma-Gamma library. It was archived read-only on 2024-06-28, and its README names PyMC-Marketing as the successor.
resources.wiki_use: Warning box for the CLV lab. LLM coding assistants trained on older code may still reach for lifetimes or btyd, so require PyMC-Marketing and show the equivalent calls.
resources.notes: btyd (https://github.com/ColtAllen/btyd, Apache-2.0) is also archived (2024-07-21) and says development moved to pymc-marketing. The claim that AI assistants suggest lifetimes is the instructor's teaching point, not a documented finding.

resources.title: CLVTools: probabilistic customer attrition and CLV models in R
resources.authors: Bachmann, P.; Kuebler, N.; Meierer, M.; Naef, J.; Oblander, E. S.; Schilter, P.
resources.summary: R implementation of Pareto/NBD (including time-invariant and time-varying covariates), BG/NBD, GGom/NBD and Gamma-Gamma spending models for non-contractual CLV.
resources.wiki_use: R option for teams that prefer R. It is also the reference implementation for covariate-extended Pareto/NBD.

resources.title: Modeling Customer Lifetime Value
resources.authors: Gupta, S.; Hanssens, D.; Hardie, B.; Kahn, W.; Kumar, V.; Lin, N.; Ravishanker, N.; Sriram, S.
resources.summary: Widely cited review of CLV and customer-equity models (RFM, probability, econometric, persistence and computer-science approaches) and their use in segmentation and in allocating spend across acquisition, retention and cross-selling.
resources.wiki_use: Assigned overview reading that places BTYD models among other CLV approaches.

resources.title: Customer-Based Corporate Valuation for Publicly Traded Non-Contractual Firms
resources.authors: McCarthy, D. M.; Fader, P. S.
resources.summary: Values non-contractual public firms by building acquisition, repeat-purchase and spend models from disclosed customer data, then summing customer lifetime values into firm value.
resources.wiki_use: Case-style extension of CLV to firm valuation. The student-friendly version is McCarthy & Fader's HBR piece.
resources.notes: Student reading: McCarthy & Fader (2020), 'How to Value a Company by Analyzing Its Customers', HBR 98(1), 51-55 (https://hbr.org/2020/01/are-you-undervaluing-your-customers). Subscription-firm version: McCarthy, Fader & Hardie (2017), JM 81(1), 17-35 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1509/jm.15.0519; SSRN https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2701093). Links taken from McCarthy's research page; the task brief's 'non-subscription' wording corresponds to this 'non-contractual' paper.

resources.title: Customer Centricity: Focus on the Right Customers for Strategic Advantage
resources.venue: Wharton School Press (Wharton Executive Essentials), paperback 2nd ed.
resources.summary: Short managerial book (about 150 pages) arguing that firms should identify and focus on their most valuable customers using CLV, with examples such as Starbucks and Nordstrom. The 2020 edition adds a new preface and afterword.
resources.wiki_use: Managerial framing for the CLV module, and a source of discussion prompts for blog-post write-ups.
resources.notes: The original edition dates from 2012 (from recollection). The Wharton School Press URL redirects to Penn Press.

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Uniting the Tribes: Using Text for Marketing Insight
resources.authors: Berger, J.; Humphreys, A.; Ludwig, S.; Moe, W. W.; Netzer, O.; Schweidel, D. A.
resources.summary: Framework paper on how marketers can extract insight from text: text as a reflection of producers versus an influence on audiences, plus a tour of methods from dictionaries to topic models and embeddings.
resources.wiki_use: Assigned opening reading for M5. Its 'what text reflects vs. what text affects' framing can organize the module page.
resources.notes: Citation and DOI confirmed on the AMA press release page. The open PDF is on Columbia's site. Won the 2025 Sheth Foundation/JM Award (per an AMA press-release title seen in search).

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Automated Text Analysis for Consumer Research
resources.summary: A step-by-step methodological guide to dictionary-based and other automated text analysis for consumer research: building constructs, operationalizing them, and checking validity.
resources.wiki_use: Background reading on construct validity for dictionary methods. Its stages (question, data, construct, operationalization, validation) can be reused as a checklist for team projects.
resources.notes: Metadata from IDEAS/RePEc. Full text is subscriber-only, so use UIUC library access. LIWC-22, the commercial dictionary tool used in much of this work, is at https://www.liwc.app/ (paid; Python/R integration mentioned).

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Comparing automated text classification methods
resources.authors: Hartmann, J.; Huppertz, J.; Schamp, C.; Heitmann, M.
resources.venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing 36(1), 20-38
resources.license: CC BY-NC-ND (publisher version, per University of Groningen repository)
resources.summary: Benchmarks lexicon methods against machine-learning classifiers (random forests, SVM, naive Bayes, neural nets and others) across dozens of social media and review datasets, and gives guidance on which to use when.
resources.wiki_use: Reading behind a 'dictionary vs. ML classifier' in-class comparison. Students can rerun a mini version with scikit-learn on Yelp or Amazon reviews.
resources.notes: Pre-LLM benchmark. Pair it with Hartmann et al. (2023) and Krugmann & Hartmann (2024) to show how the ranking of methods changed.

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: More than a Feeling: Accuracy and Application of Sentiment Analysis
resources.authors: Hartmann, J.; Heitmann, M.; Siebert, C.; Schamp, C.
resources.venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing 40(1), 75-87
resources.summary: Shows that sentiment-method accuracy varies widely and that inaccurate sentiment scores can bias downstream marketing conclusions. Transfer learning (fine-tuned RoBERTa) performs best, and the authors release SiEBERT, a ready-to-use model.
resources.wiki_use: Core reading for sentiment. The released SiEBERT model fits in a 3-line Colab demo, so students can compare it with VADER on the same reviews.
resources.notes: Model card: https://huggingface.co/siebert/sentiment-roberta-large-english (binary pos/neg; trained/evaluated on 15 datasets; license not stated on card). Usage: pipeline('sentiment-analysis', model='siebert/sentiment-roberta-large-english'). ScienceDirect blocked fetching, so the article's open-access status is unverified. Metadata confirmed on IDEAS and Univ. Hamburg page.

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Mine Your Own Business: Market-Structure Surveillance Through Text Mining
resources.authors: Netzer, O.; Feldman, R.; Goldenberg, J.; Fresko, M.
resources.summary: Mines forum posts for brand co-mentions to build perceptual and market-structure maps, then compares them with survey and sales-based maps.
resources.wiki_use: Case example linking text to M4 perceptual mapping. Students can replicate a simple brand co-occurrence network from Reddit or review text.
resources.notes: Metadata from IDEAS/RePEc. A natural bridge to the network-analysis part of M5 (co-mention networks).

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Mining Marketing Meaning from Online Chatter: Strategic Brand Analysis of Big Data Using Latent Dirichlet Allocation
resources.summary: Applies LDA to product reviews to extract quality dimensions and their valence, and tracks brand positions on those dimensions over time.
resources.wiki_use: Anchor reading for the topic-modeling lesson. Students run gensim LDA or BERTopic on Amazon Reviews 2023 and compare their output with the paper's quality dimensions.
resources.notes: DOI metadata confirmed via Crossref.

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Identifying Customer Needs from User-Generated Content
resources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (author's final manuscript on MIT DSpace)
resources.summary: Uses a CNN to filter non-informative review sentences and embeddings to cluster the rest, so human analysts can find customer needs in Amazon reviews more efficiently. UGC proves at least as rich a source of needs as interviews.
resources.wiki_use: Case example on human-machine workflows. A natural team-project template: filter reviews with embeddings or an LLM, then have humans code needs.
resources.notes: Plain-language summary for students: https://insight.kellogg.northwestern.edu/article/how-companies-can-mine-online-reviews-for-product-development-gold (seen in search). An updated LLM version of this workflow would make a good team project.

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Text as Data
resources.authors: Gentzkow, M.; Kelly, B.; Taddy, M.
resources.summary: Economics survey of representing text numerically (document-term matrices), dictionary methods, penalized regression, topic models and word embeddings, with applications.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor-only background for the 'text to numbers' lecture. Optional reading for students who want more depth.
resources.notes: DOI metadata confirmed via Crossref. Predates LLMs. For a more recent econ survey see Ash & Hansen (2023), 'Text Algorithms in Economics', Annual Review of Economics 15:659-688, doi 10.1146/annurev-economics-082222-074352 (Crossref-verified).

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Sentiment Analysis in the Age of Generative AI
resources.summary: Compares zero-shot GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama 2 with established transfer-learning sentiment models on marketing text. The LLMs often match or beat them, accuracy depends on data source and text features, and Llama 2 gives the most useful explanations.
resources.wiki_use: Core, accessible reading for the 'LLM as sentiment classifier' lab. Students replicate a mini version (VADER vs. SiEBERT vs. an LLM API) on 200 hand-labeled reviews.
resources.notes: Open access; authors hold copyright.

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Frontiers: Determining the Validity of Large Language Models for Automated Perceptual Analysis
resources.authors: Li, P.; Castelo, N.; Katona, Z.; Sarvary, M.
resources.summary: Tests whether LLM responses can stand in for survey respondents in perceptual mapping. LLM-based brand similarity and attribute ratings agree with human data over 75% of the time.
resources.wiki_use: Bridge between M4 (perceptual maps) and M5: students ask an LLM for brand-similarity judgments and compare the result with a map built from review co-mentions.
resources.notes: Metadata from IDEAS/RePEc. INFORMS press release: https://www.informs.org/News-Room/INFORMS-Releases/News-Releases/Can-Large-Language-Models-Replace-Human-Participants-in-Some-Future-Market-Research (seen in search).

resources.section: LLMs as annotators: methods and validation
resources.title: Correcting Toward the Wrong Target: LLM-Annotated Regressors Under Noisy Human Benchmarks
resources.authors: Overgoor, G.; Knight, S.; Bart, Y.
resources.venue: SMU Cox Marketing working paper / SSRN
resources.summary: Argues that validating LLM labels against noisy human labels can mislead, because corrections pull estimates toward an attenuated target. Uses about 10k TV ads and proposes a diagnostic plus an IV estimator that uses a second human rater.
