resources.wiki_use: Instructor background and an advanced reading that links M3 measurement error to LLM labeling. Shows why human 'gold' labels are not automatically gold.
resources.notes: Working paper (Sept 2025); journal publication not confirmed.

resources.section: LLMs as annotators: methods and validation
resources.title: To Err Is Human; To Annotate, SILICON? Toward Robust Reproducibility in LLM Annotation
resources.authors: Cheng, X.; Mayya, R.; Sedoc, J.
resources.summary: Shows how LLM-based annotation becomes irreproducible when proprietary models are retired, and proposes the SILICON workflow: decompose measurement error, choose open-weight backup models, and route low-confidence labels to auxiliary models.
resources.wiki_use: Reading for the 'non-reproducibility' failure mode. Supports a course rule that teams log the model version, prompt, temperature and date, and keep an open-weight fallback.
resources.notes: Preprint by business-school (NYU Stern) authors; no journal ref listed.

resources.section: LLMs as annotators: methods and validation
resources.title: ChatGPT outperforms crowd workers for text-annotation tasks
resources.authors: Gilardi, F.; Alizadeh, M.; Kubli, M.
resources.summary: On 2,382 tweets, zero-shot ChatGPT beat MTurk crowd workers on four of five annotation tasks, had higher intercoder agreement than crowd workers and trained annotators, and cost under a third of a cent per annotation (about 20 times cheaper).
resources.wiki_use: Short core reading that motivates LLM labeling. Pair it with Reiss (2023) and Baumann et al. (2025) for the cautionary side.
resources.notes: DOI and license confirmed via Crossref. arXiv version: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15056. Results are for ChatGPT as of early 2023, so newer models differ.

resources.section: LLMs as annotators: methods and validation
resources.title: Large Language Models: An Applied Econometric Framework
resources.authors: Ludwig, J.; Mullainathan, S.; Rambachan, A.
resources.summary: Distinguishes prediction uses of LLMs, which need no training leakage, from estimation or measurement uses. For measurement, valid inference requires a small validation sample, because otherwise arbitrary choices such as the model or prompt can change results a lot.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor anchor for the module's validation rule: every LLM-coded variable needs a human-labeled validation subsample. Assign a simplified slide version to students.
resources.notes: The NBER page is open. Was presented at the NBER SI 2026 ML session (conference PDF seen in search).

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Using natural language processing to analyse text data in behavioural science
resources.authors: Feuerriegel, S.; Maarouf, A.; Bär, D.; Geißler, D.; Schweisthal, J.; Pröllochs, N.; Robertson, C. E.; Rathje, S.; Hartmann, J.; Mohammad, S. M.; Netzer, O.; Siegel, A. A.; Plank, B.; Van Bavel, J. J.
resources.summary: Review of the NLP pipeline for behavioral research, from dictionaries through supervised ML to LLMs. Discusses interpretability versus accuracy and gives recommendations for rigor and reproducibility.
resources.wiki_use: Core modern overview reading that updates Berger et al. (2020) for the LLM era. Its pipeline figure can serve as the M5 roadmap.
resources.notes: Published online 4 Feb 2025; volume and pages not verified. Co-authors include marketing scholars Hartmann and Netzer. The open-access PDF is on the Columbia Business School site (seen in search).

resources.section: LLMs as annotators: methods and validation
resources.title: Best Practices for Text Annotation with Large Language Models
resources.summary: Practical guidelines for LLM-based text annotation: model choice, prompt design and iteration, stability testing, validation against human labels, transparency, and ethics.
resources.wiki_use: Basis for an 'LLM annotation checklist' callout on the wiki and for the grading rubric of LLM-coded variables in team projects.
resources.notes: Openly licensed, so short excerpts can be quoted on the wiki with attribution.

resources.section: LLMs as annotators: methods and validation
resources.title: Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference: Design-based Supervised Learning for Social Science Applications of Large Language Models
resources.authors: Egami, N.; Hinck, M.; Stewart, B. M.; Wei, H.
resources.summary: Shows that plugging LLM labels straight into regressions can bias estimates and confidence intervals even at 80-90% accuracy. Proposes DSL, a doubly robust estimator that combines surrogate labels with a random gold-standard subsample.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background and an advanced optional reading on why and how to correct regressions that use LLM-coded variables.
resources.notes: Related: Angelopoulos et al. (2023), 'Prediction-powered inference', Science 382(6671):669-674, doi 10.1126/science.adi6000 (Crossref-verified). The authors' DSL software was not verified here.

resources.section: Failure modes of LLM text analysis
resources.subtopic: Failure modes: prompt sensitivity and consistency
resources.title: Testing the Reliability of ChatGPT for Text Annotation and Classification: A Cautionary Remark
resources.summary: Repeated runs and small prompt or setting changes produce inconsistent ChatGPT classifications, so unsupervised use without validation against human labels is not advisable.
resources.wiki_use: Motivates an in-class exercise: rerun the same LLM classification with 3 prompt wordings and 2 temperatures and measure agreement (Krippendorff's alpha).
resources.notes: See also Atreja et al. (2024), 'Prompt Design Matters for Computational Social Science Tasks but in Unpredictable Ways', https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11980 (likely ICWSM 2025; fetched), and Pangakis et al. (2023), 'Automated Annotation with Generative AI Requires Validation', https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00176 (fetched).

resources.section: Failure modes of LLM text analysis
resources.subtopic: Failure modes: LLM hacking / false conclusions
resources.title: Large Language Model Hacking: Quantifying the Hidden Risks of Using LLMs for Text Annotation
resources.authors: Baumann, J.; Röttger, P.; Urman, A.; Wendsjö, A.; Plaza-del-Arco, F. M.; Gruber, J. B.; Hovy, D.
resources.summary: Across many replicated hypotheses, about 31% of tests using state-of-the-art LLM annotations reached incorrect conclusions, and the risk is highest near significance thresholds. Human annotations were the best safeguard of the 21 mitigations tested.
resources.wiki_use: Key cautionary reading. It links naturally to M6 on p-hacking: changing models or prompts until results look significant is a form of p-hacking.
resources.notes: Preprint (v2, Oct 2025); no journal ref yet.

resources.title: Natural Language Processing with Python: Analyzing Text with the Natural Language Toolkit
resources.authors: Bird, S.; Klein, E.; Loper, E.
resources.venue: nltk.org (online edition updated for Python 3 / NLTK 3)
resources.summary: The free online NLTK book: tokenization, corpora, word frequencies, tagging, text classification and more, in 12 chapters.
resources.wiki_use: Reference reading for the preprocessing lesson (chapters 1-3). Link specific sections rather than assigning the whole book.
resources.notes: The original O'Reilly edition is from 2009 and the online edition was updated for Python 3. Some content is dated, but it remains the canonical NLTK reference. NLTK also bundles VADER (nltk.sentiment.vader).

resources.title: VADER: A Parsimonious Rule-Based Model for Sentiment Analysis of Social Media Text (vaderSentiment)
resources.summary: Lexicon- and rule-based sentiment scorer tuned for social media. It handles negation, intensifiers, punctuation, capitalization, emoticons and slang, and returns compound and pos/neu/neg scores.
resources.wiki_use: First hands-on sentiment demo in Colab (pip install vaderSentiment). Serves as the baseline that transformer and LLM classifiers are compared against.
resources.notes: The paper DOI was confirmed via Crossref. The repo includes the lexicon and the evaluation datasets.

resources.title: Advanced NLP with spaCy (free online course)
resources.summary: Free interactive four-chapter course: finding words, phrases, names and concepts; large-scale data analysis; processing pipelines; and training a neural network model.
resources.wiki_use: Self-paced lab for named-entity recognition (e.g., extracting brands and products from reviews). Link chapter 1-2 as optional homework.
resources.notes: Year approximate, not stated on page. Source: https://github.com/ines/spacy-course (license not checked, so no download). For LLM-backed spaCy components see spacy-llm (MIT, marked experimental): https://github.com/explosion/spacy-llm (fetched).

resources.title: Working With Text Data (scikit-learn tutorial)
resources.summary: Official tutorial on bag-of-words with CountVectorizer, TF-IDF weighting, naive Bayes and linear SVM in a Pipeline, evaluation with classification reports and confusion matrices, and grid search, using 20 Newsgroups.
resources.wiki_use: Template for the in-class TF-IDF classifier activity. Students swap 20 Newsgroups for Yelp star ratings and use an AI assistant to adapt the code.
resources.notes: Living documentation; the year is the current docs version. Its exercises include movie-review sentiment and language identification.

resources.title: LDA Model tutorial (Gensim)
resources.summary: End-to-end LDA on a 1,740-paper NIPS corpus: tokenizing, lemmatizing, bigrams, dictionary filtering, training, and UMass topic coherence.
resources.wiki_use: Classic topic-model lab, paired with Tirunillai & Tellis (2014). Contrast it with BERTopic on the same review corpus.
resources.notes: Gensim is in 'stable maintenance mode' (bug and doc fixes only), per its GitHub README: https://github.com/piskvorky/gensim.

resources.title: BERTopic: Neural topic modeling with a class-based TF-IDF procedure
resources.summary: Modular topic modeling: sentence-transformer embeddings, UMAP, HDBSCAN, then c-TF-IDF topic descriptions. Supports dynamic and semi-supervised topics and LLM-generated topic labels, e.g., via OpenAI models.
resources.wiki_use: Main topic-modeling tool for the course. The README's Colab 'Best Practices' notebook can be embedded as a starting lab, and the LLM labeling step shows the AI angle.
resources.notes: GitHub: https://github.com/MaartenGr/BERTopic (README links about 9 Colab notebooks, including LLM-based ones). The README license badge points to a different repo, so confirm the LICENSE file before redistributing.

resources.title: Sentence Transformers (SBERT) documentation
resources.authors: UKP Lab (TU Darmstadt); maintained by Aarsen, T. (Hugging Face)
resources.summary: Library and docs for computing sentence embeddings and rerankers. Covers semantic search, clustering, paraphrase mining and fine-tuning.
resources.wiki_use: Use for an 'embeddings + k-means' lab that links M4 segmentation to text, e.g., clustering review sentences into customer-need themes.
resources.notes: GitHub: https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers (Apache-2.0).

resources.title: Transformers Pipelines documentation (text-classification, zero-shot-classification)
resources.summary: Reference for pipeline(), the one-line way to run pretrained models for sentiment, text classification, zero-shot classification and more, with batching and GPU options.
resources.wiki_use: Code reference for the sentiment lab. Students run pipeline('sentiment-analysis', model=...) on reviews and tweets in Colab.
resources.notes: Good social-media model: https://huggingface.co/cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment-latest (RoBERTa trained on about 124M tweets and fine-tuned on TweetEval; neg/neu/pos labels; CC-BY-4.0; fetched). For few-label fine-tuning see SetFit (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/huggingface/setfit (fetched).

resources.subtopic: LLM text classification and topic modeling notebooks
resources.title: Hands-On Large Language Models (official code repository)
resources.summary: Colab-ready notebooks for the book's 12 chapters, including Ch. 4 Text Classification (pretrained, embedding-based and generative/prompted approaches), Ch. 5 Text Clustering and Topic Modeling (BERTopic), and Ch. 6 Prompt Engineering.
resources.wiki_use: Embed or adapt Ch. 4-6 notebooks as M5 labs. They run on a free Colab T4 GPU and directly compare classic, embedding and LLM classifiers.
resources.notes: The book itself is paid (O'Reilly); the notebooks are free. Chapter folder names were not verified, so keep chapters 4-6. Year is approximate (book published 2024). Alternative: 'NLP with Transformers' notebooks (Apache-2.0), https://github.com/nlp-with-transformers/notebooks (fetched; some chapters no longer maintained).

resources.title: Introduction to Cultural Analytics & Python
resources.summary: Open online textbook teaching Python to humanities and social science students with song lyrics, news, tweets and Reddit. Covers TF-IDF, sentiment, topic modeling, NER and POS tagging.
resources.wiki_use: Gentle, non-CS-friendly chapters to link from the wiki. A good model for the wiki's own Jupyter Book-style design.
resources.notes: Year is approximate. Pages launch in Binder (Colab not mentioned). Some Twitter-collection chapters predate the X API changes. R alternative: Silge & Robinson, 'Text Mining with R: A Tidy Approach', https://www.tidytextmining.com/ (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 US; fetched). Free course materials from ETH: Elliott Ash's 'NLP for Law and Social Science' repos, e.g. https://github.com/elliottash/nlp_lss_2023 (GPL-3.0; fetched).

resources.section: Text analysis in marketing: anchor papers
resources.title: Text as Data: A New Framework for Machine Learning and the Social Sciences
resources.authors: Grimmer, J.; Roberts, M. E.; Stewart, B. M.
resources.summary: Research-design-first textbook organized around representation, discovery, measurement, prediction and causal inference with text.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor backbone for structuring M5 (discovery vs. measurement vs. prediction). Assign selected chapters, e.g., on validation, through the library.
resources.notes: Paid ($49.95 paperback; ebook formats). No free full text was verified, so check the UIUC library for e-book access.

resources.title: X API pricing (pay-per-usage)
resources.summary: Current X API docs describe only prepaid, pay-per-usage credits: about $0.005 per post read and $0.010 per user read, capped at 3M post reads per month (Enterprise above that), with 24-hour deduplication.
resources.wiki_use: Use in a 'data access reality check' callout: a 10,000-tweet student project costs real money, which is why course labs use Bluesky, Reddit or archived datasets.
resources.notes: Fetched Oct 2026. The intro page (https://docs.x.com/x-api/introduction) says 'No subscriptions—pay only for what you use' and does not describe a free research tier. Prices may change.

resources.title: Reddit Data API Wiki
resources.summary: Official rules for the Reddit Data API: OAuth required (unauthenticated traffic is blocked), 100 queries per minute per OAuth client on the free tier, a descriptive User-Agent, and the Responsible Builder Policy and Data API Terms.
resources.wiki_use: Setup guide for a Reddit-comments lab with PRAW. Students register a script app, then pull a subreddit's posts for sentiment and topic analysis.
resources.notes: Page updated May 11, 2026. Python wrapper: PRAW 8.0.3 docs, https://praw.readthedocs.io/en/stable/. Checked 2026-10-23: even non-commercial Data API use is limited to approved developers after a request and app review, so plan for lead time or use Bluesky's open API for class labs.

resources.title: Bluesky API Directory: public endpoints (no authentication)
resources.summary: Many Bluesky (AT Protocol) endpoints are public and need no authentication via public.api.bsky.app. Bluesky also offers a JSON 'Jetstream' firehose, making it one of the most open major platforms for classroom data collection.
resources.wiki_use: Default platform for live social-media labs: students collect posts on a brand or hashtag with the Python SDK, then run sentiment, topic and reply-network analyses.
resources.notes: Jetstream announcement (Oct 2024; not a formally stable API): https://docs.bsky.app/blog/jetstream. Community Python SDK: https://atproto.blue/en/latest/ (pip install atproto). Main docs: https://docs.bsky.app/. All fetched. Remind students of ethics: public posts are not consent for redistribution.

resources.title: Meta Content Library and Content Library API
resources.summary: Controlled-access research archive of public Facebook and Instagram content (posts, Pages, comments, groups, events and more), with a web UI and an API. Analysis runs in Meta's Secure Research Environment (Python/R JupyterHub) or an approved cleanroom.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor-facing context on post-CrowdTangle research access. Too heavy for a semester project, but useful in a lecture on who can see platform data.
resources.notes: Requires an approved application (via ICPSR or CASD) and agreement to Meta's research terms. The ICPSR page failed to load, so fees and eligibility are not verified. Compute in the SRE is stated as free. Related: TikTok Research API for academic researchers in the US, EEA, UK, Switzerland and Canada (applications take about 4 weeks), https://developers.tiktok.com/products/research-api/ (fetched).

resources.title: YouTube Data API v3: Getting Started (and quota costs)
resources.license: Docs CC BY 4.0; code samples Apache 2.0
resources.summary: How to get an API key and use the YouTube Data API. The default quota is 10,000 units per day; most list calls such as commentThreads.list and videos.list cost 1 unit, and search.list has its own 100-calls-per-day cap.
resources.wiki_use: Easy free source for a comments-sentiment or influencer-video lab. Students pull comments on a brand's or creator's videos and classify them.
resources.notes: Quota table: https://developers.google.com/youtube/v3/determine_quota_cost (fetched Oct 2026; quotas reset at midnight Pacific). Scaled academic access: YouTube Researcher Program, https://research.youtube/ (fetched).

resources.title: Influencer Marketing Effectiveness
resources.authors: Leung, F. F.; Gu, F. F.; Li, Y.; Zhang, J. Z.; Palmatier, R. W.
resources.summary: Empirical study of what drives influencer marketing effectiveness, covering influencer, content, follower and brand factors and how they shape engagement.
resources.wiki_use: Anchor reading for the influencer subsection. Students operationalize its content factors using text and LLM coding of influencer posts or YouTube videos.
resources.notes: DOI metadata confirmed via Crossref; the summary is generic because the abstract was not fetched. Also see Hughes, Swaminathan & Brooks (2019, JM 83(5):78-96), doi 10.1177/0022242919854374 (Crossref-verified). FTC influencer disclosure guidance: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers (fetched).

resources.title: The Effect of Word of Mouth on Sales: Online Book Reviews
resources.summary: Classic differences-in-differences comparison of Amazon and Barnes & Noble reviews, showing that review ratings affect relative book sales and that negative reviews weigh more.
resources.wiki_use: Classic case linking review text and ratings to sales. A good bridge to M6 identification logic.
resources.notes: DOI metadata confirmed via Crossref.

resources.title: The Market for Fake Reviews
resources.authors: He, S.; Hollenbeck, B.; Proserpio, D.
resources.summary: Documents the online market for buying fake Amazon reviews (organized via Facebook groups) and its effects on ratings, sales and product outcomes.
resources.wiki_use: Case for discussing review-data validity before running sentiment on reviews. Pairs with the FTC's 2024 fake-review rule.
resources.notes: DOI metadata confirmed via Crossref; summary is from general knowledge of the paper. Also see Luca & Zervas (2016), 'Fake It Till You Make It', Management Science 62(12):3412-3427, doi 10.1287/mnsc.2015.2304 (Crossref-verified).

resources.title: Federal Trade Commission Announces Final Rule Banning Fake Reviews and Testimonials
resources.summary: Final rule banning fake reviews, including AI-generated ones, insider reviews, review suppression, incentives conditioned on sentiment, and buying or selling fake social media indicators such as bot followers and views.
resources.wiki_use: Short case for an M5/M8 discussion: generative AI makes fake reviews cheap, so what does that mean for review analytics and detection?
resources.notes: Takes effect 60 days after Federal Register publication.

resources.title: NetworkX Tutorial
resources.summary: Official hands-on tutorial: creating graphs, nodes and edges with attributes, directed and multigraphs, generators, file I/O, basic analysis (components, degree, clustering, shortest paths) and drawing.
resources.wiki_use: Code reference for the network lab: build a retweet or reply network from Bluesky, or a brand co-mention network from reviews, then compute degree and betweenness centrality.
resources.notes: Community notebooks at NX-Guides, https://networkx.org/nx-guides/ (fetched), include a 'Facebook network analysis' exploratory notebook (Binder-ready) suitable as a ready-made in-class exercise. NetworkX is BSD-licensed per general knowledge; the license was not stated on the fetched page.

resources.title: Network Analysis Made Simple
resources.summary: Jupyter-notebook course on NetworkX: graph basics, visualization, hubs and paths, structures, bipartite graphs, and case studies (Game of Thrones, airports).
resources.wiki_use: Adapt the hubs/centrality and bipartite (customer-product) notebooks as M5 labs. Bipartite graphs link to recommendation in M7.
resources.notes: Binder supported; Colab not mentioned. The ebook (PDF/EPUB) on LeanPub is paid, but the notebooks are free. Year reflects the live site.

resources.title: Networks, Crowds, and Markets: Reasoning About a Highly Connected World
resources.summary: Introductory, no-prerequisite text that combines economics, sociology and computing. Ch. 16 (information cascades) and Ch. 19 (cascading behavior in networks, thresholds, weak ties) fit WOM and seeding.
resources.wiki_use: Assign Ch. 19 as conceptual reading before the seeding/influencer lecture. Its threshold models can be simulated in NetworkX.
resources.notes: A complete pre-publication draft PDF is free on the page. Alternative: Barabási, 'Network Science', http://networksciencebook.com/ (online; license and access terms not confirmed by fetch).

resources.title: Seeding Strategies for Viral Marketing: An Empirical Comparison
resources.authors: Hinz, O.; Skiera, B.; Barrot, C.; Becker, J. U.
resources.summary: Compares seeding strategies (high-degree hubs, bridges, random) with field experiments and real referral data. Seeding well-connected people can far outperform random seeding.
resources.wiki_use: Core marketing reading for the network subsection. Students simulate hub vs. random seeding on a SNAP network in NetworkX and compare reach.
resources.notes: DOI metadata confirmed via Crossref; summary is from general knowledge of the paper. Related: Goldenberg, Han, Lehmann & Hong (2009), 'The Role of Hubs in the Adoption Process', JM 73(2):1-13, doi 10.1509/jmkg.73.2.1; Trusov, Bucklin & Pauwels (2009), 'Effects of WOM versus Traditional Marketing', JM 73(5):90-102, doi 10.1509/jmkg.73.5.90; Katona, Zubcsek & Sarvary (2011), JMR 48(3):425-443, doi 10.1509/jmkr.48.3.425. All Crossref-verified.

resources.title: Identifying Influential and Susceptible Members of Social Networks
resources.summary: Randomized experiment on Facebook (product adoption via an app) estimating who is influential and who is susceptible to influence, by demographics.
resources.wiki_use: Case example for 'influencers are not just high-degree nodes'. Bridges to M6 on why experiments are needed to separate influence from homophily.
resources.notes: DOI metadata confirmed via Crossref; summary is from general knowledge of the paper. Other Aral work: Aral, Muchnik & Sundararajan (2009), 'Distinguishing influence-based contagion from homophily-driven diffusion in dynamic networks', PNAS 106(51):21544-21549, doi 10.1073/pnas.0908800106; Aral & Dhillon (2018), 'Social influence maximization under empirical influence models', Nature Human Behaviour 2(6):375-382, doi 10.1038/s41562-018-0346-z. Both Crossref-verified.

resources.section: LLMs as annotators: methods and validation
resources.title: Classification with Claude: Insurance Support Ticket Classifier (Claude Cookbook)
resources.summary: Worked notebook comparing simple prompting (74%), retrieval of similar labeled examples (94%) and retrieval plus chain of thought (97%) on a 10-category text classifier. Includes a scikit-learn classification report and confusion matrix, and Promptfoo tests across temperatures.
resources.wiki_use: Template for the M5 'LLM classifier' lab. Students swap in their own label set (e.g., complaint types in reviews), keep the evaluation harness, and report accuracy against human labels.
resources.notes: Uses synthetic data (68 train / 68 test tickets). Requires API keys, so set a classroom budget. Companion guide on when to use an LLM vs. traditional ML and on known failure modes (implicit requests, emotion overriding intent, multi-issue texts): https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/ticket-routing (fetched).

resources.section: Classifying text at scale with LLM APIs
resources.subtopic: Bulk LLM classification: OpenAI Batch API
resources.title: OpenAI Batch API guide
resources.summary: Asynchronous bulk requests at 50% lower cost with a 24-hour completion window. Input is a JSONL file (up to 50,000 requests, 200 MB) with custom_id for matching outputs, and it uses a separate rate-limit pool.
resources.wiki_use: Reference for scaling a validated prompt from 200 to 50,000 reviews cheaply. Teach the pattern: pilot synchronously, validate, then batch.
resources.notes: platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch now redirects here. Output order may differ from input, so match on custom_id. Output files are deleted after 30 days.

resources.section: Classifying text at scale with LLM APIs
resources.subtopic: Bulk LLM classification: Anthropic Message Batches
resources.title: Batch processing (Message Batches API)
resources.summary: Asynchronous batches at 50% of standard price. Most finish within an hour and expire at 24 hours; limits are 100,000 requests or 256 MB; prompt-caching discounts stack. Includes a full Python example.
resources.wiki_use: Code reference for the batch-labeling step. Its tips (match by custom_id, validate request shape first, cache the shared instruction prompt) belong in the wiki's LLM-annotation checklist.
resources.notes: docs.anthropic.com URLs now redirect to platform.claude.com. Results are retained 29 days. Prices are on the page and change over time, so check them before setting a class budget.

resources.section: Classifying text at scale with LLM APIs
resources.subtopic: Bulk LLM classification: Gemini Batch Mode
resources.title: Gemini API Batch Mode
resources.summary: Batch jobs at 50% of standard price with a 24-hour target (expiring after 48 hours). Requests go inline (under 20 MB) or as a JSONL file (up to 2 GB) with keys, and the page includes a Python example using the google-genai SDK.
resources.wiki_use: Low-cost option for students. The Gemini free tier (via Google AI Studio) lets them prototype classification prompts without a credit card before scaling.
resources.notes: Pricing page, https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing (fetched Oct 2026): a free tier exists for some Flash/Flash-Lite models, but free-tier content is used to improve Google products. Students must not send confidential or personal data on the free tier.

resources.section: LLMs as annotators: methods and validation
resources.title: Structured Outputs guide
resources.summary: Makes model outputs conform to a supplied JSON Schema (strict mode), with Pydantic models in the Python SDK. Enum fields restrict outputs to a fixed label set, so the model cannot invent categories.
resources.wiki_use: Teach 'labels as a schema': define a Pydantic class with an enum sentiment, a list of aspects and a confidence field, so LLM classification outputs load straight into pandas.
resources.notes: Anthropic and Gemini offer comparable structured-output features (not separately verified here). Schema enforcement fixes formatting but not validity, so a human-labeled check is still needed.

resources.title: Causal Inference: The Mixtape
resources.summary: A widely used, readable textbook on DAGs, potential outcomes, matching, IV, RDD, DiD and synthetic control. The free web edition runs alongside the print book.
resources.wiki_use: Assign chapters as background reading per method, e.g. the DiD and synthetic control chapters before the pyfixest and pysyncon labs.
resources.notes: The online edition says its code is in R and Stata, not Python. Its datasets reach Python through the causaldata package (see the-effect entry). The Yale UP publisher and 2021 date come from the print ISBN (9780300251685) in search results; the web page itself doesn't state them. Companion page: https://www.scunning.com/mixtape. The author also runs 'Scott's Mixtape Substack' (https://causalinf.substack.com/), which describes itself as covering how AI agents are changing empirical research. I couldn't confirm individual AI posts there.

resources.title: Causal Inference in Python: Applying Causal Inference in the Tech Industry
resources.summary: Written for managers, data scientists and business analysts. It measures the effects of marketing spend, discounts and pricing through A/B tests, regression, propensity scores, meta-learners, DiD, synthetic control, geo and switchback experiments, and noncompliance/IV.
resources.wiki_use: The core business-facing text for M6. The geo/switchback chapter covers interference and marketplace settings, and its MIT-licensed code can be loaded straight into Colab.
resources.notes: ISBN 9781098140243, 408 pages, July 2023. The O'Reilly page is paywalled. Students can probably reach it through O'Reilly Learning via the library; I haven't checked UIUC access.

resources.title: Causal Inference: What If
resources.authors: Hernán, M. A.; Robins, J. M.
resources.summary: The epidemiology-rooted standard reference on potential outcomes, confounding, selection bias, IP weighting, standardization and g-methods. The book and its code and data are free to download.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor-only background on confounding and selection bias. Chapters 1-3 can serve as an optional deep-dive reading.
resources.notes: Python code for Part II (chapters 11-17) by James Fiedler: https://github.com/jrfiedler/causal_inference_python_code. That repo shows no license, so it isn't marked for download. The PDF link is the April 2024 version found in search.

resources.title: Difference-in-Differences Designs: A Practitioner's Guide
resources.authors: Baker, A.; Callaway, B.; Cunningham, S.; Goodman-Bacon, A.; Sant'Anna, P. H. C.
resources.summary: A framework for classifying DiD designs and estimators: covariates, weighting, multiple periods and staggered adoption. It explains why naive two-way fixed effects can mislead.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor reference for the staggered-DiD lab. Students can use its checklist to audit DiD code an AI assistant writes.
resources.notes: The arXiv page lists no journal reference. The paper is widely reported as forthcoming or published in the Journal of Economic Literature, which I haven't verified.

resources.title: Causal inference in economics and marketing
resources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113(27), 7310-7315
resources.summary: Google's chief economist gives a short, non-technical tour of counterfactual thinking, experiments, IV, RDD, DiD and 'train-test-treat-compare' with predictive models, illustrated with advertising and marketing examples.
resources.wiki_use: First assigned reading for M6. It frames 'what would have happened otherwise' for business students.

resources.title: Conducting Research in Marketing with Quasi-Experiments
resources.authors: Goldfarb, A.; Tucker, C.; Wang, Y.
resources.summary: A JM methods guide to quasi-experimental designs in marketing (DiD, synthetic control, RDD and related designs): when they are credible and how to probe their assumptions.
resources.wiki_use: Assigned academic anchor for the quasi-experiments week. Its checklist of identification threats can feed a student project rubric.
resources.notes: Metadata confirmed through the Crossref record for the DOI. The SAGE landing page blocked automated fetching. I didn't find an open-access copy.

resources.title: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing
resources.authors: Kohavi, R.; Tang, D.; Xu, Y.
resources.summary: The standard practitioner reference on online experiments from the Microsoft, Google and LinkedIn experimentation leaders: metrics/OEC, guardrails, SRM, trust checks, variance, interference and experimentation culture.
resources.wiki_use: Core text for the A/B testing week. Assign the free Chapter 1 PDF from experimentguide.com and pull SRM and pitfall examples for exercises.
resources.notes: experimentguide.com offers a free Chapter 1 PDF (English plus translations), errata, an FAQ and a bibliography. Cambridge Core page: https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/trustworthy-online-controlled-experiments/D97B26382EB0EB2DC2019A7A7B518F59. Kohavi's interactive Maven courses are paid.

resources.title: ExP Platform: Kohavi et al. papers, talks and pitfalls on online controlled experiments
resources.summary: Free PDFs of the classic Microsoft/Bing experimentation papers: Practical Guide (KDD 2007), Seven Pitfalls, Rules of Thumb, Puzzling Outcomes, A Dirty Dozen metric-interpretation pitfalls, continuous monitoring and trigger dilution.
resources.wiki_use: Reading bank. Assign the KDD 2007 'Practical Guide' (HiPPO) as an intro piece and 'A Dirty Dozen' for metric-interpretation pitfalls.
resources.notes: Year marks roughly the latest listed item. Direct pages found on the hub: Practical Guide https://exp-platform.com/practical-guide/ ; Seven Pitfalls https://exp-platform.com/seven-pitfalls/ ; Rules of Thumb https://exp-platform.com/rules-of-thumb/ ; Dirty Dozen PDF https://exp-platform.com/Documents/2017-08%20KDDMetricInterpretationPitfalls.pdf

resources.title: A/B Testing Intuition Busters: Common Misunderstandings in Online Controlled Experiments
resources.authors: Kohavi, R.; Deng, A.; Vermeer, L.
resources.summary: Debunks common, intuitive but wrong beliefs about A/B tests that some tool vendors promote, such as misreadings of p-values and statistical power. It recommends platform designs that make the mistakes harder to commit.
resources.wiki_use: Discussion reading. Students check whether an AI chatbot repeats any of the misconceptions, then correct it.

resources.title: Improving the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments by Utilizing Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED)
resources.authors: Deng, A.; Xu, Y.; Kohavi, R.; Walker, T.
resources.summary: The original CUPED paper, which reduces A/B test variance by regressing out pre-experiment covariates. It is now standard on most experimentation platforms.
resources.wiki_use: Pair with a Colab exercise in which students implement CUPED as OLS with a pre-period covariate and compare confidence-interval widths, linking back to M3 regression.
resources.notes: The page links a free PDF at exp-platform.com/Documents/2013-02-CUPED-ImprovingSensitivityOfControlledExperiments.pdf

resources.title: Deep Dive Into Variance Reduction
resources.authors: Cosgrove, L.; Townsend, J.; Litz, J. (Microsoft Experimentation Platform)
resources.summary: Explains CUPED as a regression adjustment that leaves the estimator consistent, shows its equivalence to Lin's ANCOVA estimator, and introduces the 'effective traffic multiplier' 1/(1-R^2) with real Microsoft numbers.
resources.wiki_use: A readable companion to the CUPED paper. The traffic-multiplier idea makes a good short quiz question.
resources.notes: The ExP articles index (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/group/experimentation-platform-exp/articles/) also has 'A/B Interactions: A Call to Relax' (2023) and pieces on experimenting with GenAI features.

resources.title: Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch in Online Controlled Experiments: A Taxonomy and Rules of Thumb for Practitioners
resources.authors: Fabijan, A.; Gupchup, J.; et al. (incl. Vermeer, L.; Dmitriev, P.)
resources.summary: Defines SRM (observed group sizes deviate from the designed split), shows how often it invalidates results, and gives a taxonomy of causes across assignment, execution, logging, analysis and interference.
resources.wiki_use: Use with a Colab chi-square SRM check. Lukas Vermeer's SRM Checker site (https://lukasvermeer.nl/srm/) has a manual checker, a FAQ and the cause taxonomy.
resources.notes: The full author list isn't shown in what I fetched; the abbreviated list follows the PDF filename. The SRM Checker Chrome extension has been retired, but the website, docs and manual check remain (MIT-licensed repo).

resources.title: Statistical Challenges in Online Controlled Experiments: A Review of A/B Testing Methodology
resources.authors: Larsen, N.; Stallrich, J.; Sengupta, S.; Deng, A.; Kohavi, R.; Stevens, N. T.
resources.summary: A review of open statistical problems in A/B testing: variance reduction, heterogeneous effects, sequential testing and peeking, interference and network/marketplace effects, and long-term effects.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background for the pitfalls lecture, especially the interference section.
resources.notes: Published online Oct 2023. exp-platform.com links a supplement at https://bit.ly/ABTestingStatChallengesSupplement

resources.title: Decision Making at Netflix (Part 1 of the Netflix A/B testing series)
resources.authors: Tingley, M.; Zheng, W.; Ejdemyr, S.; Lane, S.; McFarland, C. (Netflix Technology Blog)
resources.summary: A multi-part, non-technical series on how Netflix uses A/B tests. Later parts cover hypotheses, primary/secondary/guardrail metrics, false positives and power.
resources.wiki_use: Assign Parts 1-3 as the A/B testing primer before the first coding lab. The upside-down box art example works well in class.
resources.notes: Part 2 'What is an A/B Test?': https://netflixtechblog.com/what-is-an-a-b-test-b08cc1b57962 ; Part 3 'Interpreting A/B test results: false positives and statistical significance': https://netflixtechblog.com/interpreting-a-b-test-results-false-positives-and-statistical-significance-c1522d0db27a (URL taken from a syndicated copy of the post). A later part on false negatives and power exists, but I didn't verify its original URL.

resources.title: Choosing a Sequential Testing Framework: Comparisons and Discussions
resources.summary: Compares group sequential tests, always-valid inference (mSPRT/GAVI), corrected-alpha and Bonferroni as fixes for the peeking problem, using Monte Carlo evidence on power.
resources.wiki_use: Follow-up reading after a peeking simulation in Colab, where students see the false-positive rate inflate when they stop at the first p<0.05.
resources.notes: Related Spotify posts: 'Bringing Sequential Testing to Experiments with Longitudinal Data (Part 1): The Peeking Problem 2.0' (2023) and 'Risk-Aware Product Decisions in A/B Tests with Multiple Metrics' (2024), https://engineering.atspotify.com/2024/3/risk-aware-product-decisions-in-a-b-tests-with-multiple-metrics

resources.title: Encouragement Designs and Instrumental Variables for A/B Testing
resources.summary: Explains how to randomize a nudge (e.g., a banner) when the feature itself can't be withheld, and then use IV to estimate the complier effect. Covers monotonicity, exclusion and relevance, with practical trade-offs.
resources.wiki_use: The best business-facing intro to IV for this audience. Pair with a linearmodels IV2SLS exercise on simulated nudge data.

resources.title: How to Accurately Test Significance with Difference in Difference Models
resources.authors: Doll, B.; Li, J.; Oztan, T. (Spotify)
resources.summary: Simulations show that naive DiD standard errors on serially correlated time series give over 30% false positives. Compares clustered SEs, averaging and permutation tests, and says when to use each.
resources.wiki_use: A concrete check for AI-written DiD code. Students verify that the assistant clustered standard errors at the unit level, then rerun a placebo or permutation test.

resources.title: Better Experiments with LLM Evals: A funnel, not a fork
resources.summary: Argues that offline LLM evals (LLM-as-judge) should screen candidates and generate hypotheses, while A/B tests validate real user impact. LLM judges have to be calibrated against online results.
resources.wiki_use: Current-practice reading on how A/B testing fits AI product development. It works as a discussion starter on why an LLM judge isn't a causal estimate.
resources.notes: The post reports that Spotify rolls back about 42% of launched experiments to prevent regressions in secondary metrics.

resources.title: Democratizing online controlled experiments at Booking.com
resources.authors: Kaufman, R. L.; Pitchforth, J.; Vermeer, L.
resources.summary: Describes how Booking.com built an experimentation culture and infrastructure in which anyone can run trustworthy A/B tests at scale, with safeguards and shared tooling.
resources.wiki_use: A case example of experimentation culture, to pair with the Netflix series.
resources.notes: Lukas Vermeer's publications page dates it July 2018. I couldn't find a separate Booking.com engineering blog post on CUPED or power.

resources.title: Evan's Awesome A/B Tools: Sample Size Calculator
resources.summary: A free web calculator for the sample size a conversion-rate A/B test needs, given baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, power and significance. It is part of a small suite of A/B tools.
resources.wiki_use: In-class demo. Students check the calculator's answer against statsmodels code, possibly written with an AI assistant.
resources.notes: No year given; the tool has been around since the early 2010s.

resources.title: How Not To Run an A/B Test
resources.summary: The classic short explainer showing that repeatedly checking significance and stopping early inflates false positives. It recommends fixing the sample size in advance or using sequential methods.
resources.wiki_use: Pre-reading for a peeking simulation exercise.
resources.notes: No year given; usually dated 2010.

resources.title: statsmodels.stats.power: tt_ind_solve_power / NormalIndPower
resources.summary: API reference for solving for sample size, power or effect size in two-sample t-tests and z-tests (proportions via effect sizes) in Python.
resources.wiki_use: Reference for a power-analysis Colab cell. Students prompt an AI assistant for the code and then check its arguments (effect size in Cohen's d, not raw lift) against the docs.
resources.notes: The BSD-3 license is statsmodels' standard license; this doc page doesn't state it. The version-pinned URL came from search, and the 'stable' docs path should also work.

resources.title: Consumer Heterogeneity and Paid Search Effectiveness: A Large-Scale Field Experiment
resources.authors: Blake, T.; Nosko, C.; Tadelis, S.
resources.summary: eBay switched off brand-keyword and non-brand search ads in randomized geographic tests and found much smaller returns than naive observational estimates suggested, especially among frequent, loyal users.
resources.wiki_use: Headline case study for M6. Contrast the 'correlational ROI' story with the experimental one and discuss selection on intent.
resources.notes: NBER working paper version: https://www.nber.org/papers/w20171

resources.title: The Unfavorable Economics of Measuring the Returns to Advertising
resources.authors: Lewis, R. A.; Rao, J. M.
resources.summary: Using a large set of field experiments, shows that individual-level sales are so noisy relative to ad effects that even huge experiments are badly underpowered to measure ad ROI.
resources.wiki_use: Pair with the power calculators. Students compute the sample size needed to detect a realistic ad lift and see the 'unfavorable economics' for themselves.
resources.notes: The oa_url is an earlier AEA 2014 conference draft found in search, not the published version. The open-access link is the December 2013 working paper 'On the Near Impossibility of Measuring the Returns to Advertising', not the published QJE text (QJE 130(4), 1941–1973; DOI 10.1093/qje/qjv023).

resources.title: A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook
resources.authors: Gordon, B. R.; Zettelmeyer, F.; Bhargava, N.; Chapsky, D.
resources.summary: Benchmarks matching, regression adjustment and propensity-score methods against large Facebook RCTs. Observational methods often miss the experimental lift by large margins.
resources.wiki_use: Assigned anchor. Students try to recover an RCT effect with observational methods on a dataset like Hillstrom and reflect on why it fails.
resources.notes: A non-technical Kellogg/Facebook white paper is also available: https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/gordon_b/files/kellogg_fb_whitepaper.pdf

resources.title: Close Enough? A Large-Scale Exploration of Non-Experimental Approaches to Advertising Measurement
resources.authors: Gordon, B. R.; Moakler, R.; Zettelmeyer, F.
resources.summary: Uses a large set of Facebook RCTs to test whether double/debiased ML and rich user-level data let observational methods recover experimental ad effects. Mostly they don't, even with rich data.
resources.wiki_use: Follow-up to Gordon et al. (2019) that shows ML doesn't solve confounding. Good for a debate on 'can AI replace experiments?'.
resources.notes: Volume and issue not verified. Check the exact number of experiments against the abstract before quoting.

resources.title: Ghost Ads: Improving the Economics of Measuring Online Ad Effectiveness
resources.authors: Johnson, G. A.; Lewis, R. A.; Nubbemeyer, E. I.
resources.summary: Introduces 'ghost ads', which log the ads control users would have seen, to build an exposed-vs-would-have-been-exposed comparison. It is cheaper and more precise than PSA or intent-to-treat ad experiments.
resources.wiki_use: Explains how platform lift studies (Meta/Google conversion lift) actually work, and links ITT vs. treatment-on-treated to the IV material.
resources.notes: I didn't see a DOI. Won the 2022 AMA Weitz-Winer-O'Dell award, per AMA search results.

resources.title: csdid: Callaway and Sant'Anna difference-in-differences for Python
resources.summary: A Python port of R's did package. It estimates group-time ATT(g,t) under staggered adoption (with doubly robust options) and aggregates to event-study, calendar or group effects, with plots.
resources.wiki_use: Staggered-adoption lab on the mpdta minimum-wage example in the README. Students compare its results with naive TWFE from pyfixest.
resources.notes: Needs the drdid library installed separately from GitHub. Docs: d2cml-ai.github.io/csdid/. No year given.

resources.title: differences: difference-in-differences estimation and inference for Python
resources.summary: Implements Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) ATT(g,t) through an ATTgt class, plus Sant'Anna and Zhao (2020) DR-DiD, multi-valued treatments and triple differences.
resources.wiki_use: An alternative to csdid for students who want a richer API. Use for cross-checking estimates.
resources.notes: Docs: https://bernardodionisi.github.io/differences/latest/ . The repo has few commits (58), so recent maintenance is unclear.

resources.title: pysyncon: a Python module for the synthetic control method
resources.summary: Implements classic, robust, augmented and penalized synthetic control with placebo tests and confidence intervals. Example notebooks reproduce Basque, Texas (from the Mixtape) and German reunification.
resources.wiki_use: Synthetic control lab. Start from the Mixtape Texas notebook, then apply it to a brand or market-level marketing intervention.
resources.notes: No year given.

resources.title: SparseSC: Fit sparse synthetic control models in Python
resources.summary: An ML-enhanced synthetic control that penalizes feature and unit weights. It is useful when there are many donor units or many predictors.
resources.wiki_use: Optional advanced alternative for project teams with many control markets.
resources.notes: Docs: https://sparsesc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ . Last commit date unclear and the repo is modestly active (about 90 stars). Background: Quistorff, Goldman and Thorpe (2020). No year given.

resources.title: CausalPy: causal inference for quasi-experiments in Python
resources.summary: One API (Bayesian via PyMC, or scikit-learn) for synthetic control, GeoLift, DiD, staggered DiD, RDD, regression kink, interrupted time series, IV and IPW. It ships agent skills that teach AI coding assistants to use it.
resources.wiki_use: The one-stop quasi-experiment toolkit for the wiki. Students can try its bundled AI-assistant skills (in Claude Code or Cursor) and critique the analyses they produce.
resources.notes: Docs: https://causalpy.readthedocs.io . Per the docs, the skills live in causalpy/skills/ and are distributed through Decision AI Hub (hub.decision.ai). Year approximate.

resources.title: rdrobust: robust bias-corrected inference for regression discontinuity (Python)
resources.authors: Calonico, S.; Cattaneo, M. D.; Farrell, M. H.; Masini, R.; Titiunik, R.
resources.summary: The reference RDD implementation (`pip install rdrobust`), with local polynomial estimates, robust bias-corrected CIs, data-driven bandwidths and rdplot. Ships Python illustration scripts and the US Senate example data.
resources.wiki_use: RDD lab, e.g. loyalty-tier thresholds or rating cutoffs. Compare an AI-written 'OLS with a cutoff dummy' against rdrobust.
resources.notes: PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/rdrobust/ (v2.1.1, released 2026-10-07, GPL-3.0-only). The old rdpackages.github.io/rdrobust page now just says the project moved to GitHub.

resources.title: TFP CausalImpact: Python port of Google's CausalImpact
resources.summary: A Python/TensorFlow Probability implementation of CausalImpact. It estimates the effect of a marketing intervention on a time series against a Bayesian structural time-series counterfactual built from control series.
resources.wiki_use: Demo for 'did the campaign lift sales?' with only aggregate time series. Includes a quick-start notebook.
resources.notes: Quick start is docs/quickstart.ipynb. Marked 'not an officially supported Google product'. The original R package (Apache-2.0) is at https://github.com/google/CausalImpact, with docs at https://google.github.io/CausalImpact/CausalImpact.html; its README points Python users to tfp-causalimpact. No year given.

resources.title: GeoLift: geo-level lift measurement with synthetic control
resources.summary: An end-to-end R toolkit for geo experiments: market selection and power analysis, then lift estimation with (augmented) synthetic control, including multi-cell tests.
resources.wiki_use: Explains how brands run geo holdouts. Demo the walkthrough vignette, or reproduce the GeoLift idea in Python with CausalPy.
resources.notes: R only (R >= 4.0); no Python version. Site: https://facebookincubator.github.io/GeoLift/ . No year given.

resources.title: Meridian: Google's open-source Bayesian marketing mix model
resources.summary: An in-house MMM framework with reach/frequency and search-volume features and ROI priors that can be calibrated with experiments. Comes with Colab notebooks.
resources.wiki_use: Shows how MMM estimates are made 'causal' by calibrating to lift tests. Run the Getting Started Colab live.
resources.notes: Getting started: https://developers.google.com/meridian/notebook/meridian-getting-started ; ROI priors and calibration guide: https://developers.google.com/meridian/docs/advanced-modeling/roi-priors-and-calibration . The repo citation lists v2.0.0; needs Python 3.11-3.13. The demo/ path is inferred from a Colab link to demo/Meridian_Full_Funnel.ipynb.

resources.title: Meridian GeoX: open-source geo experiments for incrementality and MMM calibration
resources.summary: Google's geo-experiment tool (holdback, go-dark and heavy-up designs, multi-treatment) that turns experiment results into priors for Meridian MMM and recommends which channels to test.
resources.wiki_use: Current-practice example of the 'experiment, then calibrate the MMM' loop. Its Colab notebooks can serve as an instructor demo.
resources.notes: Source: https://github.com/google/meridian-geox (license not verified). Notebooks: https://developers.google.com/meridian/geox/notebook . Year is when I found the 'now available' announcement; exact release date not verified. Google's older trimmed_match geo library (https://github.com/google/trimmed_match, Apache-2.0, research-only) covers matched-pair geo designs.

resources.title: PyMC-Marketing: Bayesian MMM, CLV and choice models in Python
resources.summary: A Python Bayesian MMM with adstock/saturation, a DAG-based causal identification guide, lift-test and ROAS calibration and budget optimization, plus CLV/BTYD models that also tie into M4.
resources.wiki_use: Main Python MMM. Assign the notebook 'Mitigating Unobserved Confounders in MMMs with Lift Test Likelihoods' (https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/mmm/mmm_roas.html), where an omitted confounder flips the channel ROAS ranking and lift tests fix it.
resources.notes: AI angle: the README links MMM-GPT (https://mmm-gpt.com/), an AI assistant for marketing analytics built on PyMC-Marketing. The repo also contains skills/mmm-modeling, .claude and .cursor directories, but GitHub blocked fetching them, so their contents are unverified. Lift-test integration notebook: https://www.pymc-marketing.io/en/stable/notebooks/mmm/mmm_lift_test.html . Requires Python >= 3.12.

resources.title: EconML: heterogeneous treatment effect estimation with ML (PyWhy)
resources.summary: Estimates CATE with double ML, causal forests, meta-learners, orthogonal IV and dynamic DML, with interpretability and policy-learning tools. Built in Microsoft's ALICE project.
resources.wiki_use: HTE and personalization lab: who responds to a coupon or email? The notebooks folder has worked examples to adapt in Colab.
resources.notes: GitHub's robots rules blocked listing the notebooks folder, so I couldn't verify individual notebook names (e.g. the customer-scenario case studies). No year given.

resources.title: DoWhy: causal inference with explicit modeling and testing of assumptions (PyWhy)
resources.summary: A four-step workflow (model a DAG, identify, estimate, refute) with refutation tests and graphical causal models for attribution and root-cause analysis.
resources.wiki_use: Teaches 'draw the DAG first'. Use the 'Estimating the Effect of a Member Rewards Program' and online-shop root-cause notebooks as marketing exercises.
resources.notes: Example notebook index: https://www.pywhy.org/dowhy/main/example_notebooks/nb_index.html (includes member rewards, online shop root-cause, time-decay attribution, and hotel booking cancellations). No year given.

resources.title: CausalML: uplift modeling and causal inference with ML (Uber)
resources.summary: Uplift trees and forests, S/T/X/R/DR meta-learners, and Qini and uplift curves for estimating who to target with a marketing treatment from experimental data.
resources.wiki_use: Main uplift lab package. Start with the meta-learner and uplift-tree example notebooks, then apply them to the Hillstrom data.
resources.notes: Examples index: https://causalml.readthedocs.io/en/latest/examples.html (uplift trees, meta-learners, Qini curves with costly treatments, SHAP interpretation). No year given.

resources.title: scikit-uplift (sklift): uplift modeling in scikit-learn style
resources.summary: Lightweight uplift models (solo, two-model, class transformation), uplift/Qini metrics and plots, and one-line loaders for Hillstrom, Criteo, X5, Lenta and Megafon uplift datasets.
resources.wiki_use: Easiest uplift entry point for non-CS students. Use fetch_hillstrom() and the RetailHero tutorial notebook in Colab.
resources.notes: Tutorials: https://www.uplift-modeling.com/en/latest/tutorials.html . Author name inferred from the GitHub handle; not verified. No year given.

resources.title: DoubleML: an object-oriented implementation of double machine learning in Python
resources.authors: Bach, P.; Chernozhukov, V.; Kurz, M. S.; Spindler, M.
resources.summary: A scikit-learn-based DML package for partially linear, interactive and IV models. It is the companion software to the Chernozhukov et al. causal ML book.
resources.wiki_use: Optional advanced lab: use ML for nuisance functions without biasing the treatment effect, e.g. the effect of promotions with many controls.
resources.notes: Docs: https://docs.doubleml.org

resources.title: MineThatData E-Mail Analytics and Data Mining Challenge (Hillstrom dataset)
resources.summary: 64,000 customers randomized to a men's email, a women's email or no email, with two-week visit, conversion and spend outcomes plus recency, history and channel covariates.
resources.wiki_use: Workhorse dataset for M6: A/B analysis, CUPED-style adjustment, power, heterogeneous effects and uplift targeting. It is about 5 MB and easy to load in Colab.
resources.notes: The blog post links a direct CSV. scikit-uplift loads it with fetch_hillstrom() (https://www.uplift-modeling.com/en/latest/api/datasets/fetch_hillstrom.html). No explicit license; it was released publicly for the 2008 challenge.

resources.title: Retention Futility: Targeting High-Risk Customers Might Be Ineffective
resources.summary: Field experiments show that targeting customers with the highest churn risk is not the same as targeting those most responsive to a retention offer. Uplift-based targeting beats risk-based targeting.
resources.wiki_use: Key marketing anchor linking M7 prediction to M6 causal targeting. Pair with an uplift exercise on the Hillstrom data.
resources.notes: Metadata confirmed through Crossref. I didn't verify an open-access copy.

resources.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects and Optimal Targeting Policy Evaluation
resources.authors: Hitsch, G. J.; Misra, S.; Zhang, W.
resources.summary: A framework for building and evaluating customer targeting policies from one randomized dataset using off-policy evaluation. In catalog mailing data, direct CATE methods (including their treatment effect projection) beat outcome-model methods on profit.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background and an advanced reading on why you evaluate targeting policies by profit, not by prediction accuracy.
resources.notes: The SSRN page (revised Nov 2023, first posted 2018) shows no journal. I believe a version appeared in Quantitative Marketing and Economics (2024) but haven't verified it.

resources.title: Causal Reasoning and Large Language Models: Opening a New Frontier for Causality
resources.authors: Kıcıman, E.; Ness, R.; Sharma, A.; Tan, C.
resources.summary: GPT-4-class models do very well on text-based causal tasks (pairwise causal discovery, counterfactuals, necessary/sufficient causes) but show unpredictable failure modes. The authors suggest pairing LLMs, which supply domain knowledge and DAG drafting, with formal causal methods.
resources.wiki_use: Frames the AI-assisted workflow for M6: let the LLM propose a DAG and confounders, then verify with data and refutation tests (see PyWhy-LLM).
resources.notes: By DoWhy contributors (Microsoft Research). Current version v3, Aug 2024.

resources.title: CLadder: Assessing Causal Reasoning in Language Models
resources.authors: Jin, Z.; Chen, Y.; Leeb, F.; Gresele, L.; Kamal, O.; Lyu, Z.; Blin, K.; Gonzalez Adauto, F.; Kleiman-Weiner, M.; Sachan, M.; Schölkopf, B.
resources.summary: A 10K-question benchmark of associational, interventional and counterfactual queries built from causal graphs. LLMs find formal causal inference rules hard, even with a custom CausalCoT prompt.
resources.wiki_use: Counterpoint to Kıcıman et al.: LLMs talk causality fluently but stumble on formal rung-2/3 reasoning, so students should check identification themselves.
resources.notes: The arXiv page lists no venue; widely cited as NeurIPS 2023 (not verified). The companion 'Can Large Language Models Infer Causation from Correlation?' (Corr2Cause; Jin et al., arXiv:2306.05836, https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05836) finds 17 LLMs near random at inferring causation from correlations.

resources.title: PyWhy-LLM: integrating LLM capabilities into causal analysis
resources.summary: An experimental library that uses LLMs as a stand-in domain expert: it suggests confounders, edges and DAGs, proposes backdoor, mediator and IV sets, and critiques a given DAG with suggested negative controls.
resources.wiki_use: Exercise: students let PyWhy-LLM (or a chat assistant) propose a DAG for a marketing question, then defend or reject each edge.
resources.notes: Experimental; install with `pip install pywhyllm`. No published release shown. No year given.

resources.title: Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus?
resources.authors: Horton, J. J.; Filippas, A.; Manning, B. S.
resources.summary: Treats LLMs as implicit computational models of humans ('Homo silicus') that can be given endowments and preferences and run through classic behavioral-economics experiments. Results are broadly similar to the originals.
resources.wiki_use: Anchor for the debate 'can a simulated experiment replace a real A/B test?'. Students run a small LLM-simulated survey and compare it with real data.
resources.notes: Originally sole-authored by Horton (2023); the NBER page now lists three authors and a Feb 2026 revision.

resources.title: Using Large Language Models to Simulate Multiple Humans and Replicate Human Subject Studies
resources.authors: Aher, G.; Arriaga, R. I.; Kalai, A. T.
resources.summary: Proposes 'Turing Experiments' that simulate representative samples of participants. Replicates the Ultimatum Game, garden-path sentences and Milgram, but finds a 'hyper-accuracy distortion' in wisdom-of-crowds tasks for newer models.
resources.wiki_use: Pair with Horton. The hyper-accuracy distortion is a concrete failure mode for simulated consumer panels.
resources.notes: First posted 2022; current v5 July 2023. Widely cited as ICML 2023, though the arXiv page lists no venue.

resources.title: ISLP_labs: Python lab notebooks for ISLP
resources.summary: Twelve Jupyter notebooks, one per ISLP chapter (Ch02 to Ch13: linreg, classification, resample, baggboost, deeplearning, unsup and so on), with small datasets and a requirements.txt pinned at tag v2.2.2.
resources.wiki_use: Embed or fork the classification, resampling and baggboost notebooks as Colab in-class coding activities. Students can also ask an AI assistant to explain or extend a lab cell.
resources.notes: Labs are versioned (v2.2.2). Pin that tag so the notebooks match the requirements file.

resources.title: scikit-learn User Guide 3.1: Cross-validation, evaluating estimator performance
resources.summary: The canonical reference for cross_val_score and cross_validate, K-fold, stratified, grouped (GroupKFold) and time-series (TimeSeriesSplit) splitters, and permutation tests.
resources.wiki_use: Link from the M7 'how to evaluate a churn model' page, and use GroupKFold (customers) and TimeSeriesSplit (forecasting) as marketing-relevant splitting examples.
resources.notes: The full User Guide index is at scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html (also verified). The license is scikit-learn's well-known BSD-3. I did not re-check it in this session.

resources.title: scikit-learn User Guide 12: Common pitfalls and recommended practices
resources.summary: Short worked examples of inconsistent preprocessing, data leakage (for example feature selection on the full data inflates accuracy from 0.5 to about 0.76 on pure noise) and random_state control, with Pipeline as the fix.
resources.wiki_use: Required reading before students let an AI assistant write an ML pipeline. Use it as an audit checklist: 'find the leakage in this AI-generated notebook'.
resources.notes: These are exactly the bugs LLM-written notebooks often contain: fit_transform before the train/test split, and feature selection on the full data.

resources.title: Machine learning in Python with scikit-learn (Inria MOOC)
resources.summary: A free MOOC by scikit-learn maintainers covering predictive modeling pipelines, overfitting and underfitting, hyperparameter tuning, linear models, trees, ensembles and evaluation, with runnable notebooks and quizzes.
resources.wiki_use: Self-paced backup for students without an ML background. Embed specific notebooks (for example 'ensemble' or 'evaluation') as pre-class work.
resources.notes: The CC-BY license is stated in the repo README. The year is approximate because the repo is continuously updated.

resources.title: Machine Learning Crash Course (refreshed edition)
resources.summary: A fast-paced, visual intro to ML: linear and logistic regression, classification metrics (thresholds, confusion matrix, AUC), data prep, overfitting, neural nets, embeddings, an intro to LLMs, and new AutoML and ML-fairness modules.
resources.wiki_use: Link the classification-metrics and AutoML modules (about 30 min) as pre-reading. The interactive visuals suit non-CS students.
resources.notes: The AutoML module is at developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/automl (verified; about 30 minutes, covers benefits and limitations). The 2024 refresh date comes from a Google blog result in search, not from the course page itself.

resources.title: XGBoost Documentation (incl. 'Introduction to Boosted Trees' and scikit-learn interface)
resources.summary: Official docs for XGBoost, with a get-started page, a Python intro, the scikit-learn estimator interface, and a well-written conceptual tutorial on boosted trees (tutorials/model.html).
resources.wiki_use: Assign 'Introduction to Boosted Trees' for intuition, then have students swap XGBClassifier into their sklearn churn pipeline.
resources.notes: The Apache-2.0 license was confirmed on github.com/dmlc/xgboost.

resources.title: LightGBM Documentation (Python quick start)
resources.summary: Docs for LightGBM, a fast, memory-efficient gradient-boosting library that is a common Kaggle and industry default for tabular prediction. Includes a Python-Intro quick start.
resources.wiki_use: Present it as the alternative to XGBoost, and have students compare speed and AUC on the same churn data with cross-validation.
resources.notes: MIT license confirmed on github.com/microsoft/LightGBM. That page now points to a lightgbm-org/LightGBM location, so the repo may have moved organizations.

resources.title: SHAP documentation: 'An introduction to explainable AI with Shapley values'
resources.summary: The official SHAP intro notebook. It builds from linear models to tree ensembles and explains global and local feature attributions with beeswarm, waterfall and dependence plots.
resources.wiki_use: Use it for the 'why is this customer predicted to churn?' segment. Students can produce SHAP plots for their XGBoost model and write a manager-facing interpretation.
resources.notes: The underlying paper is Lundberg & Lee (2017), 'A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions', arXiv 1705.07874 (fetched; NIPS venue not shown on arXiv). The repo license (MIT) and notebooks folder were confirmed by fetch. The notebooks folder may be large, so download it selectively.

resources.title: Interpretable Machine Learning: A Guide for Making Black Box Models Explainable (3rd ed.)
resources.summary: A free book on interpretability methods: permutation feature importance, partial dependence, Shapley values and SHAP, and their pitfalls.
resources.wiki_use: Background reading behind the SHAP lab, especially the chapters on PDP, permutation importance and SHAP limitations.
resources.notes: The page says 3rd edition but shows no year, so 2025 is approximate. Examples appear to use R, so pair it with the SHAP Python docs.

resources.title: Defection Detection: Measuring and Understanding the Predictive Accuracy of Customer Churn Models
resources.authors: Neslin, S. A.; Gupta, S.; Kamakura, W.; Lu, J.; Mason, C. H.
resources.summary: Reports a churn-modeling tournament (Teradata Center at Duke) in which many teams modeled the same telecom data. It shows that method choice matters for predictive accuracy and that accuracy translates into substantial retention profit.
resources.wiki_use: Academic anchor for the churn unit. Use the tournament framing to motivate holdout evaluation (top-decile lift, Gini) on students' own churn models.
resources.notes: The tournament detail (Teradata Center at Duke) is from background knowledge and was not verified; the fetched page confirmed only the title, authors, volume and pages. IAOR lists the authors in a different order.

resources.title: Bagging and Boosting Classification Trees to Predict Churn
resources.summary: A classic marketing paper showing that ensemble tree methods (bagging, stochastic gradient boosting) beat logistic regression for churn prediction, and discussing how to handle oversampled (balanced) training data.
resources.wiki_use: Pair it with the XGBoost lab. It is an early marketing-journal case for boosting, and its correction for balanced sampling is a useful discussion point.
resources.notes: The Tilburg repository record lists a PDF (lemmens_bagging.pdf), but open access was not confirmed.

resources.title: In Pursuit of Enhanced Customer Retention Management: Review, Key Issues, and Future Directions
resources.authors: Ascarza, E.; Neslin, S. A.; Netzer, O.; Anderson, Z.; Fader, P. S.; Gupta, S.; Hardie, B. G. S.; Lemmens, A.; Libai, B.; Neal, D.; Provost, F.; Schrift, R.
resources.summary: A review from a Choice Symposium on retention management. It argues for moving from 'who will churn?' to 'whom should we target and with what?', covering churn prediction, targeting, interventions and CLV links.
resources.wiki_use: Framing reading for the churn module. It connects M4 (CLV) to M7 (prediction) and M6 (targeting experiments).
resources.notes: The LBS eprint record appeared in search results; I did not fetch it to confirm the full text.

resources.title: Know What Your Customers Want Before They Do
resources.authors: Davenport, T. H.; DalleMule, L.; Lucker, J.
resources.summary: A managerial article on 'next best offer' (NBO) analytics. It gives a four-step framework (define objectives, gather data, analyze and execute, learn and evolve) with Tesco, Zappos, Microsoft and Walmart examples.
resources.wiki_use: Short practitioner reading that frames response, propensity and recommender models as one NBO decision system.

resources.title: Surprise: a Python scikit for recommender systems
resources.summary: A scikit-style library for explicit-rating recommenders (SVD and other matrix factorization, kNN baselines) with built-in MovieLens and Jester data and cross-validation helpers.
resources.wiki_use: Quick in-class lab: replicate a Netflix-Prize-style SVD on MovieLens 100k in about 20 lines.
resources.notes: Maintenance-only since v1.1.0 (2019), with no new features. Check NumPy 2 compatibility in Colab before class. For implicit feedback (clicks, purchases), use 'implicit' (github.com/benfred/implicit, MIT; ALS, BPR; verified).

resources.title: Recommenders: Best Practices on Recommendation Systems
resources.authors: Recommenders team (Linux Foundation AI & Data; originally Microsoft)
resources.summary: A large collection of notebooks and utilities for about 33 recommender algorithms (ALS, BPR, SAR, NCF, LightGCN, SASRec, content-based and others), with data prep, offline evaluation and tuning.
resources.wiki_use: Source of quick-start notebooks for team projects that want a recommender, and instructor reference for evaluation metrics (precision@k, NDCG).

resources.title: Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars (Part 1)
resources.summary: Netflix's own account of the Netflix Prize. SVD and RBM from the Progress Prize went into production, but the winning ensemble was never deployed because the accuracy gains did not justify the engineering cost, and the business goal shifted from RMSE to engagement and retention.
resources.wiki_use: Case discussion: offline metric vs business objective. It also pairs with privacy (M8), since the Prize sequel was cancelled after a lawsuit and FTC concerns.
resources.notes: For history: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix_Prize (fetched) covers the 2006-2009 timeline, the $1M prize to BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos, the Narayanan-Shmatikov de-anonymization, the 2009 lawsuit and the 2010 cancellation of the sequel.

resources.title: StatsForecast: fast forecasting with statistical and econometric models
resources.summary: Fast AutoARIMA, AutoETS, Theta, MSTL, Croston-type intermittent-demand models and baselines for many series at once, with built-in time-series cross-validation.
resources.wiki_use: Main tool for the demand-forecasting lab: forecast SKU-store sales with AutoETS vs seasonal naive and evaluate with rolling-origin CV.
resources.notes: The 'nbs' folder probably holds the source notebooks, but the page does not say so. The docs quick guide is at nixtlaverse.nixtla.io/statsforecast/docs/getting-started/getting_started_short.html.

resources.title: Prophet: Forecasting at scale
resources.authors: Meta (Facebook) Core Data Science; Taylor, S. J.; Letham, B.
resources.summary: An additive trend, seasonality and holiday forecasting procedure for R and Python, popular in marketing and business teams for daily data with promotions and holidays.
resources.wiki_use: Easy first forecasting demo (quick start in Colab), then contrast it with statsforecast baselines to show that Prophet is not always the most accurate.
resources.notes: The site links a PeerJ preprint (peerj.com/preprints/3190), but that fetch failed, so the authors and the journal version (American Statistician 2018) are unverified. The site has a '2023 Update' on Prophet's future (not read). The license was not stated on the page.

resources.title: Forecasting: Principles and Practice, the Pythonic Way
resources.authors: Hyndman, R. J.; Athanasopoulos, G.; Garza, A.; Challu, C.; Mergenthaler, M.; Olivares, K. G.
resources.summary: The Python edition of Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's forecasting textbook, built on Nixtla's open-source 'nixtlaverse' libraries. It is free online.
resources.wiki_use: Assigned reading for the forecasting week (benchmarks, ETS, ARIMA, evaluation), with code that matches the statsforecast lab.
resources.notes: Preface dated May 2026. No license is stated (only a copyright symbol), so link to it rather than copy it.

resources.title: Machine Learning: An Applied Econometric Approach
resources.summary: An accessible explanation of how supervised ML differs from econometrics: it is good at prediction (y-hat) but not at recovering parameters (beta-hat), illustrated with house-price prediction and regularization.
resources.wiki_use: The opening reading for M7, connecting M3 (regression) and M6 (causal) to prediction.
resources.notes: JEP offers a free PDF. Replication data is on openICPSR (project 113993, seen in search).

resources.title: Prediction Policy Problems
resources.authors: Kleinberg, J.; Ludwig, J.; Mullainathan, S.; Obermeyer, Z.
resources.summary: A short piece separating 'umbrella' problems, where only a prediction is needed, from 'rain dance' problems, where the causal effect matters.
resources.wiki_use: A five-page reading for an in-class exercise: classify marketing decisions (churn targeting, ad budget, pricing) as prediction or causal problems.
resources.notes: The oa_url PDF came from search results and was not fetched.

resources.title: Machine learning and AI in marketing: Connecting computing power to human insights
resources.venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing 37(3): 481-504
resources.summary: A review of ML methods (supervised, unsupervised, deep learning, reinforcement learning) for marketing problems, including text, image and behavioral data, and how they complement theory-driven models.
resources.wiki_use: Instructor background, plus an optional reading for students who want a map of ML applications in marketing research.
resources.notes: The CKGSB page hosts the extracted full text of the paper.

resources.title: Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples
resources.authors: Argyle, L. P.; Busby, E. C.; Fulda, N.; Gubler, J. R.; Rytting, C.; Wingate, D.
resources.summary: Introduces 'silicon samples': GPT-3 conditioned on demographic backstories reproduces subgroup response patterns from US political surveys ('algorithmic fidelity').
resources.wiki_use: Foundational reading for the 'LLMs as simulated consumers' session. Students can run a small persona-prompting replication in Colab.
resources.notes: The volume, issue and pages come from the IDEAS URL seen in search. The DOI appears on the Cambridge page as the supplementary-material DOI. Replication data is at doi 10.7910/DVN/JPV20K.

resources.title: Using large language models to generate silicon samples in consumer and marketing research: Challenges, opportunities, and guidelines
resources.authors: Sarstedt, M.; Adler, S. J.; Rau, L.; Schmitt, B.
resources.summary: A marketing-specific review of when LLM 'silicon samples' agree with human respondents, with practical guidelines on where they are useful (pilots, item generation) and where they are not (final estimates).
resources.wiki_use: Assigned reading and checklist for any team that wants to use LLM respondents in its project.
resources.notes: The LMU ePub record links a PDF but states no license. That record lists three authors, while the Columbia page lists all four.

resources.title: MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering
resources.authors: Chan, J. S.; Chowdhury, N.; Jaffe, O.; Aung, J.; Sherburn, D.; et al. (OpenAI)
resources.summary: A benchmark of 75 Kaggle competitions for AI agents. o1-preview with AIDE scaffolding reached medal level in 16.9% of competitions at release, and agents on the repo's paused leaderboard now score above 60%.
resources.wiki_use: Discussion of how far 'AI does the ML for you' has come. Show the leaderboard and the rule-violation and plagiarism detectors as evidence of how agents can cheat.
resources.notes: The full dataset is about 3.3 TB and the Lite split about 158 GB, so do not download it; use it for discussion only. The AIDE agent is at github.com/WecoAI/aideml (MIT; verified).

resources.title: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science
resources.summary: Documents leakage errors in hundreds of ML-based papers across many fields, gives an eight-type leakage taxonomy, and proposes 'model info sheets' to rule leakage out.
resources.wiki_use: Use the taxonomy and model info sheet as a required appendix in student project write-ups, especially when AI wrote the pipeline.
